Title: Six Unpatched Danfoss Refrigeration Controller Flaws Could Allow Remote Takeover Without Login
Context: 0 does not patch the flaws: "It's not really possible either because according to the file timestamp this firmware was likely built on October 29, before the second wave of...
Full Text:
Six flaws in Danfoss AK-SM800A refrigeration controllers could let a remote attacker take over a controller without logging in, Dutch security consultancy Midnight Blue said earlier this week.

No patch is available, and the researchers say the newest firmware, version 5.4.0, does not fix the flaws.

Government cybersecurity agencies in Belgium, Ireland and Germany told operators this week to take the controllers' management interfaces off the internet.

For a controller left on the internet, updating the firmware, changing default passwords or turning on Strict mode is not enough on its own, the Belgian and Irish agencies said. Strict mode is a login protection that requires encrypted connections and session tokens, but one of the six flaws is in the gateway that enforces it.

The AK-SM800A runs a store's fridges and freezers, and maintenance firms can manage it remotely. Such controllers were targeted in attacks in France starting October 11, and in a second wave across Europe that began last week. The attacks caused unwanted defrost cycles and destroyed stock.

Germany's federal IT security agency, the BSI, says in a security notice that the AK-SM800A was involved in earlier incidents in which refrigeration units in several countries were tampered with.

The agency has no information about any exploitation of the six new flaws, and neither other agencies nor researchers link the flaws to those incidents.

The researchers examined firmware version 5.3.2, then the newest, and say every version up to and including it is affected.

No CVE identifiers have been assigned. The researchers are keeping technical details private while they work on disclosure with Danfoss, the Danish company that makes the controllers.

The vendor lists software package 5.4.0, dated November, as its newest release for the AK-SM800A. Its 5.4.0 readme and November update guide cover upgrade steps, and the guide adds a stricter password rule. Neither mentions a fix for any vulnerability.

In a follow-up statement carried by trade publication Cooling Post, the researchers said 5.4.0 does not patch the flaws: "It's not really possible either because according to the file timestamp this firmware was likely built on October 29, before the second wave of cyber attacks and well before our vulnerability reports."

The German agency first said in a press release this week that 5.4.0 was not affected. Later the same day, it changed that in a corrected statement: it cannot rule out for now that 5.4.0 is affected.

The vendor's advisory page lists no advisory for the six flaws as of today, and no date for a fix has been published.

Midnight Blue researcher Carlo Meijer found the six flaws in less than an hour of manual review, using firmware the vendor offers for download, and described them in a technical write-up.

Five of the flaws are in web request handlers that do not require a login, inside a program that runs as root. Through one of them, the researchers ran code as root on older firmware, version 3.3.0, and they found the same bugs in 5.3.2.

Strict mode closes almost all of the controller's web attack surface to users who have not logged in, including the flaw used in that demonstration. The sixth flaw is in the gateway that enforces Strict mode, a separate program that blocks every request except the login until a user has logged in.

When the researchers ran firmware 5.3.2 in an emulator with Strict mode on, that flaw crashed the gateway. The crash could be turned into code execution with more work, the researchers say, and the gateway lacks basic exploit defenses such as stack canaries.

With code running as root, an attacker could change the controller's settings, start defrost cycles and hide that activity from its logs.

The controllers do not use secure boot, the researchers found, so an attacker could plant code that survives a factory reset and a firmware update. An attacker could also make a controller unusable until it is replaced.

The researchers say the code almost certainly holds more flaws like these, and they call patching flaws one by one or turning on Strict mode "a misallocation of scarce security and personnel resources."

What Operators Can Do

Removing internet exposure must not wait for a patch, and it is needed even where firmware is current and Strict mode is on, the Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium says.

The Belgian advisory and a similar Irish advisory recommend these steps:

Find every controller whose management interface can be reached from the internet, including through a 4G or 5G modem, and remove that exposure.

Give remote access only through a secure VPN or a protected internal network. Allowing only a service company's IP addresses through a firewall is a short-term measure.

Check temperature setpoints, defrost schedules, alarm settings, user accounts and remote-access settings for changes you did not make.

The German agency adds that anyone who suspects a compromise should change all credentials and check that equipment connected to the controller works properly.

Before cutting off the data a controller sends to its refrigeration service company, operators should check contract and insurance terms, the Belgian advisory says. They should also set up protected remote access so that monitoring can continue.

Danfoss's own update guide says the AK-SM800A should not be directly reachable from the public internet, adding: “This recommendation applies to all software versions, including those with Strict Mode enabled.”

Ireland's National Cyber Security Centre also advises running the latest supported firmware, changing default passwords and turning on Strict mode, but says operators should not rely on those steps alone.

Danfoss told Cooling Post on October 12 that most units hit in France were either older models that no longer receive updates or current AK-SM800A units running outdated firmware.

The vendor fixed earlier flaws in the AK-SM800A in 2023 and 2025, including login bypass and command injection bugs. Version 5.3.2, which the researchers examined, is newer than all of those fixes.

Title: AI Cuts Vulnerability Discovery from Nine Months to 90 Hours
Context: A new report by the cybersecurity firm, Finding Critical Infrastructure Bugs with Off-the-Shelf AI, details how publicly available models can help teams working with a small...
Full Text:
Forescout Technologies has added its voice to the growing number urging security teams to embrace AI, revealing how the technology helped it accelerate vulnerability discovery.

A new report by the cybersecurity firm, Finding Critical Infrastructure Bugs with Off-the-Shelf AI, details how publicly available models can help teams working with a small budget unearth vulnerabilities in open source software and proprietary binaries.

The researchers used a specially built AI-assisted vulnerability research harness to find bugs in 10 popular TCP/IP stacks.

This approach reduced analysis time from around nine months to 90 hours and helped the team uncover 99 vulnerabilities, including 66 zero days, Forescout said.

Read more on AI in security: Hackers Observed Using AI to Develop Zero-Day for the First Time

After 10 hours of AI analysis, the team then spent around 80 hours manually validating the findings. Static analysis across the 10 stacks cost around $935, which means just $2.58 per finding, the report claimed.

However, it added that binary analysis was around six times more expensive and took twice as long as source-code analysis.

“AI did not eliminate the need for expert vulnerability researchers, but it dramatically compressed the work. With access to an effective AI-assisted workflow, vulnerabilities in complex embedded software can be found much faster and at a fraction of the cost, by security researchers and attackers alike,” said Daniel dos Santos, VP of Research at Forescout.

“Our research demonstrates that AI is changing the economics of vulnerability discovery and accelerating the pace at which security teams need to identify, prioritize, and mitigate cyber risk. This is especially impactful for critical infrastructure, where legacy and difficult-to-patch devices may remain in service for years.”

AI Tips for Security Teams

However, AI is not a silver bullet. Research by ReliaQuest pointed to the technology helping threat actors make attacks cheaper, faster to scale, easier to customize and harder to spot.

However, this some have warned that it can make attacks less efficient. One security expert from Proofpoint recently described AI-generated exploits as highly flawed.

To mitigate risk in this new world of AI everywhere, Forescout urged security researchers to:

Assess and prioritize risk based on reachability, exploitability, and operational impact rather than treating all vulnerabilities equally

Reduce unnecessary exposure of connected devices by disabling services such as FTP, Telnet, IPv6 and web administration interfaces

Isolate devices that cannot be patched such as those that have reached end of life

Accelerate patching timelines when fixes exist to account for a faster rate of vulnerability disclosure.

Build security into procurement by requiring suppliers to define support lifetimes, publish vulnerability disclosure policies, provide software bills of materials (SBOMs), and demonstrate ongoing security testing

Title: AI-written patches are becoming attack maps for hackers
Context: Then the first agent attacked the patched programs again, looking for a different way to trigger the same flaw
Full Text:
This summer, the maintainers of vm2, an open-source JavaScript sandboxing library with 1 million downloads per week, shipped fixes for 34 separate sandbox-escape vulnerabilities and Anthropic’s Claude co-wrote 19 of them. Weeks later, a security researcher pointed an AI agent at one of the advisories and asked for a way around the patch. The agent delivered.

Shayaun Nejad, lead product security engineer at Rubrik, ran vulnerability variant analysis on the vm2 patch while preparing for a talk he held at the recent [un]prompted AI security conference in San Francisco. He wanted to highlight the challenges his development team faced when dealing with a flood of AI-discovered vulnerabilities, and noted that the same bugs kept being rediscovered later in new testing runs despite being fixed by AI-assisted pipelines.

“Sometimes the [vulnerability] variant wouldn’t be caught until the model variation got better or the model used chaining analysis at a higher degree once it improved in order to find those variants,” he said. “Sometimes it was in the exact same spot, sometimes it was something that was related, that was a neighbor, but variant analysis is basically something that has been popping up, and it’s a context magnet, too.”

With the rate of published CVEs higher than ever due to AI assistance, software developers are actually disclosing the types of vulnerabilities their platforms are susceptible to, and the patches for these flaws can serve as blueprints for attackers, Nejad warned. Sometimes it’s as simple as pointing an AI agent at a codebase with its historical vulnerabilities as context and telling it to go hunt for variants, he said.

Rubrik’s experience reflects a broader asymmetry that other researchers have observed in recent months: AI models have become very good at offense — finding vulnerabilities and building exploits — while their defensive skills, such as writing secure code and correct patches, have lagged behind.

Also at the [un]prompted conference, OpenAI security researcher Tim de Waal showed how an AI agent patched two vulnerabilities in the firmware of a network access point. For one issue, the agent rebuilt the vulnerable function without the stack canaries the original code had, silently removing a defensive protection. For the other, the generated patch filtered out double-quote characters in the attacker input but missed that using single quotes would have bypassed the fix.

Controlled studies found the same issue at scale. When researchers at 1Password’s Off-by-1 Labs used AI agents to repeatedly generate patches for the same six known vulnerabilities in complex open-source projects, about half of the 6,080 resulting patch candidates left at least one attack path open, with agents sometimes missing identical instances of the same bug in other parts of the code.

More recently, in a benchmark test called P2Patch, researchers pitted two AI agents against each other: one wrote exploits for 101 real vulnerabilities, and the other patched the code until the exploits stopped working. Then the first agent attacked the patched programs again, looking for a different way to trigger the same flaw. In 41 of the 101 cases, it succeeded, sometimes multiple times for subsequent patches.

Of course, human-written patches are not infallible either. Security firm Trail of Bits reviewed the fixes developers submitted for 2,265 vulnerabilities found during its consulting assessments over several years and one in eight failed to fully resolve the reported issues.

In one case the company documented, a human maintainer and an AI agent working as part of the Patch the Planet initiative separately wrote patches for the same memory-safety bug in the freenginx web server, and both patches introduced the same crash during request cleanup.

Organizations turn to AI patching because humans can’t keep up

The issue is not that AI always writes worse patches than humans, although the failure rate of AI-written patches might be higher, but that the rate of vulnerability discovery is now so fast that humans alone can’t keep up. This is combined with the offensive capabilities of AI agents that enable attackers to analyze and reverse engineer patches at machine speed.

Seven months after launching its Mythos-powered Glasswing vulnerability-hunting program, Anthropic’s public ledger counted 37,966 findings. Only 217 of the 7,349 flaws that were made public had been fixed, according to a recent analysis from vulnerability intelligence firm VulnCheck. Not all findings turn out to be security vulnerabilities, but Anthropic claims a true positive rate of 94.2%, which, given the small number of fixes, highlights the deluge of reports that maintainers have to triage and deal with.

“Progress on software security used to be limited by how quickly we could find new vulnerabilities,” Anthropic wrote in its initial Glasswing update. “Now it’s limited by how quickly we can verify, disclose, and patch the large numbers of vulnerabilities found by AI.”

And this is not just a problem for open-source projects. After Bank of America let Anthropic’s models loose on its own systems, the bank added 1,000 outside contractors in the second quarter of this year to help with the patching work, on top of the roughly 3,000 existing staff. They were still on the job in October, CEO Brian Moynihan told CNBC.

By July, Meta was using AI to write fixes for 40% of its critical vulnerabilities, and almost half of those patches landed in production unchanged. Despite that, the exposure time did not go down, Meta software engineer David Molnar said in a separate presentation at [un]prompted. That’s because the AI-proposed patches still had to be reviewed by humans, while the amount of new code grew more than 100% year over year, with more than 80% of it attributed to AI coding agents.

“Everyone is drowning in stuff to review,” Molnar said, adding that his team has worked with directors and product managers internally to find more places where automation can be introduced, including in the review process, shifting it from human-in-the-loop to human-on-the-loop.

“You can automate everything upstream of AI, and then just completely overwhelm your poor humans on the other end,” he said. “Which is why you have to take a look at the entire pipeline and automate all of it.”

In June, the Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams (FIRST) projected around 66,000 CVE assignments for this year. With two months left, the number is already approaching 100,000. Microsoft’s October Patch Tuesday alone addressed 1,415 vulnerabilities compared to only 180 in October 2025.

Closed-source patches are not safe from AI analysis

If AI agents are scouring code repositories for vulnerability variants, one might be inclined to think that closed-source sofware, where the patch is usually inside a compiled binary, are safer. That’s not necessarily the case given that AI models are now also great at reverse engineering, and some people use them to create open-source replicas of complex proprietary products, for example Adobe Photoshop.

In June, when Anthropic’s researchers tested what an attacker can do with AI-assisted patch diffing, they gave a model nothing beyond what’s public on patch day. It produced a working exploit within an hour of a Firefox fix landing. On Windows, given vulnerable and patched binaries plus decompilation output, the same approach built eight full privilege-escalation chains from 21 kernel vulnerabilities for roughly $2,000 each.

“In some ways, N-days are the more dangerous of the two [compared to zero-days], because the patch itself provides a roadmap to the bug,” the Anthropic researchers said at the time.

A team of researchers from Fudan University in Shanghai, China, built an LLM-assisted binary diffing framework and analyzed 76 recent patches from 62 closed-source applications across 25 vendors. According to their paper published this month, the framework flagged 63 of the patches as incomplete and manually confirmed 56, of which 26 could be bypassed into new vulnerabilities, resulting in 19 CVE assignments and $28,100 in bug bounties.

Comparing a vulnerable build against a patched one to locate the changed code has been a standard practice for security researchers for years. The difference now is the speed and lack of skill needed thanks to AI. And even though the latest frontier AI models might have API guardrails that make reverse engineering or binary diffing harder, the open-weight models have become capable enough.

Taesoo Kim, vice president of security research at Microsoft, also warned during the [un]prompted conference that AI has drastically reduced the time needed for binary-diff analysis and exploit creation, and noted that Microsoft has to also be extremely careful when publishing CVEs and push updates quickly to customers.

The more recent frontier models have started refusing such binary analysis work due to stricter guardrails, but a lot of people use open-weight models instead, such as Qwen, Kimi, and GLM, because “they are extremely capable,” he said.

Exploiting the patch gap is now easy

Last month, the Microsoft Edge Security team warned that attackers are increasingly taking advantage of the time gap between when information about a potential vulnerability becomes available in a code commit or test release in one project and when the patch trickles down to other projects. Their report included examples of attackers exploiting security fixes revealed in Chromium builds, the open-source browser that serves as the base for Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, and other browsers, before those fixes were integrated in those downstream browsers.

“This is patch-gap abuse,” the Edge team said. “The technique is not new, but the speed and expertise required is changing. AI-assisted analysis and exploit development could compress work that once took weeks into hours, increasing the chance that a usable exploit emerges while either exposure window remains open.”

Researchers from Epoch AI recently used GLM 5.3 to emulate an unsophisticated attacker and target the Firefox patch gap. Using about $1,000 in API credits and as little as 12 hours of work per target, it compromised every Firefox release shipped between Sept. 17 and Oct. 26. “We did not trigger any safeguards or refusals from any provider,” the researchers wrote.

In response, the Mozilla team has decided to take several actions to prevent patch gap abuse, for example by no longer releasing the regression tests associated with security fixes.

“We’ve observed that GLM 5.3 is much less effective at patch-gapping when a regression test is not present, so we’ve reintroduced a practice of keeping these confidential until after the fix has shipped,” Firefox CTO Bobby Holley wrote.

More diligence in patching, not less disclosure

In a report last month dubbed PatchSlop, security firm Terra found that the rate of incomplete or broken fixes across open-source projects increased eightfold this year.

“A patch that only blocks the reported input can give the impression the bug is addressed even if it’s still there in the underlying code,” the company’s researchers said. “It functions as a map for attackers, marking out both vulnerable code and what the defender thought the bug was. Looking just outside the diff (another encoding, another address range, another path into the same function) is one of the cheapest forms of bug hunting. We believe a growing share of attacker effort, and AI tokens, goes into exactly this.”

The answer is not for open-source projects and software companies to hide vulnerability details and stop publishing security advisories, but to produce better patches. And some researchers believe this is possible, even when patching gets automated with the help of AI agents.

In Rubrik’s case, after the company noticed that bugs it had marked as fixed kept coming back, Nejad’s team added its own variant hunting step that runs automatically in the pipeline after fixes are developed. The company began routing simple bugs to AI patching while reserving complex flaws, such as authentication bypasses, for human engineers.

“Yes, attackers do have that context, but you have that context first, and you can act on that,” Nejad said.

In a blog post this month, OpenAI noted that its Linux vulnerability research and patching pipeline needed iterative testing and variant analysis because initial patches “failed to examine related code for variants of the same vulnerability, leading to incomplete patches.”

“We recommend using models for adversarial review of human and AI-generated patches, which can identify issues such as the patch being bypassable, missing other attack paths or variants, and more,” the company’s researchers said.

The Open Source Security Foundation’s guidance for AI-assisted patching also advises teams to “have a new discovery agent probe the patch as an attacker” and Trail of Bits has released an agent skill that requires testing at least one distinct variant based on the bug’s root cause before a patch can be submitted.

“It is clear there needs to be greater diligence and rigor when patching vulnerabilities,” Terra CEO Shahar Peled told CSO. “This means finding the root cause of any flaw, searching across the codebase for similar bugs and re-testing the system to ensure the patch itself doesn’t introduce a new vulnerability.”

Title: BO Team Exploits Log4Shell in VMware vCenter, Compromises Russian Firm's Code-Signing Server
Context: "We found numerous traces of BO Team connecting to various Windows servers, though the attackers only used malware in one case," Kaspersky explained
Full Text:
An investigation into suspicious activity within a Russian software developer's network has uncovered a months-long compromise of its development infrastructure and a software code-signing server.

The activity, documented by Kaspersky's ICS CERT team after it was contacted by the affected developer in June 2025, has been attributed to a threat actor named BO Team (aka Black Owl, Hoody Hyena, and Lifting Zmiy). The name of the targeted company was not disclosed, but it operates from within Russia and develops software that has a "customer base in the Russian Federation," according to Kaspersky.

Over the course of several months, the intrusion resulted in the theft of confidential information and the compromise of all components of the organization's IT infrastructure, including Windows and Linux servers, workstations, hypervisors, backup servers, security solution management servers, and network equipment.

Active since at least 2023, BO Team focuses on cyber espionage and hacktivism, and has a history of targeting Russian entities to steal valuable data and break into compromised infrastructure using tools like Mythic and Cobalt Strike, along with its own malware such as BrockenDoor and ZeronetKit. The group is assessed to be of Ukrainian origin.

"Their primary motivation is to degrade the Russian military-industrial complex to weaken Moscow's operational capabilities on the battlefield," Orange Cyberdefense said in an analysis of the group. "They also engage in cognitive warfare aimed at humiliating Russian institutions and demonstrating their vulnerability to Ukrainian digital resistance."

While BO Team is known to deploy ransomware and publicize its activities on a dedicated Telegram channel, the attack targeting the unspecified software developer did not involve any data destruction or public posts claiming responsibility for it.

"Instead, the attackers worked to entrench themselves in the victim's network by setting up convenient command channels and planting backdoors to restore access in case it was lost," Kaspersky said. "The compromise of the software development (CI/CD) infrastructure and the software code-signing server indicated that the attack would likely develop into a supply chain scenario."

The attack, per the Russian cybersecurity company, involved the threat actors compromising the organization's Linux terminal server by taking advantage of an exposed SSH service, and using it to conduct reconnaissance of the internal network to flag systems with accessible SMB, Kerberos, SSH, Telnet, FTP, HTTP, HTTPS, WinRM, and LDAP services.

The adversary has also been found unsuccessfully attempting to access internal portals, along with websites like proxy-sale[.]com, start.duckduckgo[.]com, vcsa.vmware[.]com, and vulners[.]com, among others.

Event logs show that the attackers further attempted to connect from the compromised terminal server to the virtualization system servers, including logging in to the VMware vCenter web interface. These sign-in efforts ended in failure.

However, the threat actor managed to successfully target a VMware vCenter server (version 7.0.3) vulnerable to CVE-2021-44228 (aka Log4Shell and LogJam), obtain a remote command line with root privileges, connect to the hypervisor over SSH, and identify accessible hosts.

This phase also involved the deployment of a backdoor on the hypervisor that was run every hour by planting a shell script in the "/etc/cron.hourly/" directory. The script carried the name "pgcache" in a likely attempt to disguise it as a legitimate PostgreSQL component.

The primary responsibility of the backdoor is to download and run a secondary shell script from "lo1yaizaeghaevarooD1ahtaichootae.nofrillsdns[.]com." The shell script is designed to download and run the Global Socket (GSocket) utility, enabling the attacker to gain remote control of the compromised host.

Select variants of the script have been found to point to a hostname-specific payload staged on "lo1yaizaeghaevarood1ahtaichootaz.nofrillsdns[.]com" to deliver an as-yet-undetermined next-stage payload.

"The attackers used the nofrillsdns[.]com service, which allows domain names to be created for free by calling the curl utility," Kaspersky said. "By default, when the malware's command-and-control server is not operating, the attackers set the corresponding DNS record to 127.0.0.1, which is what the script checks. Activating the backdoor requires only a change to the DNS record -- the script will then download and run the malware."

Some of the other post-exploitation actions undertaken by the BO Team following the backdoor deployment are listed below -

Gaining access to the corporate proxy server.

Abusing the certificate of the compromised hypervisor to connect to servers associated with a second virtualization cluster and place a similar backdoor.

Collecting information about virtual machines and firewall rules, accessing some of them via a command-line interpreter in the guest OS from the hypervisor.

Running an obfuscated bash script to decrypt and run an ELF binary designed to provide remote control over SSH.

Searching for secrets on the compromised virtual machines, allowing the attackers to breach the virtual machine of the GitLab software development platform, as well as gain access to some of the repositories containing source code and seize the server's private key.

Using the private key of the GitLab virtual machine to connect to the organization's Ansible orchestration system.

Using access to the Linux terminal server to locate credentials of several domain accounts and connect to the domain controller using the account of one of the system administrators after likely accessing the memory of virtual machines running on the compromised hypervisors.

Changing the security attributes of the user's Windows Downloads directory.

Using legitimate binaries like tasklist.exe, findstr.exe, taskmgr.exe, and ipconfig.exe to identify which security solutions were running on the system and to gather details about network interfaces.

Attempting to take a dump of the lsass.exe process using the Nanodump utility and obtain the credentials of domain administrators and other privileged users with access to the domain controller. The attackers deleted the event logs after the activity was detected and blocked by a security solution.

Using system utilities such as comsvcs.dll rather than established utilities like Mimikatz and Nanodump to create a memory dump of the lsass.exe process.

Dumping the system registry using the regedit.exe utility, and using it to decrypt the Active Directory domain database ("ntds.dit") to extract the credentials of all domain users.

Launching the OpenSSH scp.exe utility to transfer the collected information to the terminal server.

Logging in to the domain controller using the Kerberos ticket of one of the domain administrators and ultimately compromising the organization's entire Windows infrastructure by taking advantage of the fact that the same password was used for system administrator accounts in different domains.

Connecting to the terminal server over SSH using root account credentials after possibly stealing them from a system administrator's computer post obtaining domain administrator privileges.

Modifying "/usr/bin/nxnode-login" to intercept and write user credentials to a shared-memory file at "/dev/shm/pulse-shm-3088612174."

Successfully brute-forcing the password of the administrator's terminal server after about 2,500 failed attempts to place the private key of the Ansible system.

Complicating detection efforts by timestomping, obfuscation of malware code, usage of living-off-the-land (LotL) techniques, systematic deletion of event logs, and dressing up malware files as legitimate software.

"We found numerous traces of BO Team connecting to various Windows servers, though the attackers only used malware in one case," Kaspersky explained. "The server which apparently held particular interest for hackers, was used to sign compiled builds of the commercial software developed by the attacked organization."

"Attackers may be interested in such a server for two reasons. First, they may try to carry out a supply chain attack by injecting malicious code into a product build right before it is signed. Second, the attackers may try to steal the organization's digital signature to use later to sign malware."

It's suspected that the attackers likely attempted to execute a malicious WMI script and install a backdoor similar to the Linux variant in the temporary files directory.

But after the incident was detected and countermeasures were enacted, the attackers, after having lost access to the compromised infrastructure, orchestrated a phishing campaign towards the end of July in an attempt to collect employee credentials. The phishing email contained the "Account disconnected from the mail server" subject line and sought to trick the recipient into clicking on a link to change their password.

What's more, the email managed to bypass SPF and DKIM checks, indicating the attackers had in their possession a private key that was obtained after gaining control of the organization's mail server. The phishing attack was detected and prevented.

"The attackers used a service that automatically generates phishing pages," Kaspersky said. "The service loads the content of a targeted organization's official website and displays a password entry form on top of the official site's layout. After entering the password, the user sees an error message. However, the information is actually sent to the attacker."

"We repeatedly noted that the attackers tried not to use malware and hacking utilities in order to evade detection," Kaspersky said. "Instead, they actively used system tools such as RDP, SSH, and SCP, as well as system utilities to steal user credentials. This enabled them to develop the attack using legitimate accounts, which also matches the BO Team profile."

The activity has been found to originate from IP addresses 193.3.23[.]236 and 80.76.42[.]139, both of which belong to a provider in Ukraine. Further analysis into the malicious activity has revealed that the attackers followed a standard work schedule and operated in a time zone that differed "only slightly" from that of the victim Russian entity.

"Based on the totality of the circumstantial evidence, such as the attackers' interest in the source code repository and software build signing server, as well as their use of a software composition analysis (dependency analysis) platform, we believe that BO Team may have set out to inject malicious code into a solution released by the attacked organization in order to subsequently compromise its customers, i.e., carry out a so-called supply chain attack," Kaspersky concluded.

"Thanks to the rapid response measures applied after the incident was discovered, the attackers lost access to the compromised infrastructure and were apparently unable to bring the attack to its intended conclusion."

Title: Introducing GravityZone Exposure Management: Close Attack Paths Before They're Exploited
Context: A sysadmin closes the maintenance window with every Critical and High vulnerability patched
Full Text:
A sysadmin closes the maintenance window with every Critical and High vulnerability patched. One of the remaining mediums sits on a workstation. The workstation's user has administrative rights on a domain controller and signs into it interactively, so their credential material stays in its memory while the session lasts. On the same subnet, a web service still opens to the internet on a port opened during a migration two years ago. None of these findings is worth escalating on its own. Together they are a route to domain compromise, and automated attack tooling now performs the reconnaissance and chaining between steps faster than any ticket queue moves.

Bitdefender GravityZone Exposure Management is a prevention-first product built to remove those attack opportunities before they are used. It unifies visibility across critical exposures, prioritizes them by the attack routes they create, and reduces the attack surface through hardening.

What Does Exposure Management Bring Together?

Exposure Management shifts your strategy toward prevention without replacing what you run today. It works natively with the Bitdefender GravityZone platform and alongside third-party endpoint protection (EPP) and endpoint detection and response (EDR) products.

The product combines five capabilities, each answering a different question:

Endpoint Risk Management: What is weak on your servers and workstations?

User Risk Management (part of Risk Management): Which identities, and which user behaviors, put the environment at risk?

External Attack Surface Management (EASM): What can an attacker see from the internet?

Attack Path: Which weaknesses combine into a route to a critical asset?

Proactive Hardening and Attack Surface Reduction (PHASR): Which risky tools and actions can be blocked without disrupting work?

Fig1. Continuous Exposure Management loop.

Together, these capabilities form one continuous loop in three stages: visibility, prioritization, and reduction. The reduced surface is then scanned again, so the ranking always reflects the current environment.

How Does Exposure Management See Your Environment?

Exposure Management understands your environment by correlating two directions of visibility into a single inventory of findings.

Inside-out: Endpoint Risk Management continuously assesses Windows, macOS, and Linux endpoints for operating system misconfigurations, local and group policy weaknesses, and installed applications mapped to CVE identifiers. Each finding is assigned a risk score and a remediation option: automated mitigation task, manual remediation steps, or application patch. User Risk Management assesses identity-related behaviors such as password reuse and credential exposure.

Outside-in: EASM is agentless and runs from Bitdefender infrastructure. Starting from your domains, email addresses, and IPv4 and IPv6 ranges, it discovers internet-facing assets and artifacts (services, certificates, CIDR ranges, DNS records) and reports publicly exposed services, open ports, CVE-mapped services, name servers vulnerable to zone transfer, and certificates that expire within 30 days.

How Does Exposure Management Decide What to Fix First?

Visibility alone produces longer lists. Scanning produces findings; correlation produces routes. A medium-severity CVE on a privileged user's workstation outranks a critical CVE on an isolated test server. The first ends in domain compromise, the second in a rebuilt test server. Attack Path Analysis turns raw findings into an ordered workflow by asking from which starting points could an attacker reach a valuable asset, and through which steps?

Each answer is a directed graph that ends at a target asset. Nodes include user accounts, workstations, servers, cloud resources such as security groups and load balancers, and derived resources such as an SMB file-sharing service that depends on a specific server. Every edge is labeled with the mechanism that makes the hop possible, and selecting it shows the CVEs and findings behind that step. Four risk factors appear as badges: Public Exposure, Exploitable CVE, High-Severity CVE (a risk score of 70% or higher), and Critical Asset. The target carries a risk score from 0 to 100. The practical result is the choke point: a node that several routes depend on. Fixing a choke point closes every branch below it.

Fig. 2. The demo attack path in the Graph tab, with the Assets panel grouped by attack stage and the details of DEMO-WS4 open.

The Top 5 attack path entry points widget on the ASM Dashboard surfaces these quickly, because the same account appearing at the start of several paths is usually the fix with the widest effect. A Shortest Path control highlights the most direct route while keeping alternate branches visible, so you can confirm whether a fix actually puts the target out of reach.

Fig. 3. The Attack Path view of the ASM dashboard.

How Does Exposure Management Shrink the Attack Surface?

Some attacker routes cannot be closed today: a patch waits for a maintenance window, or the hop relies on something working as designed, such as credentials held in memory or built-in tools like WMIC and PowerShell. Exposure you cannot remove is exposure you constrain. PHASR is the module where Exposure Management moves from reporting to enforcement.

PHASR builds a behavioral profile for each machine-user combination and compares it against more than 1,100 monitored rules covering Living off the Land binaries, tampering tools, remote administration tools, crypto miners, and piracy tools. When a profile never uses a capability attackers rely on, PHASR restricts that action or the entire tool. WMIC can remain available for system queries while remote process execution is blocked, and PowerShell can remain available while obfuscated or encoded actions are blocked.

The hardening is dynamic in both directions. After a learning phase, you approve recommendations in Direct Control or let Autopilot apply them. If a user's behavior changes, PHASR generates new access recommendations.

The same model extends to AI. On Windows, PHASR treats more than 50 local AI tools and each AI agent is treated as a behavioral profile of its own, an identity independent of the user operating the endpoint, with its own permissions and restrictions. The AI agent gains access to the tools required to perform its tasks, while user permissions remain strictly tied to the user's role. For instance, a user whose role never calls for PowerShell keeps that restriction on their own profile, even while the AI assistant running on their workstation is allowed to use it.

Exposure Management in Practice: A Hybrid Exchange Example

Consider a company that moved its mail to Exchange Online but still runs one Exchange 2019 server on-premises to manage hybrid recipients, with Outlook on the web published to the internet. EASM flags the exposed service, and Risk Management flags an exploitable vulnerability on the server. Attack Path Analysis shows why it matters: help desk administrators sign in to that server to manage recipients, so their credentials are cached there, just as they are on a phished user’s workstation where one of them fixed a problem last week.

Two entry points, one from the internet and one from the inbox, lead to the same account, and from that account several routes lead to the servers that run your domain. The fix with the widest effect is that one account, not the machine with the most CVEs. While the Exchange server waits for its migration, PHASR restricts what an attacker could do next: it blocks encoded PowerShell and PowerShell Remoting and WMIC remote execution on workstations that never need them, while your administrators keep the tools they use every day.

Fig. 4. Exposure Management in practice with hybrid Exchange example.

Summary

GravityZone Exposure Management moves risk reduction from periodic reporting to continuous prevention. Risk Management and EASM give you unified inside-out and outside-in visibility across CVEs, misconfigurations, identity risks, and internet-facing assets. Attack Path Analysis correlates those findings into routes that end at critical assets and identifies the choke points where one fix closes several routes. PHASR constrains what cannot be patched, removing unnecessary access to risky tools and actions at the level of individual behaviors, including AI agents.

Bitdefender Exposure Management works with the GravityZone platform alongside third-party EPP and EDR, allowing you to adopt a prevention-first strategy without rebuilding your stack. Learn More About GravityZone Exposure Management

Title: Updating our coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy timelines
Context: We’re shortening the disclosure window in our coordinated vulnerability disclosure (CVD) policy from 90 days to 30 days for high- and critical-severity issues, and to 45 days...
Full Text:
Over the last several months, frontier models have become much better at discovering vulnerabilities. We remain optimistic that this will help defenders find and fix vulnerabilities faster than ever before. However, the speed at which AI is improving has changed how we think about our own disclosure practices.

We’re shortening the disclosure window in our coordinated vulnerability disclosure (CVD) policy from 90 days to 30 days for high- and critical-severity issues, and to 45 days for all other issues. The new timelines apply to vulnerabilities reported to vendors and maintainers on or after January 1, 2027. In-progress reports as of that date will keep their existing deadlines.

In addition to shortening the disclosure window, we are making two related changes. First, we will aim to escalate to an external vulnerability coordinator after 15 days instead of 30 if a maintainer does not respond to our initial vulnerability report. Second, we will wait 30 days instead of 45 after a patch is available before sharing full technical details. The rest of our policy remains the same.

Finally, there are high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities that we reported over 90 days ago and that now exceed the deadline in our current CVD policy that have not yet been disclosed publicly. We are now notifying the maintainers of these projects that we are providing them an additional 30 days, after which time we will publish these reports on our dashboard in line with our updated policy starting January 1, 2027.

Responding to AI-enabled vulnerability discovery

Many coordinated disclosure norms, including those found in our own policy, were developed well before AI could discover vulnerabilities. These policies assumed that fixes moved at human speed and that independent rediscovery of the same bug was unlikely. Neither assumption holds today. Models can now help develop fixes, and a bug that one model can find is increasingly likely to be found by another. We are seeing a higher rate of vulnerability rediscovery as these capabilities increase. A 90-day window made sense when a vulnerability could be expected to stay private for months. We no longer believe it can, and these changes are intended to keep pace with progress in AI capabilities and strike the right balance for defenders.

Some vulnerabilities still can’t be fixed quickly. Flaws in hard-to-deploy software, such as critical infrastructure, and flaws that require changes to a specification or RFC can’t always be resolved in 30 or 45 days. In these cases, we will work with the vendor on a remediation timeline. Our seven-day disclosure window for any vulnerability under active exploitation remains unchanged. This new policy update will not apply to AI-discovered findings that have not received human review, such as those found by OSS Scanner.

We recognize that shorter timelines may put more pressure on software maintainers. To reduce that burden, we will continue to include actionable guidance with each report, along with a patch or mitigation where possible, to best enable the maintainer to confirm a finding and fix the vulnerability. We will also continue to agree on a sustainable pace with maintainers before sending a large volume of findings to a single project.

We offer programs to help maintainers and defenders work at this new pace. Maintainers of critical open-source projects can apply to OSS Scanner, a no-cost service that periodically scans their code with our strongest models and sends them findings directly. Eligible maintainers and contributors can apply to the Claude for Open Source Program for six months of Claude Ultra at no cost. And security professionals, including open-source maintainers, can apply to our Cyber Verification Program, which tailors Claude’s safeguards to enable legitimate defensive work.

Title: Attackers Exploit UnrealIRCd Flaw That Enables Server-Level Command Injection
Context: The maintainer described the vulnerability as the "most critical issue" found in UnrealIRCd over the past 15 years
Full Text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Friday added a high-severity security flaw impacting UnrealIRCd, an open-source Internet Relay Chat (IRC) server, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, following reports of active exploitation.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-114713 (CVSS score: 8.6), is a case of improper neutralization of delimiters that could be used to execute arbitrary commands with server/IRCOp privileges.

"The labeled-response module in UnrealIRCd 6.0.0 before 6.2.7.1 does not escape the IRCv3 'label' message tag when echoing it into replies, which allows any user on a network with two or more linked servers to inject server-to-server commands that are executed with server authority," reads the description of the flaw in the NIST National Vulnerability Database (NVD).

The addition comes nearly a week after UnrealIRCd's project leader, developer, and maintainer, Bram Matthys (aka Syzop), released UnrealIRCd 6.2.7.1 to address multiple security vulnerabilities identified with the help of artificial intelligence, including CVE-2026-114713.

"We are seeing bad guys exploiting this issue on the internet right now," Matthys said. "Hopefully everyone has hot-patched or updated their server, or at the very least has the spamfilter workaround deployed. If not, do so ASAP!"

Exploitation attempts are said to have commenced a day after the release of the hotfix on November 7, 2026. That said, the exact details of the malicious activity and its end goals are presently unknown. The maintainer described the vulnerability as the "most critical issue" found in UnrealIRCd over the past 15 years.

Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies have time until November 16, 2026, to apply the fixes under Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk.

Title: This year’s bug count just passed 100K
Context: Similarly, VulnCheck found the median time from CVE publication to exploitation falling from 120 days in 2025 to 80 days during the first half of 2026
Full Text: Chalk up a new record for vulns. The number of Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) found and disclosed so far in 2026 surpassed 100,000 on Friday - more than double 2025’s total - and the reason can be summed up in two letters: AI. “It’s kind of wild,” Josh Bressers, VulnCheck’s director of coordinated vulnerability disclosure, told The Register. “The thing that almost scares the bejesus out of me is while 100K sounds like a lot, in a couple years we're going to say, remember when it was only 100K?” As of the time of our interview, about 4 pm UTC on Friday, VulnCheck counted 100,222 CVEs, he said. Microsoft alone added 1,094 security flaws to the total count on Tuesday, following 1,474 vulnerabilities the month before. “There's no denying the fact that vulnerability hunting with AI is driving a majority of what we're seeing.” All the major CVE Numbering Authorities (CNAs) - these are the organizations authorized by the CVE program to assign unique identifiers to security vulnerabilities - like VulnCheck, Microsoft, Oracle, GitHub, and other large enterprise IT vendors “are just screaming into the atmosphere right now,” Bressers said. “It’s AI.” Meanwhile, the percentage of these bugs that are exploited in the wild remains relatively consistent. About 1.4 percent (1,363) of the CVEs published this year have been added to VulnCheck’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. “But obviously, as the number of CVEs grows, [1 percent] of 1,000 is a lot different than [1 percent] of 100,000,” Bressers said. Plus, as other security researchers have documented, the window between the public release of a security patch and attackers developing working exploits – often by reverse engineering the patch while end users are still applying the fix – is rapidly shrinking. This is also thanks to AI. From CVE to KEV From January to June, 88 percent of the exploitation observed by CrowdStrike using public proof-of-concept (PoC) code occurred within 48 hours of the code's release. The security firm said China-linked groups such as Vault Panda and Genesis Panda moved even faster, launching attacks within 24 hours of disclosure. Similarly, VulnCheck found the median time from CVE publication to exploitation falling from 120 days in 2025 to 80 days during the first half of 2026. This window has closed even further during the second half of the year, which also seems to coincide with the AI-induced vulnpocalypse. “It’s often just hours,” Bressers said, noting 14 make-me-root vulnerabilities that VulnCheck disclosed on Friday in Copeland refrigeration controllers. Two are under active exploitation. These are the devices that Iranian hackers abused to spoil food and spark fires in supermarkets across Europe. “We published those CVEs, and literally minutes later, we were seeing hits on our honey pots,” Bressers said about the Copeland device vulnerabilities. “We’ve hit a point where with anything that looks interesting, someone is taking that information and seeing what they can do with it. Is it AI driven? Probably. It'd be hard to say it's not, because we've seen it really ramp up recently.” This influx of software bugs requires a sea change in how the entire industry approaches vulnerability disclosure and patching. “We don't have a security problem anymore,” Bressers said. “We have a data problem now. Instead of obsessing over vulnerabilities, we need to start looking at things like heat maps for infrastructure, and figure out the vulnerabilities that actually affect you. The CISA BOD helps with that.” What to prioritize in a patchpocalypse The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) in June issued a cybersecurity directive that replaces flat-deadline vulnerability management policies. Instead of prioritizing patching based solely on CVSS severity scores, the directive instructs organizations to prioritize based on specific risk criteria, including whether the asset is internet-exposed, under active exploitation, and whether an attacker can automate the exploit. “It's telling people to figure out the vulnerabilities that actually affect you, and then put those at the top of the list, instead of just saying we're going to fix all the criticals,” Bressers said. AI-generated vulnerability disclosures also create huge headaches for open source software developers and maintainers, which Bressers describes as a security problem “super close to my heart.” “You've got individual developers that are drowning in vulnerability reports,” he said. “You have foundations being crushed by AI agents scraping their data or downloading their packages, millions of times a day, and it's straining the seams absolutely everywhere you look. The one thing I can say with certainty is: The way we currently do things has to change, and it's going to have to change fairly soon.” Different open source projects have taken different approaches to solving this issue. The Eclipse Foundation, which houses the Open VSX Registry, in April launched a “managed tier” for enterprise customers and other organizations running Open VSX at scale. Instead of using the free, open source version, the managed version guarantees a 99.95 percent uptime SLA backed by service credits. Its customers include AWS, IBM, Google, Cursor, and Windsurf. This paid option means commercial users who rely on the registry help fund its ongoing maintenance - and their own platforms’ security and performance. Meanwhile, curl’s maintainer, Daniel Stenberg, citing an “avalanche of vulnerability reports," updated its bug reporting rules last month. As of October 26, all low- and medium-severity reports go directly into the public GitHub repository, with only the high- and critical-flaws receiving private handling. Stenberg already shuttered curl's bug bounty program this year as AI-generated submissions piled work onto its security team. “A lot more needs to happen, and I think it is going to be a challenge to enact some of this change,” Bressers said. “When a package registry drastically changes something, people start freaking out, and the world is going to end, and people on LinkedIn are complaining - a lot of people are hesitant. No one wants to be the first to jump into the alligator-filled pool. That's one of our challenges.”®

Title: PostgreSQL Patches 52 Flaws, Including 22-Year-Old Bug Enabling Authenticated RCE
Context: " The project's security advisory describes the attacker only as someone who can create objects, without saying which privileges that takes
Full Text:
A type confusion flaw in PostgreSQL lets a database user who can create objects run code on the server. Updates released yesterday fix it, along with 51 other security flaws. Full protection from this flaw also requires rebuilding any C-language extensions installed on the server.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-6460, has a CVSS score of 8.8. Any code run this way has the rights of the operating system user that runs PostgreSQL. All versions before 18.7, 17.12, 16.16, 15.20, and 14.25 are affected.

The PostgreSQL Global Development Group, which publishes the database's releases, has not reported any attacks using the flaw. CISA's assessment in the CVE record also lists exploitation as none.

The flaw involves composite types, which are types built from named fields, each with its own data type. A field's type can be changed while older values of that type are still held in other parts of the server.

The server could then read an old value as if it had the new type. The fix, described in the project's release notes, adds version checks so the server can detect a value that no longer matches its type.

Security researcher Mehmet Ince described a working exploit for the flaw, demonstrated on PostgreSQL 18.6, in a technical writeup published this week.

His method is to prepare a query that holds a value, change the type of one of the value's fields, and then run the query. The writeup includes the SQL that crashes an unpatched server this way and a second step that leaks memory addresses. It does not include the SQL for the final step, which makes the server run a command.

He wrote that he could "trigger this crash as a lowest-privileged login role." The project's security advisory describes the attacker only as someone who can create objects, without saying which privileges that takes.

Red Hat, which ships PostgreSQL packages, says in its CVE assessment that an attacker needs a database login with the ability to create or modify objects. None of these sources says whether an account with only default privileges can go beyond the crash to run code.

Ince traces the root of the flaw to May 5, 2004, when PostgreSQL gained the ability to change a column's type. His technique for running code relies on a later change made on May 14, 2015.

He also adapted the exploit for managed PostgreSQL services and privately shared proofs of concept with their security teams in August. The providers he worked with include AWS (Aurora and RDS), Microsoft (Azure PostgreSQL), Google (AlloyDB), Supabase, Databricks, and Ubicloud. The writeup does not give each service's current patch status.

The project credits more than a dozen reporters for CVE-2026-6460, including the researcher, and credits him on five other flaws in the same release.

The project rates 32 of the 52 flaws at 8.8, the highest score in the release. Based on the scores in its vulnerability index, only one flaw in the server requires neither a login nor any user action. That flaw, CVE-2026-116322, lets an unauthenticated client trigger a restart of PostgreSQL 18 servers.

Several other fixes are in client tools. A crafted archive can make pg_restore run code as the user running it. A compromised source server can make psql run code through the restore script in pg_dump's tar output.

What Administrators Should Do

Update the server to 18.7, 17.12, 16.16, 15.20, or 14.25, matching your major version.

Rebuild or update every C-language extension at the same time as the server. Extensions built against older releases still load, but they "may not be protected from the vulnerabilities fixed in this release," according to a repository notice from the project's RPM package maintainers. Some extensions will also need source-code changes.

Extensions rebuilt for the new releases can fail to load on older servers. Extension packages in the project's RPM repositories now require the new minor release.

If PostgreSQL runs outside its package's own service unit, for example under Patroni, restart it right after updating, a maintainer of the RPM packages says in a packaging blog post.

Update client tools such as pg_dump, pg_restore, reindexdb and vacuumdb on every machine that runs them.

Do not use the new composite_type_mismatch setting to turn off the checks. The project says doing so carries security risks.

The project's advisory and release notes offer no workaround for servers that cannot be updated yet.

PostgreSQL 14 is now end-of-life, and 14.25 is its last release. Older major versions are also affected and received no update.

After updating, follow the reindexing steps in the release announcement. If you use incremental backups, take a new full backup and base later incremental backups on it.

Title: CISA Adds Two Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
Context: While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog...
Full Text:
CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-114713 UnrealIRCd Improper Neutralization of Delimiters Vulnerability

CVE-2026-123039 Check Point Multiple Products Incorrect Permission Assignment for Critical Resource Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Title: Policy and Disclosure: 2026 Edition
Context: A vulnerability’s severity does not affect the likelihood that it will be discovered by attackers, only its impact on users
Full Text:
Since 2021, Project Zero has followed a “90 + 30” vulnerability disclosure policy, allowing vendors up to 90 days to remediate a vulnerability plus an extra 30 days “soak time” for patch rollout. Our goal was to encourage faster patching and give vendors time to deliver patches to users. The advent of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploitation has changed the threat landscape such that the vulnerability remediation timeline encouraged by our disclosure policy is clearly insufficient.

LLMs have increased the speed at which attackers can find and exploit vulnerabilities, alongside the risk that multiple parties, including malicious ones, discover the same bug. A vulnerability reported today presents a much higher immediate risk to users than one reported last year. In this new environment, it is crucial that vendors move towards remediating vulnerabilities faster.

LLMs have also decreased the time it takes for attackers to reverse engineer and exploit a vulnerability based on a patch, to the extent that zero patch-to-exploitation time is a reasonable, though imperfect, model of attacker behavior. Patch soak time is no longer meaningful in a world where attackers can almost immediately determine bug details from a patch, and can put users at risk by creating a false sense of secrecy. “Patch gap” is the time between a fix being released for a security vulnerability and the user installing the relevant update. It is equally crucial that vendors reduce patch gap, either by reducing patch rollout time or using other strategies to protect users while remediation is in progress.

LLMs have also increased the volume of vulnerabilities that Project Zero reports. We are finding several vulnerabilities a week in targets where we once found a few vulnerabilities a year. Aspects of our policy that require vendor negotiation or agreement, including determining whether a bug is fixed and whether grace period applies, are quickly becoming unmanageable.

Today, we are announcing a new vulnerability disclosure policy, created with the following goals in mind:

Encourage faster vulnerability remediation

Encourage vendors to reduce “patch gap”

Allow for the policy to be automated by both Project Zero and vendors

Our new policy: “Full X”

Vulnerabilities will be disclosed X days after they are reported to the vendor.

Starting today, our policy is “Full 90”, i.e. vulnerabilities will be disclosed 90 days after they are reported to the vendor.

On February 2, 2027, we will move to a “Full 60” policy where vulnerabilities are disclosed after 60 days.

On January 3, 2028, we will move to a “Full 30” policy where vulnerabilities are disclosed after 30 days.

We are also removing most ‘special cases’ from our disclosure policy, including grace period and variant policy. The only exceptions to our new policy are:

Vulnerabilities actively exploited in the wild -- ITW vulnerabilities will be handled according to Google’s application security vulnerability disclosure policy

Public vulnerabilities -- Project Zero may make details of a vulnerability public, at our discretion, if the details have already been made public by others

Vendor request -- We will make vulnerability details public if the vendor we reported it to requests it

Why reduce remediation time gradually?

Project Zero solicited feedback from the vendors we report the most vulnerabilities to as a part of developing this new policy. An overarching concern was that immediately changing the policy could harm users by making unfixed vulnerabilities available to attackers while vendors are in the process of improving their remediation processes and technology. While the benefits of delaying disclosure are declining due to the increased probability that attackers will discover a vulnerability during the embargo period, we still feel there are benefits in the short term.

In addition, vendors mentioned two more subtle concerns. One was that an overly-aggressive disclosure policy would encourage fixing bugs reported under the new policy with more priority, even if they are less severe than other reported vulnerabilities. The other was that immediately enforcing a policy that some vendors aren’t equipped to meet might lead to a state where vendors accept that they cannot fix bugs within the deadline and don’t attempt to.

We decided on a policy that encourages vendors to improve remediation time on a schedule that is challenging but realistic, with the hope that this will lead to vendors broadly improving their remediation processes and infrastructure in a way that eventually enables them to fix all reported vulnerabilities quickly.

What about severity?

While our analysis isn’t always perfect, Project Zero only reports vulnerabilities with substantial severity and demonstrated security impact in our tracker. That said, we don’t feel severity is an effective metric for making disclosure decisions, especially in the current environment. A vulnerability’s severity does not affect the likelihood that it will be discovered by attackers, only its impact on users.

When vendors determine severity and use it to prioritize bug fixes, they are making decisions about what risks they are willing to expose their users to, and it is reasonable to accept the risk of low-severity bugs, like unexploitable null pointer crashes or minor info leaks in a lot of circumstances. But this doesn’t change the availability of these vulnerabilities to attackers, and we want our policy to reflect this reality.

It’s also important to acknowledge that Project Zero holds itself to high standards with regards to the reproducibility, readability, reachability and reported security impact of the vulnerabilities we report. This policy assumes bugs reports are of this quality, and it is reasonable for vendors to treat low quality-bug reports differently.

What about hardware?

We encourage all vendors to consider how they would respond to imminent disclosure of a serious vulnerability, including non-patch strategies, as there is no guarantee that defenders will be the first to find a bug. That said, Project Zero has occasionally granted exceptions to our policy on rare occasions, including Spectre and Meltdown, and will continue to do so in the future.

Are you really not going to check whether bugs are fixed?

The question of whether a bug is fixed for the purposes of our policy has always been challenging and somewhat unresolved, particularly with regards to code that is not shipped directly to users and not publicly available. It is not unusual for Project Zero to communicate with vendors multiple times for each bug report to come to an agreement on whether a vulnerability is fixed. As more vendors experiment with vulnerability remediation strategies that are not patching like temporarily disabling code paths, we expect this to become even more complex.

We still plan to track whether bugs are fixed and communicate if they are not, however, this will not be a decision point in our policy. This will enable us to share technical details of how users are protected without needing to make a binary judgement with consequences for the vendor.

Title: Linux Kernel TCP Flaw (CVE-2026-98432)
Context: On October 25, 2026, the National Vulnerability Database published CVE-2026-98432, a vulnerability in the Linux kernel's IPv4 TCP stack
Full Text:
What happened?

On October 25, 2026, the National Vulnerability Database published CVE-2026-98432, a vulnerability in the Linux kernel's IPv4 TCP stack. The flaw is a use-after-free: when a server handles a retransmitted SYN for a connection request, it can read IP options from memory that has already been freed. This can lead to a crash or memory corruption. The Linux kernel fix defers freeing these IP options until after an RCU (read-copy-update) grace period, so no thread can still be using them when they are released.

Okta's response

Security Patching: All Okta and Auth0 environments are fully patched or mitigated against this issue.

No Evidence of Exploitation: To date, Okta and Auth0 have observed no evidence of exploitation.

Do I need to do anything?

For customers running Okta Access Gateway (OAG), we recommend upgrading to the latest version and restarting your appliance to ensure the patched kernel is loaded.

Title: HTTPd (CVE-2026-119618): Detecting heap corruption and RCE in Apache HTTP Server mod_http2
Context: Threat Intelligence entries show where affected Apache hosts are running, Vulnerability Management maps to each distribution’s vendor advisory, and Runtime Detections catch what...
Full Text:
On November 11, 2026, Apache released HTTP Server 2.4.71 to fix CVE-2026-119618, a critical severity heap corruption flaw in mod_http2 that Apache’s security advisory said can lead to remote code execution (RCE). The flaw sits in assign_headers(), affects versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70, and can be triggered over HTTP/2 with no authentication. Red Hat and Amazon have scored the vulnerability 9.8 on CVSS v3.1, though CISA rates it at 8.1.

Two teams found the bug independently, eight days apart. Anthropic's OSS Scanner is an opt-in, model-driven scanner for open-source projects. It reported the bug on October 26, 2026. Anthony Weems and Simon Scannell of Google Cloud Vulnerability Research reported it eight days later on November 3, according to the CVE record.

The day after Apache disclosed it on oss-security, a public proof-of-concept (PoC) was published on GitHub showing the heap corruption, though no PoC has been released for the RCE as of the publication of this blog. Additionally, no confirmed in-the-wild exploitation has been reported, and the CVE does not appear in CISA's KEV catalog.

The bug lives in Apache's own HTTP/2 implementation, not in any application the server hosts. Only servers that enable HTTP/2 are exposed. Affected organizations are encouraged to upgrade to version 2.4.71 or turn off HTTP/2 if patching is delayed.

The Sysdig Threat Research Team (TRT) analyzed the publicly available research and simulated a successful exploit to help defenders understand four key details: who is affected, what has been demonstrated versus claimed, what runtime visibility can detect, and what mitigation steps should be taken until a patch can be applied. They also tested and found that Sysdig’s existing runtime detections caught every post-exploitation step.

Affected Apache HTTP Server versions

The flaw is in mod_http2, the HTTP/2 module of Apache HTTP Server. The same module is released separately as mod_h2 on GitHub and also affected.

While the Apache advisory rates the vulnerability as critical. The CVE record, which Apache maintains as the CVE Numbering Authority (CNA), doesn’t actually carry an associated CVSS score. However, Red Hat and Amazon both rate the vulnerability as critical and score it at 9.8 on CVSS v3.1 and CISA rates it as a high severity vulnerability at 8.1 on CVSS v3.1.

Red Hat rates its own RHEL 9 and 10 builds Important rather than Critical. Those builds allocate each HTTP/2 stream from "a separate allocator, which substantially increases the complexity of exploiting the flaw."

The severity and prioritization of this vulnerability in an organization’s environment depends first on whether HTTP/2 is on.

The version number alone won’t confirm exposure, check these additional factors:

Distribution packages: Vendors often backport fixes without changing the upstream version, so check your vendor's advisory and not only httpd -v or apache2 -v.

As of November 13, fixes are out for Debian 12 and 13 (2.4.71-1~deb12u1 and 2.4.71-1~deb13u1), Ubuntu 22.04 through 26.10, Alpine, Fedora, Amazon Linux 2 and 2023, and Wolfi and Chainguard.

SUSE, openSUSE, Photon OS, and several RHEL rebuilds were still waiting on vendor fixes.

Downstream products: Vendors that repackage httpd, such as Red Hat JBoss Core Services (jbcs-httpd24-mod_http2) and Red Hat Hardened Images, may be listed as affected on version number alone. Whether you are exposed depends on what the product ships. Check that mod_http2 is actually present and loaded. For example, Sysdig’s scan of the Red Hat Hardened Images httpd image shows it listed as affected, but the image has no mod_http2, so the risk can be accepted. Check the vendor’s advisory for fix status.

Recent upgrades: Servers upgraded to 2.4.67 for the HTTP/2 flaw in May, CVE-2026-23918, are still inside this CVE's affected range.

How the HTTPd RCE flaw works

HTTP/2 carries many requests over one connection as parallel streams and that concurrency is where this flaw lies.

The Apache advisory calls the flaw "Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization" in assign_headers(), and the CVE record lists CWE-362. Red Hat lists CWE-20 instead. Red Hat describes the root cause as "a worker thread writes into memory owned by the connection thread through a shared, lock-free allocator." In practice, two threads can corrupt the same heap.

The fix is a one-line change in assign_headers(). Before the fix, a request with a content type that had already ended had its zero Content-Length header written into the HTTP/2 request's own header table (req->headers). The fix writes it into the per-request table (r->headers_in) instead. The commit message gives no explanation. Red Hat's statement supplies the threading context.

What is reachable

Exposure depends on configuration. Red Hat states that only servers with HTTP/2 enabled through the Protocols directive are affected:

Path

Does it reach the vulnerable code?

Details

Protocols includes h2

Yes

HTTP/2 over TLS.

Protocols includes h2c

Yes

HTTP/2 over cleartext TCP. The public PoC targets this.

Protocols set in a virtual host

HTTP/1.1 only

According to RedHat, servers serving only HTTP/1.1 are not affected.

Red Hat's Bugzilla entry says an unauthenticated attacker triggers the flaw "by sending specially crafted HTTP/2 frames." That puts internet-facing, HTTP/2-enabled httpd in the first patch tier. This table does not cover reverse proxies in front of httpd.

HTTPd RCE exploitation: What's been demonstrated vs. claimed

According to Red Hat’s CVE page, public research has shown "a reliable exploit against a default-configured server." However, without a researcher name or links to details, this can’t be verified. As of the publishing of this blog, no other security researchers or vendors have confirmed exploitation.

As of about 16:00 UTC on November 12, a GitHub search for the CVE returned four repositories: a proof of concept, a patch-status tracker, and two detection or assessment tools.

The PoC reports heap corruption, not code execution. Its README describes the impact as "Heap corruption in an httpd child process; potential remote code execution."

Its evidence comes from a lab build:

Setup: httpd 2.4.70 built from upstream source on a debian:bookworm container, running the prefork MPM with Protocols h2c http/1.1.

Results: The PoC sent 6,080 requests. AddressSanitizer reported five crashes, including a heap use-after-free allocated in assign_headers(). ThreadSanitizer reported 31 allocator races.

Fixed build: A 2.4.71 build showed none.

Trigger: A request that ends without a body and carries a Content-Type but no Content-Length triggers the bug. The fix commit changes exactly that code path.

The README doesn't show control of the corrupted memory, and the author has published no exploit.

The bottom line is that unauthenticated HTTP/2 traffic can crash and corrupt the heap of a vulnerable httpd. Remote code execution is possible, but nobody has publicly demonstrated it yet. Treat the crash as likely wherever HTTP/2 is on, and code execution as a credible risk.

HTTPd RCE impact

Nothing publicly disclosed as of November 13, 2026, shows in-the-wild exploitation, a mass-scanning campaign, or a public RCE exploit. The primary sources do establish the following:

Risk of unauthenticated RCE: Red Hat says a remote attacker who can reach the server could execute arbitrary commands with no authentication. Bugzilla adds that commands run as the httpd process.

Worker crashes: The public PoC crashes httpd child processes on a vulnerable build.

Long-lived exposure: The affected range starts at 2.4.55, so servers patched for earlier HTTP/2 bugs can still be exposed.

Paths with no fix yet: Standalone mod_h2 has no fixed release. Several distributions, including SUSE, openSUSE, Photon OS, and CentOS Stream 10, were still waiting on vendor fixes as of November 13.
