Runtime detection

The Sysdig TRT simulated a successful exploit inside a vulnerable Apache server, both inside a container and as a host service. Existing runtime threat detections caught every step without rule modifications, including:

Failed exploit attempts that crash web server workers

Commands or a shell started by the web server, including reverse shells

Tools downloaded and run by the web server

The web server process replaced by attacker code

A successful attack would give the attacker code execution as the httpd worker. From there, attackers do what they do after any web server RCE: open a reverse shell, download and run a tool, start a miner, steal cloud credentials, or try a kernel local privilege escalation.

Detecting HTTPd RCE with open source Falco

Falco sees syscalls, not HTTP/2 frames. It cannot see the malicious request itself, but it can see what the request causes on the host. That includes a shell or unexpected binary spawned by an httpd process, an unexpected outbound connection, or a write to a sensitive path.

Web servers fork helpers legitimately, so rules scoped to httpd need tuning to stay quiet. The post-exploitation strategies above apply.

Recommendations

Patch

Update httpd on every server: Move to 2.4.71, or to your vendor's patched package. On RHEL 9 that is mod_http2-2.0.26-7.el9_9.1, on RHEL 10 mod_http2-2.0.29-5.el10_3.1, and on Debian trixie apache2 2.4.71-1~deb13u1. Patching is the only complete fix.

Restart httpd and rebuild images after you patch: A running server keeps the old module loaded. Verify the package version inside the running workload.

Replace standalone mod_h2: The project is archived, and its latest release, 2.0.42, is affected.

Interim mitigations if you cannot patch today

Disable HTTP/2: Apache's advisory and oss-security notice give no workaround. Wiz recommends removing h2 and h2c so the setting reads Protocols http/1.1. That is Wiz's guidance, not Apache's. It matches Red Hat's statement that HTTP/1.1-only servers are not affected.

Apply the change server-wide and in every virtual host.

Restart or reload httpd so the change takes effect.

Test latency-sensitive services first. Clients fall back to HTTP/1.1, which can slow multiplexed workloads.

Contain the blast radius

Run httpd workers as an unprivileged user: Limit what a compromised worker can read and write.

Keep secrets out of the server's reach: Use a secrets manager, not environment variables or files the worker can read.

Investigate and audit

Audit your environment: Find every host and workload running httpd 2.4.55–2.4.70 or mod_h2 2.0.8–2.0.42 with HTTP/2 enabled, internet-facing first. Sysdig Secure customers can use the Threat Intelligence entry and Vulnerability Management findings.

Watch for crashing httpd children: Repeated child-process segfaults on an HTTP/2-enabled server match what the public PoC produces.

Review httpd process activity: Look for shells, downloads or outbound connections from httpd workers since public disclosure on November 11.

Enable default runtime policies: Sysdig’s runtime detections will catch exploitation, even when a vulnerability scan has no findings yet.

Conclusion

CVE-2026-119618 is a threading bug in httpd's HTTP/2 module, not a flaw in the applications httpd serves. Heap corruption and crashes are public. Code execution is claimed but not yet publicly shown, but that gap is why reachability should drive patch prioritization. Defenders should start with HTTP/2-enabled, public-facing servers.

The timelines are still important to note for security teams. Two teams reported the bug independently, eight days apart. One “team" was an automated, model-driven scanner, while the other was a human team. By November 12, a day after disclosure, a public PoC that corrupts the heap was on GitHub. The window between “advisory published” and “working exploit” is small, and organizations need to be prepared to respond quickly to these notifications.

In this case, the best course of action is to patch first. Until every server is patched and restarted, disable HTTP/2 where you can and use runtime detection to close the gap. A runtime sensor will not see the heap corruption, but it will catch what a successful exploit does next.

Title: Capabilities and vulnerabilities of the Muse AI agent | Kaspersky official blog
Context: Around the same time, a researcher found a vulnerability that let an attacker take control of Muse and act on the owner’s behalf
Full Text:
That’s how the Odyssey might have opened if it were about Muse, Meta’s new AI agent. For now, the agent is available only as an iOS, Android, or macOS app and on the web. Even so, it’s already caught on: according to Meta’s official figures, Muse had been downloaded more than 10 million times by October 21.

The agent can do a lot: read your conversations and calendars, remind you about meetings and tasks, reply to messages and emails, track your spending, make purchases, search the web, generate content, and much, much more. In short, a full-blown concierge service for the chronically busy. Muse’s creators have admitted they drew heavily on the headline-grabbing AI agent OpenClaw, which researchers coincidentally found full of serious security holes.

But soon after launch, the bad news about Muse started piling up. First, a journalist discovered that the agent had gotten into his conversations without explicit permission. Around the same time, a researcher found a vulnerability that let an attacker take control of Muse and act on the owner’s behalf. And then it turned out that the calls the AI was supposedly making were actually being handed off to… human operators.

We look at how all this could happen, and how to use Muse as safely as possible.

When the agent reads more than it should

Journalist Jason Aten installed Muse on his iPhone and Mac, and deliberately didn’t give the agent access to the Messages app. Yet after he exchanged messages with a colleague about the new iPhones, Muse unexpectedly offered to draft a column on that very topic, citing his editor’s message about the deadline. Aten immediately asked the agent how it had acquired that information.

Muse’s explanation was that the Mac app had merely been passing it the text of notification pop-ups, which sounded quite plausible at first glance. But then Aten discovered that Muse had been syncing data directly from the local message database on his Mac. The sync had reached row 187 462 of the database. That number alone doesn’t reveal exactly how many messages were processed, but this was clearly far more than a few notifications.

According to a Meta employee, Muse could read conversations only if the user had separately allowed access to Messages and given the app Full Disk Access. How the agent managed to read the conversations without explicit permission remains unclear. The likely culprit was an opaque permissions interface.

Zero-day vulnerability in Muse

Just as the message-snooping scandal broke, researcher Patrick Wardle found a serious vulnerability in Muse tied to how the app stores and uses its internal settings.

Muse keeps several of these settings locally, and some of them could be changed with hardly any restrictions. One of these settings determines which server receives your voice input for speech recognition. Normally, these requests go to a Meta server, but Wardle found that almost any local app or Terminal command could change the address.

In practice, an attacker could do this in one of two ways: infect the victim’s device with malware, or talk the victim into pasting a specially crafted command into Terminal under the guise of “helpful instructions”. These dangerous instructions are often spread through fake websites or infected browser extensions that alter the content of the web pages people view.

Once the Meta server in the settings had been swapped for the attacker’s, Muse’s voice requests went there instead. Along with those requests, the attacker received an authorization token, which let them impersonate the account owner and control the agent remotely. If the user had already given Muse access to their camera, messages, files, and other data, the attacker could use all that for their own ends: take photos with the camera, write malicious files to disk, read conversations, locate linked devices, and much, much more.

Once in control of Muse, an attacker can use the same features as the agent itself: take pictures with the front camera, view photos, read files and modify or delete them, show notifications… All told, the researcher counted more than 50 such commands. Source

What’s more, the attacker could route Muse’s voice traffic through their server, and quietly slip their own instructions in with the victim’s voice commands. They would pick up the Muse token along the way, so after the first successful attack they could keep their access to the agent and go on controlling it remotely. Meta has already released an update that fixes the vulnerability, but stories like this are far from rare in the AI world.

Meatbags to the rescue

Muse has an experimental feature that calls U.S. businesses on the user’s behalf: the agent can phone a company itself, ask for the details it needs, and then show a transcript of the call. But as Reuters and 404 Media discovered, Meta had also been testing a curious add-on to this feature with its own employees: handing the calls off to trained call-center operators. Fully automated calls weren’t getting the job done: people on the other end simply hung up as soon as they heard a robotic voice. Meanwhile, many Meta employees had no idea their requests were being handed off to real people.

After a barrage of criticism, Meta shut down the human operator experiment. Company representatives said it had been a mistake to run the experiment without warning and promised to improve the feature.

Protecting your privacy: which Muse settings to check

Meta really does process a huge amount of data when people use Muse: conversations with the chatbot, photos, metadata, uploaded and generated files… This also includes information from any third-party apps you’ve connected to the agent. Meta employees can access this data on an as-needed basis.

We recommend checking the following settings and turning off any features you don’t need:

System permissions on Mac

Full Disk Access: full access to the disk and files on the computer.

Automation: lets the agent take actions in local apps, such as sending messages or deleting notes.

Notifications: lets the agent notify you when it finishes a task.

You can separately restrict access to apps that store their data on your Mac itself rather than in the cloud. Muse offers three modes for each app:

Off: the agent can neither read data nor take actions.

Read only: the agent can only read information, at your request.

Read and interact: the agent can read information and take actions in the app.

Action confirmation

By default, Muse is supposed to ask you for permission before taking important actions in third-party apps. Still, relying on an AI’s judgment for, say, shopping or conversations with coworkers is hardly a good idea, so it’s best to limit its autonomy ahead of time. In Muse, go to Settings → Permissions → Connectors, and choose either Ask for some actions (the less secure option), or Always ask. In Manage permissions, review any permissions you’ve already granted under Connectors.

Meta notes that if you use a single account, Muse connects to Facebook, Instagram, and Threads automatically, and that unlinking them cuts off access but doesn’t delete the data already collected; you have to delete it manually.

Website access

You can set up Muse’s internet access in much the same way:

Go to Settings→ Permissions → Web access defaults.

Choose Ask for some actions to have Muse ask for permission before sharing your data or opening an unfamiliar site, or Always ask to have the agent ask before visiting any site at all.

We recommend choosing Always ask and using anti-phishing protection: there’s always a chance the agent will mistakenly decide to open a fake or suspicious site.

Training on your data

Meta claims that the user data used to train Muse is anonymized and stored without being linked to an account. Unfortunately, that doesn’t mean you can’t be identified from context: the emails, messages, documents, and calendars the agent works with contain names, email addresses, home addresses, and other details that give away your identity.

Meta also says it removes certain categories of personal identifiers before training the model. But the more information goes into training, the higher the risk that one day it will surface by accident in someone else’s conversation, or become public because of a bug. Sadly, even internal safety filters sometimes fail.

And, naturally, training is on by default. To turn off training, go to Settings → Data controls → Help improve our AI models and select Turn off.

Permissions on mobile devices

On mobile devices, we recommend reviewing the permissions you’ve given the Muse app. In your phone’s settings, limit its access to your contacts, photos, location, microphone, and camera. Also turn off AI training on your data.

On iPhone, open Settings → Privacy & Security, and check which categories Muse can access. On Android, check Settings → Apps → Muse → Permissions. You can turn off training separately in Muse → Settings → Data controls.

How to use AI agents safely

Revoke permissions you don’t need, and don’t share sensitive data with the agent. The less information the agent can access, the less you risk if there’s a leak or a bug.

Don’t delegate important decisions or actions to agents. Even if the agent asks you to confirm before it buys something or sends a message, check exactly what it’s about to do, and where. Otherwise, you might end up paying for a purchase of non-existing goods or services on a fake website. Muse’s creators themselves write that the agent isn’t fully protected against prompt injections — hidden malicious commands aimed at AI.

Don’t run Terminal commands you don’t understand — especially if a website, email, or pop-up claims they’re needed for a “security check” or to “install an update”. That’s exactly how the ClickFix attacks work: they trick users into running a malicious command themselves. To protect yourself from malware and fake websites, install a comprehensive security solution on your devices.

Keep the app that runs the agent up to date. The developers have fixed the vulnerability Patrick Wardle found, but security problems in AI turn up all the time.

Title: Microsoft Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 enter their 'permanently vulnerable' era
Context: Microsoft stated: "Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 are no longer tested for vulnerabilities and there are no updates released
Full Text: Microsoft has warned customers still clinging to Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 to consider the software "permanently vulnerable" as November's security fixes arrive for Subscription Edition (SE) alone. The warning appears in the release documentation for November's Exchange Server SE security update. Looking for Exchange 2016 and 2019 information? Tough. Microsoft stated: "Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 are no longer tested for vulnerabilities and there are no updates released. If you are using those versions of Exchange, you should consider them permanently vulnerable [Microsoft's emphasis] and should upgrade your organization immediately." You have been warned. Support for Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 ended on October 14, 2025, but the company announced an Extended Security Updates (ESU) program in July 2025. The plan was that this program would end on April 14, 2026, by which time customers would surely have made the jump to a later or online version, right? The company said: "This period will not be extended past April 2026 (you do not need to ask)." And... of course it was. As April 2026 rolled around, and it became clear that some customers were still stubbornly sticking with the old versions, Microsoft did the equivalent of heaving an exasperated sigh and offered another six months of paid security updates. Those final weeks also brought a separate treat: a Windows Server update breaking Exchange Server. This time it was serious. Microsoft released the final Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 security updates on October 13. No more patches, no more vulnerability testing, and apparently no more reprieves. According to Microsoft's Security Update Guide, the November update fixed nine vulnerabilities in Exchange Server SE, including a critical remote code execution flaw, CVE-2026-118207. Microsoft isn't testing earlier versions of Exchange for the vulnerabilities. ®

Context: TSGA and TSProxy are modified variants of PhiliKit, a malware framework previously documented in attacks exploiting Ivanti vulnerabilities
Full Text:
Key findings

Beginning on 30 October 2026, an attacker executed scanning and exploitation activity against organizations with unpatched Check Point Security Gateways, using Mobile Access portals with PHP2Shell as initial access followed by CVE-2026-123039.

The first wave, on October 30, targeted Israeli organizations and included destructive activity against some of them. A broader second wave on November 2 targeted organizations across multiple countries and sectors, with no evidence of destructive activity

In the investigated intrusion, PHP2Shell provided initial access, followed by privilege escalation through the DynamicCLI interface, tracked as CVE-2026-123039. The attackers then deployed PHP webshells, the persistent TSGA backdoor and its embedded TSProxy networking component.

The attackers pivoted from the gateway to a VMware ESXi host over SSH, deployed the destroy_v6 wiper, and left politically themed DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt notes during the destructive stage.

TSGA and TSProxy are modified variants of PhiliKit, a malware framework previously documented in attacks exploiting Ivanti vulnerabilities. Both tools share distinctive code, configuration, and cryptographic material with the framework

Although ESET associated PhiliKit with China nexus UNC5221, the evidence does not allow us to assess with high confidence the true nature of this operation. Several scenarios remain plausible: the identified actor ran the entire campaign, acted solely as an initial access broker, or took part in a false-flag operation. It is also possible that the destructive activity served as a smoke screen.

The note left during the destructive activity uses the Dream Security brand. Dream had recently published research on PHP2Shell exploitation of Palo Alto Networks devices by China nexus actors. While this timing raises the possibility of retaliation, the available evidence does not establish a clear motive.

Introduction

We have now confirmed that, in late October 2026, approximately one week after a security fix became available, activity originating from 130.94.19[.]204 targeted Israeli organizations through vulnerable Mobile Access portals on Check Point Security Gateways. Evidence suggested some cases of a successful compromise, with exploitation activity consistent with PHP2Shell, associated with CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.

Following initial access, the attacker escalated privileges from the portal service account to root by exploiting CVE-2026-123039, a local privilege-escalation vulnerability in the DynamicCLI IPC interface. The attacker then used privileged command execution to deploy PHP webshells and establish persistence.

A second scanning wave on November 2nd targeted some Israeli organizations previously targeted during the first wave, alongside additional organizations worldwide, with no apparent focus on Israel. Neither wave showed a clear sector preference, suggesting opportunistic initial-access attempts rather than sector-specific targeting.

Infection Flow

On October 30, 2026, the first signs of exploitation appeared on the targeted Check Point Mobile Access gateways. PHP session artifacts were created under /opt/CPcvpn-R81.20/tmp/, including session files containing the upload_progress_pwn marker associated with the exploitation activity. During the same window, the portal’s Apache/PHP workers experienced hundreds of segmentation faults, providing additional evidence of repeated exploitation attempts against the service.

Figure 1 – Infection chain

After gaining access to the Mobile Access portal, the attackers escalated privileges to root by exploiting CVE-2026-123039, a local privilege-escalation vulnerability in the DynamicCLI interface. With privileged command execution, the attackers placed PHP webshells in <templates>, a directory used by the Mobile Access portal to construct its login pages. These webshells provide a way to send commands through the web portal, establishing a stronger foothold within the compromised environment.

printf <base64 Webshell> | base64 -d > <templates>/zz<random>.tpl

The attacker used multiple .tpl files with names matching the pattern zz*.tpl Each initially received a small command-execution shell, which was then replaced with a more capable version. The expanded shell requires the hardcoded key zz2026 and supports operating-system commands, PHP code execution, and file uploads. Uploaded files are saved to the fixed path /tmp/.up.tpl. The attackers subsequently issued commands to copy that file into the portal’s directory as challenge_render.tpl.

The attackers then moved from web-based access to a standalone passive backdoor, launching the TSGA malware (/tmp/CPconfigdaemon) in the background and redirecting its output to a hidden temporary log:

nohup /tmp/CPconfigdaemon >/tmp/.bd.log 2>&1 & printf started

When executed as root, the malware relocates itself and relaunches under the name slot_CPconfigdaemon in the boot persistence directory. The executable also carries a second component, TSProxy: an embedded shared library that it writes to /lib/libcpfwcommon.so. Its injection code loads this library into selected appliance processes, where it intercepts networking functions to handle specially marked attacker connections while allowing ordinary traffic to continue. This combines a persistent standalone backdoor with concealed access through existing appliance services.

The attackers then deployed the gogo scanner on the gateway to discover internal assets and services across the network and continued to move laterally to a VMware ESXi host over SSH, authenticating with the vpxuser service account. On the ESXi host, they staged the destroy_v6 wiper to /tmp/des wiper and executed it. Finally, the attackers left a note that accompanied the destructive activity named DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt.

Figure 2 – Destructive activity note

Technical Analysis

Webshells

The expanded PHP webshell requires a hardcoded key to access its command-execution, PHP-evaluation, and file-upload functions. It supports both plain-text and Base64-encoded, XOR-obfuscated commands, and saves uploaded files to /tmp/.up.tpl.

Figure 3 – Webshell code

Wiper

The Linux ELF wiper destroy_v6 accepts a target directory as a command-line argument. The optional -f flag enables fast deletion, while -w specifies a pipe-separated list of directories to exclude. The wiper recursively traverses the target directory, deleting files regardless of extension and skipping excluded subtrees. By default, it attempts to overwrite files with zeros before deleting them, fast mode skips the overwrite step. It also writes DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt to each processed directory. This politically themed note includes a timestamp and explicitly rejects ransom negotiations.

TSGA – slot_CPconfigdaemon

The TSGA implant, deployed as slot_CPconfigdaemon, is a Linux gateway implant with substantial Check Point-specific functionality. It provides encrypted remote access, configuration theft, backup and snapshot persistence, process injection, and binary firewall-log tampering.

TSProxy

TSProxy is a Linux shared-library backdoor embedded in TSGA and dropped as /lib/libcpfwcommon.so and supports encrypted SOCKS-style proxying.

Tools relationship

Both TSGA and TSProxy are Check Point-specific components linked to the previously reported PhiliKit-associated toolset. PhiliKit is a passive backdoor and installer targeting Ivanti VPN appliances and was previously reported following the February 25, 2026 upload of a sample named philistine to VirusTotal.

TSGA and the PhiliKit implant have roots in Tiny SHell, and share a core set of remote-control capabilities. Both implement authenticated, encrypted communications through TCP port 11072 and the Unix socket /tmp/.p_sock. The analyzed PhiliKit build restricts its TCP listener to loopback, whereas TSGA listens on all IPv4 interfaces. Both provide interactive shells with pseudo-terminal allocation, configurable terminal dimensions and bidirectional input/output. Operators can execute arbitrary shell commands and Python or Perl scripts, retrieve their output, transfer files using operator-selected paths, and collect selected or full appliance configurations over the encrypted channel.

TSProxy shares distinctive configuration with libdssafe.so, the networking component embedded in PhiliKit package: identical operator credentials, transport secrets, three matching activation-selector digests, and the same TLS certificate and private key. These overlaps strongly support a shared tooling lineage.

Attribution

The implants delivered to the gateway, TSGA and TSProxy are part of the PhiliKit malware family, which has been associated with the China-nexus group UNC5221 and previous exploitation of Ivanti appliances. In addition, gogo scanner has also been reported in connection with Chinese-nexus threat actors exploiting Ivanti vulnerabilities.

The infrastructure IP addresses used by the attacker were hosted on LightNode VPS infrastructure, a service previously associated with activity by Chinese- nexus threat actors.

The scanning activity was concentrated between 00:00 and 09:00 UTC, corresponding to 08:00–17:00 in China and broadly aligning with typical Chinese working hours.

With all the above, the following attributes that appeared in the described campaign do not appear to fully align with known Chinese-nexus groups (and specifically UNC5221) motives and interests:

Destructive operation

Focus on Israel and wiper note in Hebrew referring to the Israeli-Palestine conflict

Philikit name derived from the malware internal name philistine

Taken together, the evidence does not allow us to assess with high confidence the true nature of this operation. Several scenarios remain plausible: the identified actor ran the entire campaign, acted solely as an initial access broker, or took part in a false-flag operation. It is also possible that the destructive activity served as a smoke screen.

Title: Hackers exploiting ScreenConnect plugin flaw to spread malware across hundreds of PCs
Context: Huntress spotted the attacks at around 1747 UTC, when someone began using ScreenConnect's remote command feature to install rogue clients on machines managed by multiple IT...
Full Text: Hackers have used a dodgy third-party ScreenConnect extension to push malware onto at least 288 machines across 48 organizations, prompting ConnectWise to disable a handful of plugins in hundreds of customer environments. Security outfit Huntress first raised the alarm in a Reddit post on Wednesday, warning of an active campaign targeting cloud-hosted ScreenConnect instances. At the time, its security operations center was tracking six compromised managed service providers (MSPs) and more than 286 affected endpoints, with the numbers still climbing. ConnectWise acquired popular remote supporttool ScreenConnect in February, 2015. Huntress spotted the attacks at around 1747 UTC, when someone began using ScreenConnect's remote command feature to install rogue clients on machines managed by multiple IT service providers. All 288 endpoints were hit within 90 minutes, with roughly a third compromised in the first ten minutes. Huntress suspects more MSPs may have been compromised, as the attackers appeared to be numbering their victims sequentially, with the numbers suggesting earlier attacks that it hadn't detected. The attackers deployed a 16-file malware toolkit dubbed SCKit, which installs a separate ScreenConnect client to maintain remote access even if the legitimate connection is shut down. It also contains code designed to spread the infection to IT technicians and potentially other customers under their control. Huntress has since traced the activity to a possible authentication weakness in RMM+, a third-party extension that lets other management tools issue commands through ScreenConnect without technicians using its console. Versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 of the extension contain a flaw that means installations without a configured access key will accept a blank one. Because RMM+ operates independently of ScreenConnect's normal user accounts and authentication controls, an attacker could potentially execute commands without defeating MFA. Huntress said the findings matched what its investigators saw during the attacks, with commands reaching machines across several ScreenConnect installations despite no corresponding login activity. The researchers also confirmed that the attacks affected ScreenConnect versions 26.6.6.9747 and 26.7.6.9783, meaning administrators running the latest releases weren't necessarily safe. ConnectWise has acknowledged that third-party extensions may have been involved but has stopped short of confirming how the attackers initially gained access. In a security advisory, the company said it was investigating unauthorized access to certain partner environments and had identified approximately 400 installations containing at least one extension from the RMM+ family. It has disabled five extensions, including RMM+, RMM Plus, and Labtech Plus, wherever it can do so remotely, and urged customers running their own ScreenConnect servers to follow suit. ConnectWise stressed that the 400 environments were identified because they had the extensions installed, not because they were necessarily compromised. The company said: "At this time, we have found no evidence of a compromise of ConnectWise infrastructure or a vulnerability in ScreenConnect itself." There's another nasty trick buried in SCKit. According to Huntress, the malware is designed to turn an infected computer into a trap for the technician sent to investigate it. If the technician connects through ScreenConnect, the toolkit attempts to transfer malware back to their workstation, steal authentication cookies, and use their access to infect other machines. That could give attackers a route from one compromised customer into others managed by the same IT provider. However, Huntress says it has yet to see that part of the attack succeed. "We have not observed that method to spread work successfully. The console-takeover attempt failed in every recovered host log we have checked so far," the researchers wrote. Huntress also suspects that some of the malware's C# code was generated using an LLM, pointing to unusually detailed comments explaining what the code is supposed to do. Apparently, even malware authors appreciate a little help with their homework. Both Huntress and ConnectWise are urging administrators not to investigate suspected infections by remotely connecting through ScreenConnect, since doing so could put the technician's own machine at risk. Administrators are being advised to use other security tools to investigate affected machines, look for rogue ScreenConnect clients, and check what commands have been run. Any malware left behind will also need to be removed before the machines are brought back online. Huntress warned on Reddit that some machines were becoming reinfected within minutes of being taken out of isolation because the malware had not been properly removed. Simply disabling the vulnerable extensions won't necessarily undo the damage, either. As ConnectWise warns, "Disabling extensions and resetting credentials alone may not remove unauthorized software, persistence mechanisms, or access already established on endpoints." And with the attackers already able to install their own remote access software, kicking them out could prove considerably harder than closing the door they came through. ®

General Recommendations

As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. Terms of Use

The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use.

Recommended Practices

CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.

Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet.

Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.

When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.

CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.

CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies.

CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets.

Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies.

Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.

Summary

On October 21, 2026, the PHP project and security researchers disclosed two critical, unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerabilities in the core PHP language runtime known as "php2shell" (tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619). This advisory covers the status of impact of various Siemens software products. As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines, and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Siemens is actively monitoring the situation and assessing the implications of these vulnerabilities on our portfolio. Because this evaluation is ongoing, our findings are subject to change as new technical details and vendor updates emerge. We will publish updated findings, guidance, and remediation recommendations as soon as they become available. Siemens has released new versions for several affected products and recommends to update to the latest versions. Siemens is preparing further fixes and recommends mitigations for products where fixes are not or not yet available.

Title: Security Teams Must Shift from Patching to Mitigation in the AI Era
Context: This shift was demonstrated by the speed at which attackers exploited the recent PHP2Shell vulnerability following its disclosure in October 2026
Full Text:
Organizations “can’t patch their way out of AI” and should instead focus on mitigation post exploitation, according to Dick O’Brien, principal intelligence analyst at Symantec.

Speaking at the IRISSCON 2026 conference in Dublin, Ireland, on November 11, he highlighted the rapid closure of the patch window in the past year due to attackers’ use of AI.

This includes AI tools to discover zero day flaws and the ability of frontier models to chain together low severity vulnerabilities together to find an exploit path in a way that humans would not be able to do.

The Zero Day Clock, a live dashboard that tracks the collapse of the time-to-exploit (TTE) window from CVE disclosure to confirmed exploitation in the wild, has estimated that the average time to exploitation following public disclosure of a vulnerability fell from one week in 2025 to one day in 2026. The initiative estimates that in 2027, the average time will be a minute.

“Once you get to a minute, what can you do realistically? We need to start thinking beyond patching to address vulnerabilities,” O’Brien said.

This shift was demonstrated by the speed at which attackers exploited the recent PHP2Shell vulnerability following its disclosure in October 2026. O’Brien noted that the first reporting exploitation attempts occurred just 19 minutes after the bug was made public.

Amazon also reported that it detected an attempted exploitation attempt of PHP2Shell four days before the vulnerabilities were published.

Agentic AI Orchestration of Attacks

Post-initial access, O’Brien expects threat actors to move to an era of “end-to-end agentic orchestration of attacks” in the next year, shifting away from using AI as an assistant for various tasks towards AI agents undertaking attacks independently.

This will make it significantly harder for defenders to detect and respond to threats in their organization’s environments.

There have been a few examples of this approach taking place so far. One of these was an attack on the Dutch Institute of Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD) in September 2026, where AI agents executed the post-compromise tasks independently, operating at machine speed.

According to an analysis by Symantec of the DIVD’s assessment report, it took 19 minutes for the attack to be detected, but 19 hours before the response began, and a further nine hours to contain the threat.

“This is what we’re dealing with. It’s an excess of 24 hours and you know you’re not going to be able to compete with something operating at machine speed,” O’Brien commented.

Adopt an Assume Exploit Mindset

In this landscape, organizations should assume exploitation is inevitable and prepare for machine-speed post-compromise activity, where attackers can move from initial access to impact in minutes rather than days.

“Stop measuring your mean time to patch and start measuring your mean time to mitigate. Assume an exploit is going to happen and the plan your preparedness for that,” O’Brien advised.

He set out a number of mitigation tasks security teams can immediately focus on:

Behavior blocking

Default-deny for what runs

Least privilege for every agent and token

Inspect data before it leaves the device

Bind every agent action to a named human

“These are all things you can start doing right now before you become aware of a vulnerability,” O’Brien added.

Longer-term, organizations must integrate detection and protection technologies on multiple different control points, which are able to identify behavioral anomalies of rogue or malicious AI agents.

Title: N-able Takes N-central Platform Offline After Discovery of 33 Flaws
Context: Indeed, with public exploit code available, attackers already are scanning for vulnerable systems, although no exploitation has yet been observed, N-able reported in a security...
Full Text:
N-able is navigating a hectic crisis-management situation after the discovery of more than 30 alleged zero-day flaws in its N-central remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform, as well as the disclosure of exploits allowing attackers to execute commands, create administrator accounts, and escalate privileges to root.

Realizing the critical security nature of the situation, N-able took its hosted N-central environments offline earlier this week across the Americas, Europe, and Asia-Pacific after offensive security researcher Sean Bales on Sunday publicly revealed the flaws, collectively called Able2Shell, and subsequently published a series of exploits for them on the GitHub account "Oracle-Security." N-able also advised customers operating on-premises servers to shut them down until further notice.

"N-able sincerely appreciates the patience, flexibility, and partnership our customers have demonstrated throughout this critical security event," the company wrote in a security update Wednesday.

Related:Attackers Crash Claude's 'Office Party' Flaw to Run Malicious Code on Linux

The extraordinary scenario has major repercussions for the entire endpoint management industry, including managed service providers (MSPs) and IT managers that broadly use N-central to monitor, manage, and secure customer devices and networks remotely. The risk for users of vulnerable platforms is significant because of the "extraordinary privileges" these RMM platforms have "because they need them to do their jobs," observes Gene Moody, field chief technology officer (CTO) for autonomous endpoint management provider Action 1.

N-able and other RMM platforms can engage in critical tasks such as script execution, software deployment, and remote administration, often across many thousands of endpoints, Moody says. The downside? "That also makes them incredibly attractive targets," he says.

Indeed, with public exploit code available, attackers already are scanning for vulnerable systems, although no exploitation has yet been observed, N-able reported in a security update Wednesday. The company moved fast to remedy some of the most critical flaws, releasing N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 (build 2026.4.1.26) on Tuesday to address seven CVEs associated with them; the company says it also plans to release further security updates.

Multiple Zero-Day Security Bugs in N-able

Flaws covered by the N-able hotfix are tracked as the following: CVE-2026-125883, which covers multiple XXE vulnerabilities; CVE-2026-125878, which covers multiple OGNL Injection vulnerabilities; CVE-2026-125879, a local privilege escalation flaw; CVE-2026-125880, described as stored XSS via MMS3 patch metadata; and CVE-2026-125881, a schema validation flaw.

Related:Google, Partners Disrupt 1.3 Million-Device-Strong XCPE Botnet

The patch also addresses CVE-2026-125882, which enables remote code execution (RCE) via file repository upload path traversal and was discovered by Nate Fair of Sprocket Security; and CVE-2026-91000, which leads to local privilege escalation via insecure IPC Channels.

Though Bales disclosed 33 separate flaws, some of them are steps in longer exploit chains built from other entries on the same list, according to a report from Tenable's Research Special Operations published today. All in all, Bales listed four exploit chains, with the XXE chain emerging as potentially the most significant of the issues, according to Tenable.

"The researcher describes the XXE chain as credential-free, and N-able's record for CVE-2026-125883 lists no privileges and no user interaction as required," the Tenable team wrote. That chain exploits an unauthenticated XXE flaw in N-central's service-import functionality and can ultimately turn an unauthenticated network request into a complete compromise of a central IT management system.

Indeed, the CyberSec Guru called the credential-free XXE exploit the "centerpiece of the release" and went into detail about how it can be exploited to create an attacker entry point into a system in a blog post updated Tuesday.

Related:'Aokigahara' Stealer Targets 'Developer Keyrings' & AI Assistants

Moreover, once an attacker has compromised a platform, the other vulnerabilities can help expand their access to take over privileged internal sessions and ultimately execute commands on the underlying server, paving the way for cross-customer compromise, according to the post. This scenario is especially concerning for MSPs managing infrastructure on behalf of many organizations.

N-Central at Risk Again for Cyberattack

The recently disclosed flaws are not N-central's first time dealing with a significant security incident. In August 2025, CISA added two N-central vulnerabilities, CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog after they were exploited in the wild.

More recently, in August 2026, attackers exploited an authentication-bypass flaw (CVE-2026-18556), subsequently finding a way around N-able's initial fix through a related vulnerability, CVE-2026-18577. The second incident allowed attackers to gain administrative access to vulnerable N-central servers and use the platform's Take Control feature to access managed systems.

The recurrence of vulnerabilities in the same management platform raises broader questions about the security of RMM infrastructure, particularly given the extensive access these tools provide to MSPs and their customers, Moody says.

"I see this as yet another warning in a recent wave of attacks on these platforms; how much authority endpoint management platforms concentrate," he says. "They are essential, but MFA and role-based access cannot contain every platform compromise."

N-able Cyber-Risk Is a Ticking Time Bomb

All in all, the situation has created a significant security quagmire for N-able and its customers, who — given that exploitation of the flaws could be imminent — are advised to apply the hotfix where necessary as well as take other immediate mitigation steps.

"The clock is ticking for anyone not taking this seriously," Moody observes, advising that any affected organization "keep on-premises N-central offline until N-able provides safe restoration instructions," while preserving logs before making any changes.

Moreover, they should "review authentication and administration since at least beginning of November, just because this is exposed does not mean it was not leveraged prior to disclosure," he warns.

Researchers from Huntress also advised organizations affected to review login and authentication activity from Nov. 8 onward for unexpected or unauthorized access, according to a blog post published Monday. If they find it, they should involve incident response, as it could indicate that an attacker conducted RCE or privilege escalation on the server.

Huntress also advised organizations to examine audit logs for secondary indicators of compromise — such as anomalous remote access sessions or new scripts being deployed — since as during previous N-central exploitations, "threat actors were observed 'spraying' downstream environments with unauthorized scripts and tools."

Noting that CISA's March guidance called for least privilege, phishing-resistant MFA and second-administrator approval, Moody says he would go even further this time to protect N-able environments by keeping critical secrets and signing keys outside the platform, and making endpoints independently verify cryptographically signed approval for high-impact operations.

"Stealing a credential, or even controlling the console, should not automatically confer that authority," he says. "A login should no longer be considered enough to authorize protected operations."

Title: Critical RCE Vulnerability in Apache HTTP Server: Everything You Need To Know
Context: CVE-2026-119618 is a critical, high-severity vulnerability involving a race condition in the Apache HTTP Server, which was independently discovered by Anthropic and Google...
Full Text:
A critical synchronization vulnerability (CVE-2026-119618) has been identified in Apache HTTP Server’s HTTP/2 module (mod_http2). The flaw stems from a concurrent execution race condition within the assign_headers() function when handling shared resources. If successfully exploited, a remote, unauthenticated attacker can corrupt heap memory to achieve arbitrary code execution (RCE).

As of the time of this blog’s publication, no exploit is available and there are no reports of exploitation in the wild.

What is CVE-2026-111497?

CVE-2026-119618 is a critical, high-severity vulnerability involving a race condition in the Apache HTTP Server, which was independently discovered by Anthropic and Google Cloud’s Vulnerability Research Team.

Specifically, the flaw exists within the assign_headers() function of the HTTP/2 module (mod_http2). Due to improper synchronization when executing concurrent threads sharing resources, an attacker can trigger heap corruption. This memory corruption can ultimately be leveraged to achieve RCE on the hosting server, allowing unauthorized threat actors to execute arbitrary commands with the privileges of the web server process.

Wiz Research data: what’s the risk to cloud environments?

In cloud environments, a compromised Apache instance running containerized or virtualized workloads can serve as an entry point for lateral movement, potentially exposing adjacent microservices or cloud metadata endpoints.

According to Wiz data 64% of cloud environments have resources vulnerable to CVE-2026-119618, and 51% of cloud environments have publicly exposed instances. Note that this does not take configuration into account.

Which products are affected?

The vulnerability affects deployments utilizing HTTP/2 capabilities on the Apache HTTP Server within the version ranges outlined in the table below:

Vendor

Product

Affected Versions

Patched Versions

Apache Software Foundation

Apache HTTP Server

From 2.4.55 through 2.4.70

2.4.71 and newer

GitHub (Open Source)

mod_h2 module

From 2.0.8 through 2.0.42

2.0.24 and newer

Which actions should security teams take?

Security operations and engineering teams should execute the following remediation and mitigation steps:

1. Upgrade Deployments

Upgrade Apache HTTP Server: Update affected installations to Apache HTTP Server version 2.4.71 or later. This release addresses the race condition in assign_headers().

Update Standalone Modules: If managing standalone mod_h2 builds from GitHub, upgrade the module to a version newer than 2.0.42.

2. Implement Temporary Mitigations

If immediate patching is not possible due to operational constraints, temporarily disable HTTP/2 support to eliminate the attack vector.

Edit the configuration file (such as httpd.conf) to restrict active protocols to HTTP/1.1 by removing h2 and h2c references:

# Restrict protocols to HTTP/1.1 Protocols http/1.1

Wiz customers can use the pre-built query and advisory in the Wiz Threat Center to search for vulnerable instances in their environment.

Title: N-able Rushes Out N-central Fixes After 33 Zero-Days Go Public
Context: N-able has released a critical N-central hotfix that temporarily disables the platform's built-in remote control, after researcher Sean Bales published 33 alleged zero-days with...
Full Text:
N-able has released a critical N-central hotfix that temporarily disables the platform's built-in remote control, after researcher Sean Bales published 33 alleged zero-days with proof-of-concept (PoC) code.

N-able detailed N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2, build 2026.4.1.26, in its November 10 release notes, describing the update as a critical security release for its remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform.

The Able2Shell disclosure, published November 9, described four exploit chains that Bales said ended in code execution on an N-central server, two of them with root privileges and one he called credential-free. He said he tested the flaws on a pre-release build and that most if not all should work on earlier versions, including the current release.

Hotfix Covers Seven CVEs and Disables Remote Control

N-able took hosted N-central offline on November 9 as a precaution and told on-premises customers to keep their servers offline until they were updated.

Hotfix 2 addresses seven CVEs covering XML external entity (XXE) flaws, Object-Graph Navigation Language (OGNL) injection, privilege escalation, stored cross-site scripting, server-side request forgery and remote code execution through path traversal.

The seven records are CVE-2026-125883, CVE-2026-125878, CVE-2026-125879, CVE-2026-125880, CVE-2026-125881, CVE-2026-125882 and CVE-2026-91000. CVE-2026-125882 credits Nate Fair of Sprocket Security.

Remote control will be re-enabled in a future fix, according to the release notes, which also tell customers to update agents and probes after upgrading. N-able told Infosecurity that hosted environments have been upgraded and are back online.

N-able said the release addresses "the most critical November 9 vulnerabilities" and that a follow-up hotfix will bring further security updates.

Read more on N-central: N-able Releases Hotfix for Critical Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

N-able Disputes Disclosure as Exploitation Attempts Emerge

N-able said it was seeing scanning activity linked to the published PoC code.

Security firm WatchTowr saw exploitation attempts against its N-central honeypots overnight after the disclosure, according to an advisory updated November 10 by Beazley Security, the cybersecurity arm of insurer Beazley. The systems were decoys, not customer environments.

N-able said claims that it had ignored responsible disclosure from Bales were inaccurate, and that the vulnerabilities published on November 9 had not been disclosed through its established reporting channels.

Speaking to Infosecurity, Bales confirmed that N-able's account was accurate and that he had not disclosed any of the vulnerabilities to the company, adding that he believed the claim N-able had ignored him came from an outdated README he has since changed. He argued that publishing "makes vendors safer by forcing them to fix problems as fast as possible."

N-able president and CEO John Pagliuca took the opposite view, arguing that "publishing exploit code before customers have had the chance to act doesn't make anyone safer. It hands attackers a head start," he told Infosecurity.

Neither the release notes nor N-able's statement say how the seven CVEs map to the 33 Able2Shell issues, and PoC code for all 33 remains public.

Title: Lessons from 59 Linux Kernel Bug Reports
Context: We thank Yuan Tan of NebuSec, who also independently found this vulnerability
Full Text:
In this article

From scans to reports

Selected findings

Closing thoughts

At Microsoft’s FORGE Lab, we used codename MDASH to scan a subset of Linux kernel subsystems from late May to mid-June 2026. One full-time researcher and one intern led this three-month effort, which has so far produced 59 public upstream reports and 33 assigned CVEs. We confirmed working root privilege-escalation exploits for eight of those CVEs, and fixes for 38 of our reports have been merged into mainline.

Finding the bugs was only part of the work. The initial scans produced 26,502 raw findings in about two weeks, but turning those results into reproducible bugs, upstream reports, and patches took months of expert investigation and collaboration with Linux maintainers.

In this post, we look back at how we went from thousands of potential findings to validated vulnerabilities and upstream fixes, and what we learned about scaling vulnerability discovery with AI.

From scans to reports

We focused on several core kernel subsystems, such as networking, filesystems, and security modules. Our selection criteria were straightforward: we picked security-sensitive components with no obvious dependence on specialized hardware, making QEMU-based validation simple and unified. Code scanning mainly used Sonnet 4.6 (71.1% of code-scanning tokens), GPT-5.4 (20.1%), and GPT-5.5 (7.1%).

The codename MDASH scans produced 26,502 raw scan findings in about two weeks on two servers (64 cores/256 GB RAM and 32 cores/128 GB RAM), but turning that output into patches and reports took months of expert work. We filtered out low-confidence claims using codename MDASH’s confidence levels and separate fast screening agents we built, reducing the pool to 11,769 candidates. PoC-generating agents then attempted reproduction in QEMU, mainly using GPT-5.5 (77.3% of reproduction tokens), Opus 4.6 (13.2%), and GPT-5.5-cyber (9.4%). Experts then reviewed the 621 cases with PoC evidence to identify root causes, merge duplicates, and prepare upstream submissions.

Figure 1 . Scan-to-report workflow. 26,502 raw findings → 11,769 screened candidates → 621 PoC-backed cases → 59 upstream reports.

Where the 621 cases went

Roughly one public upstream report landed from every ten PoC-backed cases: 59 reports from 621 cases (9.5%). Across those cases, the main reasons for not filing a separate new report were:

266 (42.8%) shared a root cause with another case, so one patch could fix them together.

163 (26.2%) were not reported after review, mostly due to limited security impact.

133 (21.4%) were already reported or fixed upstream.

Submission timing explains many of the 133 overlaps. Most of the 621 cases were new when the scans finished (though some may already have been in flight by others). Our first public report went out on June 27, 2026, more than five weeks after scanning started. By September 1, 55 of the 59 had been posted to the public lists; the other four were reported privately during the same window and routed to the public lists by mid-October.

Getting fixes merged

Upstream Linux typically requires vulnerability reports to come with a working patch. Agents helped draft initial fixes, but human validation, subsystem understanding, and iterating with maintainers during review remained essential. So far, fixes for 38 of our reports have been merged into upstream mainline—half on the first submission, and the rest after one to four revisions. Reaching a mainline release from the first public patch took a median of 41 days (up to 108 days), and we are still working with maintainers on the remaining reports.

How old the bugs were

Interestingly, most of the bugs we reported had been in the kernel for years. Across the 59 reports, the average bug was 8.1 years old when we first reported it publicly. One of the oldest, a cls_u32 shift-out-of-bounds bug (CVE-2026-74544), had been there for at least 21 years.

Figure 2 . Age of reported kernel bugs, measured from the bug-introducing commit (the fix’s Fixes tag) to our first public report. Average age 8.1 years across 59 reports; six were 15–19 years old and three were at least 20 years old.

Selected findings

Among the 33 CVEs assigned so far from this batch, 24 are rated High or above (CVSS v3.1 score of at least 7.0). Below are eight CVEs for which we confirmed local root privilege-escalation exploits in controlled laboratory environments, with some cases requiring non-default settings or disabled exploit mitigations:

CVE-2026-…

Module

Summary

64554

net/ipv6

Use-after-free in bridged IPv6 fragmentation: a saved pointer into a packet was reused after the packet’s buffer was reallocated.

64563

lib/rhashtable

Use-after-free in hash-table walks: a walk resumed after the table was resized reused a pointer to a possibly freed entry.

64580

net/ipv6

Refcount underflow in IPv6 IPsec routing: an error path dropped a device reference but kept the pointer, so cleanup dropped it again.

74561

net/ipv4

Use-after-free in next-hop replacement: the route-cache flush walked an IPv6 route list without its lock, racing with route deletion.

74562

net/ipv4

Use-after-free in next-hop replacement: route checks and notifications walked an IPv6 route list without its lock, racing with route deletion.

89789

drivers/net

Use-after-free in the GTP tunnel driver: when device creation failed, its lookup tables were freed while incoming packets could still read them.

98222

security/keys

Heap buffer overflow in encrypted-key updates: long key parameters overflowed a 16-bit length, so the kernel wrote past an undersized buffer.

98364

net/xfrm

Use-after-free in IPsec routing: a network device was used without holding a reference, so deleting it at the same time could free it mid-use.

A closer look at CVE-2026-64563

CVE-2026-64563 is a one-line state-reset bug in rhashtable, the Linux kernel’s shared resizable hash table. Because callers trust the object pointers returned by a table walk, this small library flaw enabled a stable local privilege escalation on Linux—and affected Android with SELinux enforcing—without requiring special kernel configurations or user namespaces.

Many kernel subsystems store live objects, such as sockets, in rhashtable and walk the table when user space asks to list them. Because a large listing may be split across several replies, a walk can pause and resume. Its iterator saves where it stopped, including a pointer to the last visited entry (iter->p). While the walk is paused, however, the table can still change: entries can be removed and freed, and resizing can replace the underlying bucket table.

The missed reset

Before 2018, rhashtable_walk_stop() always cleared iter->p = NULL on pause. To improve walk stability across stop/start cycles, a 2018 commit (5d240a8936f6) kept iter->p across walk_stop() and moved the reset into rhashtable_walk_start_check()—but only on one of its two resume paths:

Old table freed by a resize (iter->walker.tbl == NULL): lines 877–882 switch to the new table, reset slot and skip, and return -EAGAIN early without clearing iter->p:

Old table still present (iter->walker.tbl != NULL): lines 884–919 scan the bucket chain for iter->p and reset iter->p = NULL if the entry was removed.

if (!iter->walker.tbl) { iter->walker.tbl = rht_dereference_rcu(ht->tbl, ht); iter->slot = 0; iter->skip = 0; return -EAGAIN; }

After that restart, the next call to rhashtable_walk_next() sees iter->p still set and follows iter->p->next instead of starting over at slot = 0. If that entry was freed while the walk was paused, dereferencing iter->p->next reads from freed memory.

Why did this bug go unnoticed for eight years? Triggering it requires three conditions to line up in the same walk: the caller must pause and resume the same iterator across walk_stop() and walk_start(), a table resize must free the old bucket table during that pause, and the entry at iter->p must also be removed and freed before the walk resumes. Most rhashtable walkers finish in a single pass without ever resuming a stopped iterator, and even when a caller does pause and resume, those three events rarely coincide by accident in normal workloads.

The upstream fix simply clears the stale pointer before returning:

+ iter->p = NULL;

From a socket listing to a kernel write

Because rhashtable is a shared library, its callers determine both whether this bug is reachable and how severe its security impact can be. Across the kernel, there are about two dozen files that use the rhashtable walker API, and most walk the table in a single pass and immediately exit. Among those callers, we found two that pause and resume an iterator across batches and can at least cause a crash: TIPC’s socket dump (tipc_nl_sk_walk()) and Netlink’s socket diagnostics (__netlink_diag_dump()).

Of the two, __netlink_diag_dump() is the exploitable caller. It is reachable by unprivileged users on standard kernels, and user space controls the pause between dump replies (via recvmsg()). An attacker can hold a dump paused while resizing the table and freeing the socket at iter->p, then reallocate that memory to control iter->p->next—causing rhashtable_walk_next() to return a fake socket pointer sk.

__netlink_diag_dump() then checks net_eq(sock_net(sk), net) and passes sk to sk_diag_fill() and sock_diag_save_cookie(), which initializes sk->sk_cookie if it is zero. That turns the fake sk pointer into a constrained 64-bit write (when the target 8 bytes are zero and sk->sk_net matches &init_net). Paired with other general exploitation techniques, this write is enough for local privilege escalation.

We thank Yuan Tan of NebuSec, who also independently found this vulnerability. He promptly shared its real severity with us and the maintainers, which helped the upstream fix, and later provided us with his working exploits for both Linux and Android. We also thank Frank Wu of NebuSec, who identified a viable exploitation primitive and developed a working privilege-escalation exploit.

Closing thoughts

Finding bugs and fixing them are drastically out of balance. Two weeks of codename MDASH scanning produced the initial findings, which we narrowed to 621 PoC-backed cases. But it took over four person-months to report 59 of them—and five months later, 38 fixes have been merged. For complex infrastructure like the Linux kernel, keeping humans in the loop is still necessary, making human effort the bottleneck. Both bug hunters and maintainers can be overwhelmed by the volume of real findings, so focusing on genuinely high-severity issues is essential.

More tokens may yield more bugs, but not a secure system. We scanned only a small fraction of the kernel, and further tuning and more tokens could uncover substantially more bugs. But even after fixing all of them, is the system secure? At Microsoft FORGE Lab, we’re using AI to expand the scope of vulnerability research, but our experience shows that discovery is only one part of the work. The more urgent problem is how to build practical security solutions that are operational, cumulative, and economically sensible.

These lessons also extend beyond our research. Through close collaboration with the engineering teams building codename MDASH, we’re applying what we learn from real-world vulnerability discovery and validation to inform how these capabilities evolve. The goal is to bring advances in AI-powered security research into the hands of security teams, helping them identify and address critical vulnerabilities more effectively.

The post Lessons from 59 Linux Kernel Bug Reports appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog.

Title: Anthropic's Glasswing Finds Many Vulnerabilities Yet Delivers Few Fixes, Researcher Says
Context: The researcher added that since his last analysis of Glasswing vulnerability findings in September, Anthropic had added 4613 vulnerability findings to its ledger, yet only 15...
Full Text:
The researcher added that since his last analysis of Glasswing vulnerability findings in September, Anthropic had added 4613 vulnerability findings to its ledger, yet only 15 were marked as fixed within the same period. A significant volume of findings added to the ledger between September and November (1668) were marked as duplicates.

This led the researcher to question Anthropic’s latest claimed true positive rate of 94.2%, which, he said, raises “questions about how it accounts for duplicates and withdrawn findings.”

Read more: Anthropic Expands Mythos Access to 150 More Organizations

Anthropic Launched OSS Scanner to Scale Vulnerability Disclosures

One reason that could explain the gap between the vulnerabilities claimed to be found through Glasswing and vulnerabilities publicly fixed is the pace of human vulnerability report triage.

On October 8, Anthropic said it had found more than 29,000 candidate vulnerabilities but had manually reviewed only about 6000, and that it remains "bottlenecked on our human capacity to validate these findings."

“We are working on scaling our vulnerability disclosures,” the company added.

Therefore, it launched its own Open Source Security Scanner (OSS Scanner), a self-service new tool inspired by Google's OSS-Fuzz project and that allows maintainers to request a scan and triage the findings themselves.

Anthropic also said it has already sent nearly 5000 unverified vulnerability reports directly to maintainers who asked to receive everything in bulk.

This new shift in Project Glasswing started showing issues in AI-powered vulnerability reports more clearly.

For instance, Daniel Stenberg, maintainer of the Client and URL (cURL) project, said on November 6 he received 45 vulnerability reports from Anthropic through Glasswing.

After analyzing 34 of them using Anthropic OSS Scanner and other tools, Stenberg pointed out that 19 weren't vulnerabilities at all and six have been confirmed as low severity.

“AI is a valuable tool for finding vulnerabilities, and I'm not discounting that. But seven months in, the evidence still doesn't match the launch narrative. The CVEs are a sliver of this year's total, almost none are being exploited, fixes have stalled while duplicates and withdrawals pile up, and the triage burden is shifting onto the open source maintainers Glasswing promised to help. The receipts keep coming in. They still don't reconcile,” Garrity concluded.

Infosecurity contacted Anthropic for comment, but the company had not responded by the time of publication.

Title: Microsoft Fixes 1235 Flaws in Another Record Patch Tuesday
Context: The zero-day vulnerability is CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Microsoft Outlook, exploited in attacks to steal NTLM account hashes
Full Text:
Microsoft has issued updates to fix over 1200 vulnerabilities in its products, a new record.

The tech giant’s November Patch Tuesday contained fixes for 1235 flaws, including one zero-day being actively exploited in the wild.

It makes this month the fourth this year in which Microsoft has issued a record number of patches, following previous milestones passed in July, September and October.

The zero-day vulnerability is CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Microsoft Outlook, exploited in attacks to steal NTLM account hashes.

“An attacker sends a specially crafted message file and gets the user to open it. Outlook then connects to a network location the attacker controls, but it skips the usual warning about external content,” explained Action1 director of vulnerability research, Jack Bicer.

“That quiet connection can leak the user's NTLMv2 hash, a scrambled form of their login secret, which the attacker can use to sign in as that person. It affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and Office LTSC 2021 and 2024.”

Read more on patching: Exploited Vulnerabilities Typically Take Three Months to Patch, Moody’s Finds

Although the zero-day is rated “moderate,” sysadmins should prioritize it, Bicer advised.

“Attackers are already exploiting it, it needs only one click on an email file, and it hits Outlook, which nearly every organization runs,” he added. “A stolen hash can open doors far beyond the inbox. Push the Office update to every Outlook user now, starting with administrators and high-value accounts.”

The majority (536) of CVEs patched this month are elevation of privilege (EoP), followed by remote code execution (296) and information disclosure (157).

A total of 66 are rated critical, most of these being remote code execution flaws.

SAP Patch Volumes Hit New Highs

Microsoft wasn’t the only software giant to release a record-breaking number of security updates yesterday. SAP’s November Patch Day was the biggest ever, with 43 vulnerabilities addressed, including 12 Hot News Notes and 13 High Priority.

“Hot News” is the highest priority ranking given to SAP security updates (Notes).

The patch load was twice the size of the average for 2026 and included four with a maximum CVSS score of 10.0, according to Onapsis.

These were:

CVE-2026-89103 (SAP Security Note #3798345), a broken access control vulnerability in SAP Gateway dubbed “ProxyGate”

CVE-2026-76964 (SAP Security Note #3778530), a memory corruption flaw in SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP (Internet Communication Manager)

CVE-2026-89126 (SAP Security Note #3778556), a memory corruption vulnerability in SAP Web Dispatcher

CVE-2026-120017 (SAP Security Note #3849308), a missing authentication (SAML2 authentication bypass) vulnerability in SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP and ABAP Platform (SAML2 Service Provider)

Title: ZDI-26-953: (0Day) Meta FAIRChem utils load_inference_model Deserialization of Untrusted Data Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
Context: Vulnerability Details This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Meta FAIRChem
Full Text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Meta FAIRChem. User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must visit a malicious page or open a malicious file.

The specific flaw exists within the parsing of checkpoint files. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in deserialization of untrusted data. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the current process.

Title: Able2Shell: Frequently asked questions for reported N-able N-central zero-day vulnerabilities
Context: As of November 10, there are no details available for any threat actor activity connected to Able2Shell exploitation
Full Text:
N-able released a hotfix for N-central that fixes seven CVEs after a researcher published proof-of-concept code for 33 alleged zero-day vulnerabilities. The researcher says one attack chain needs no credentials.

Key Takeaways

Able2Shell is a set of 33 alleged vulnerabilities in N-able N-central, published with proof-of-concept code. The researcher says one chain lets an unauthenticated attacker run commands on the server.

Security firms report exploitation attempts against N-central honeypots, but as of November 10, no confirmed compromise of a customer server has been reported.

N-able released N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 on November 10. It fixes seven CVEs.

Background

Tenable's Research Special Operations (RSO) team has compiled this blog to answer Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) regarding Able2Shell, a set of reported zero-day vulnerabilities in N-able N-central.

FAQ

When was Able2Shell first disclosed?

A researcher operating under the GitHub account “Oracle-Security” published a write-up titled “Able2Shell” in the account’s CVEs repository. It describes 33 alleged N-central vulnerabilities with proof-of-concept code. The earliest README commit is dated November 9, 2026 at 04:14 UTC. N-able described the release as a public disclosure by an independent security researcher. N-able does not state whether it was notified in advance and does not name the researcher.

What are the vulnerabilities associated with Able2Shell?

On November 10, N-able published seven CVE records for vulnerabilities fixed in N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2. On its status page, N-able says the release addresses “the most critical November 9 vulnerabilities” and that a follow-up hotfix will provide further security updates. The page lists all seven as related CVEs. One, CVE-2026-91000, had been reserved on September 14, before the public Able2Shell disclosure.

N-able’s CVE titles match several finding types in the researcher’s README, but N-able has not said which of the 33 findings each CVE addresses. N-able credits CVE-2026-125882 to Nate Fair of Sprocket Security, and a file repository path traversal also appears in the README.

Is Able2Shell one vulnerability or several?

Several. The README lists 33 findings, and some of them are steps in longer exploit chains built from other entries on the same list. The researcher lists four exploit chains. The rest are standalone findings.

The researcher describes the XXE chain as credential-free, and N-able's record for CVE-2026-125883 lists no privileges and no user interaction as required. The researcher’s proof-of-concept takes several identifiers as inputs, and other findings in the README describe anonymous ways to obtain some of them. The XXE step has the appliance fetch a file from an attacker-hosted server.For the MMS3 chains, the researcher says an unauthenticated attacker can plant the script, which runs when a logged-in administrator views the poisoned patch details. N-able’s record for CVE-2026-125880 lists high privileges and active user interaction.

How severe is Able2Shell?

Two of the four chains reach root: MMS3 stored XSS to Audit Export, and SIS path traversal to syslog. The XXE chain runs commands as the nable account (uid 992), and the researcher’s proof-of-concept can also create an administrator account. N-able’s CVSSv4 scores for the seven CVEs range from 8.3 to 9.3, and N-able calls Hotfix 2 a critical security update.

Has N-able confirmed the findings?

N-able has published seven CVEs and a hotfix, but it has not mapped its CVEs to the researcher’s 33 findings or commented on them individually. Before the hotfix, N-able said it was responding to the public disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in N-central by an independent security researcher.

Which versions are affected?

N-able's CVE records list N-central versions before 26.4.1 as affected (the record for CVE-2026-91000 writes this as 2026.4.1), and the fixed build is 2026.4.1.26. The researcher says all testing was done on N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31, which the researcher describes as a pre-release build, and that "most if not all vulnerabilities should work on previous versions."

Is the hosted N-central service affected?

N-able took its hosted N-central environments offline as a precaution after the disclosure, and its status page lists hosted N-central in the Americas, APAC and Europe among the affected services. On November 10, N-able said all hosted N-central servers across all global regions had been upgraded to the new release. Hosted customers still upgrade their own Agents and Probes.

Has Able2Shell been exploited in the wild?

N-able's status page says it is observing “scanning activity associated with the published proof-of-concept code.” Huntress reported N-able’s statement that it had no evidence that any customer environment had been successfully exploited, and said on November 10 that it had not observed evidence of Able2Shell exploitation in its partners’ environments.

Beazley Security Labs updated its November 9 advisory on November 10 with watchTowr’s report of exploitation attempts against its N-central honeypots. Beazley Security Labs says a confirmed compromise of a customer server “has not been reported.”

Previdian reports exploitation attempts against its N-central decoy environment, not confirmed compromise. Its decoys recorded 68 events from one source IP address starting on November 9, including XXE and sensitive-file access attempts. Previdian says these do not show a completed account takeover or command execution, or a full replay of the published chain.

Which threat actors are exploiting Able2Shell?

As of November 10, there are no details available for any threat actor activity connected to Able2Shell exploitation.

Is there a proof-of-concept (PoC) available?

Yes. The researcher’s README includes Python proof-of-concept code for the alleged vulnerabilities, tested against N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31.

How does this relate to earlier N-central vulnerabilities?

Able2Shell is a newly disclosed set of vulnerabilities, and it is not known whether any relate to earlier N-central flaws. None of the seven CVEs fixed in Hotfix 2 is in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog as of November 10. Five earlier N-central CVEs are in the KEV catalog:
