Title: A patched PHP server can still be a compromised one by Lucie Cardiet
Context: Amazon's honeypots (decoy servers built to attract attackers) recorded the first attempt on October 17, four days before disclosure, and by October 21 Amazon was seeing broad...
Full Text:
On October 20, details of two critical flaws in PHP leaked online before the fixes were ready. PHP, the scripting language behind a large share of the web, moved its patch release up a day and shipped it on October 21. The flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (nicknamed php2shell), let an attacker run commands on a web server through PHP itself, with no login needed.

Patch now. CISA added both flaws to its list of exploited vulnerabilities on October 26. That advice is right, and it leaves a gap. This post is about the gap.

Attackers were testing the flaw before the fix existed

Fixes are out for PHP 8.2 to 8.5,and PHP says PHP 8.1 and older will not get updates. One estimate counts about 884,000 such servers still online, a rough figure from a single source.

Amazon's honeypots (decoy servers built to attract attackers) recorded the first attempt on October 17, four days before disclosure, and by October 21 Amazon was seeing broad exploitation attempts in the wild. Cloudflare saw early attacks, and the UK National Cyber Security Centre warned organizations to update immediately or take systems offline. How many real servers were taken over is still unclear. Amazon says it does not know whether the attempts it saw would have worked outside a honeypot.

On October 23, CrowdStrike and Flare still reported only probing and failed attempts, many of which crash PHP rather than give an attacker control. The next day, Perplexity's Adel Karimi recorded successful remote code execution on a honeypot, and on October 26 CISA added both flaws to its list of known exploited vulnerabilities, with a federal patch deadline of October 29. Karimi's test used a deliberately favorable setup, so it shows the flaw works, not how often attacks like it succeed.

Every flaw has been out there for a while before anyone announces it

A flaw becomes news on the day it is announced, not the day it appears. PHP's own maintainers first spotted signs of this problem in a 2024 audit, and attackers reached it before the public did.

We have seen this pattern before. When Log4j hit in December 2021, Vectra wrote that the first sign of an attack was hard to spot and that the safest assumption was that at least one server in an estate was already compromised. Other flaws in the software your business runs are very likely in the same position today: known to someone, announced to no one. Patching deals with the ones you hear about. It cannot help with the rest.

The PHP servers you miss matter most

PHP runs WordPress,Drupal, Joomla and Magento sites, hosting control panels, and a lot of software that never mentions PHP. The servers you know about will get patched. The ones you do not know about are the ones attackers find first, because nobody is watching them.

Appliances and management interfaces that ship PHP are the likeliest place an attempt becomes a compromise, and they are rarely monitored like web servers. Flare, relaying one researcher's report, says some ship PHP without address randomization, which removes the main obstacle for an attacker. Ask your vendors which of their products include PHP.

No team patches everything on the day a fix ships. Knowing which servers face the internet, and which hold the most valuable data, turns a backlog into a short list of decisions, including which services to switch off until they are fixed. On any server you suspect was hit, save logs and a snapshot of memory before restarting, because a restart erases traces.

‍

What happens after a PHP server falls

An attacker who gets code running through PHP usually does not need malware. The web server already has a shell, a network connection and access to files, so they can use the tools already installed on the machine to look around, find credentials and move from one system to the next. Nothing looks wrong, because the web server is doing web server things with slightly different commands. That is the first of the three detection gaps I write about: nothing looks wrong.

What changes is where the server talks to. A web server that has served the same pages for years suddenly reaches places it never did before, calls out to unfamiliar addresses, or starts talking to internal systems. That behavior shows up in network traffic, not in patch status. A view of the network is how you see what a server is actually connecting to, whether or not anyone is watching the server itself.

What Vectra AI can and cannot see

Vectra AI is not really concerned about what the initial attack vector is. What we see is what happens afterward.

PHP is the story today. Next week it will be something else: another flaw, a phone call to a help desk, someone on the inside. What we look at does not depend on which door was used. We watch what a system does once an attacker is inside, so we do not need the way in to be known or the flaw to be published. That matters most when the entry point is unknown or the vulnerability has not been announced yet.

Uncovering Potential PHP Servers and Shadow IT

One of the challenges in securing PHP infrastructure is knowing where it exists in the first place. Forgotten applications, unmanaged servers, and shadow IT can create security blind spots, even after known vulnerabilities have been patched.

Vectra AI's PHP Server Visibility dashboard provides an additional investigative tool to help security teams identify potentially overlooked PHP servers using indicators observed in unencrypted HTTP traffic, such as .php endpoints and PHPSESSID cookies. Analysts can then investigate whether these hosts are also receiving externally originated encrypted traffic, helping prioritize potentially exposed systems for further investigation.

The dashboard is not intended to provide a complete inventory of PHP servers. It can only identify systems exhibiting observable PHP-related indicators, and encrypted traffic or limited network visibility may leave some servers undiscovered. Instead, it acts as an assistant to existing asset discovery and threat-hunting workflows, helping analysts uncover potential shadow IT, investigate exposure, and identify systems that warrant closer examination, even after patching.

Detection rules for known php2shell exploit attempts

Vectra Match now contains rules to detect the PHP2Shell attacker behaviors when proper visibility is provided to the attacker traffic. They flag known exploit attempts in network traffic when that traffic is visible to us, so they catch attempts at the door, while the detections above catch what follows. An attempt is not a compromise. A match is a reason to look at that server, not proof that it was taken over. This is available for all Vectra Match customers.

The rules, by ET rule number:

2072548: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Handler-mismatch Session Injection (CVE-2026-109619)

2072549: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Multipart Header Amplification OOM (CVE-2026-109618)

2072550: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Nested Empty File Control OOM (CVE-2026-109618)

2072551: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Chunked Multipart Request without Content-Length (CVE-2026-109618)

2072552: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Binary URL-Encoded POST for $_POST Corruption (CVE-2026-109618), commented out in the rule set, so off by default

2072553: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Multipart Request without Content-Length (CVE-2026-109618)

2072554: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Code Injection in Filename (CVE-2026-109619)

2072555: ET HUNTING PHP Generic Upload Progress Session Manipulation, a hunting rule, not an exploit rule, so treat a match as a lead

2072556: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Excessive Multipart Part Count (CVE-2026-109618)

2072557: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Excessive Empty Multipart File Controls (CVE-2026-109618)

What a compromised PHP server reveals about your resilience

The old measure of success was whether attackers get in. The better one is how far they get. Patching, a sound network design, splitting the network into zones, least privilege and knowing which systems carry your most important business processes all limit that distance. The network record can show whether anyone came through the door before it closed, and where they went next.

The three gaps are walked end to end in the Mind Your Gaps in the Age of AI-Powered Attacks white paper.

Title: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619: PHP Vulnerable to Unauthenticated RCE Attacks

Full Text: *October 26, 2026: This advisory has been updated to clarify language describing exploitability and potential impact.*October 23, 2026: This advisory has been updated with new ThreatLabz analysis and Zscaler Deception telemetry on exploitation activity observed during the first 48 hours following disclosure.IntroductionOn October 21, 2026, two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, collectively referred to as “PHP2Shell,” were publicly disclosed. Both vulnerabilities carry a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 out of 10. The PHP security team has released emergency patches and strongly encouraged all PHP users to update immediately. These flaws reside in the PHP core language runtime and successful exploitation could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to achieve remote code execution on any server running a vulnerable version, potentially enabling unauthorized access, data theft, or further system compromise. Given PHP's pervasive deployment across web infrastructure globally - including applications like WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento, as well as embedded devices and similarly overlooked public-facing platforms - the potential attack surface is significant. The vulnerabilities could enable automated exploitation of exposed, vulnerable PHP deployments without authentication or user interaction. The vulnerabilities therefore may be attractive targets for exploitation.ThreatLabz analysis indicates that attackers began rapidly targeting these vulnerabilities following public disclosure, highlighting the need for organizations to patch vulnerable PHP deployments immediately.Zscaler’s security team has analyzed this issue across both production and corporate environments and has ruled out any impact to Zscaler Cloud Platforms, products, distributed components, services, or our enterprise environment, as detailed in the Trust post. RecommendationsOrganizations running PHP should take the following actions:Patch immediately: Upgrade PHP to one of the fixed versions: 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35. Linux package maintainers received patches in advance and may already have updated packages available. PHP packages for most Linux distributions may also include the patches backported to previous versions of the software, so consult the release notes for your specific installation to ensure your systems are covered.Deactivate unpatched instances: Consider fully disabling services for any PHP instance that cannot be immediately patched. While this may seem overly cautious, any unpatched instance could be targeted by opportunistic adversaries and result in shell-level access to the vulnerable host. Inventory PHP deployments: Conduct an immediate inventory of all PHP installations across your environment, including standalone servers, vendor appliances, bundled software (WordPress, Magento, WooCommerce, Shopware), and hosting panels (cPanel, Plesk, etc).Migrate off EOL branches: Organizations running PHP 5.4+, 7.x, 8.0, or 8.1 must migrate to a supported branch immediately. No official binary patches will be released for these versions.Isolate EOL instances that cannot be immediately migrated: Migrating EOL instances is strongly recommended. If this is not possible, isolating unpatchable applications from the internet and other untrusted networks may provide some level of protection. This should be considered a high-risk mitigation and reserved only for business and mission-critical applications while implementing aggressive monitoring of these instances.Monitor for exploitation: Audit web server logs (including but not limited to Apache, Nginx, etc.) for unusual segmentation faults, crash dumps, or abnormal memory usage patterns that may indicate active exploitation attempts.Mitigate risk through PHP settings: While not a definitive fix, mission critical applications that cannot be disabled or immediately patched may benefit from reviewing and tightening memory_limit and max_execution_time settings in php.ini to avoid triggering OOM conditions. Consult additional guidance regarding mitigations through setting session.upload_progress.enabled = Off and disabling multipart uploads at the service edge. ThreatLabz Observes Exploitation Attempts Within 48 HoursThreatLabz observed scanning activity and possible exploitation attempts targeting the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities using multiple attack tools and exploitation methods, including RCE payloads, PHP object injection, and named exploitation frameworks, indicating rapid, in-the-wild exploitation attempts.In the first 48 hours after the PHP2Shell disclosure, Zscaler’s global decoy mesh observed 1,156 exploitation attempts from 156 unique attacker IPs targeting 70 organizations. As a rapid response measure, a new detection rule for PHP2Shell exploitation has been pushed to all Zscaler Deception customers.Attack chainAutomated scanning activity observed by Zscaler suggests attackers may be attempting to use a two-stage PHP2Shell exploitation chain, as shown in the figure below.Figure 1: Notional exploit chain consistent with scanning and exploit attempts observed by ThreatLabz.Stage 1: State setup and fatal triggerThe attacker sends a crafted multipart/form-data POST request containing:A PHPSESSID field to associate the request with a known session, making the session filename (sess_[PHPSESSID]) predictable.The PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS field to force PHP to begin session bookkeeping during multipart parsing, populating vulnerable global state pointers and writing attacker-controlled data into the session file.A file attachment whose filename= parameter contains either PHP code or a serialized object string.A body sized or structured to exhaust memory (CVE-2026-109618) or trigger a fatal error (CVE-2026-109619).When the fatal condition is triggered, longjmp() aborts the request, freeing per-request memory but leaving stale global pointers.Stage 2: Heap reclaim and code executionThe attacker immediately sends a second request to the same worker process. This second request contains the attacker's payload, sized and aligned to reclaim the freed memory slots. When PHP processes the new request and references the stale global state before re-initialization occurs, it reads and executes the attacker-controlled data, achieving arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the PHP worker process.Zscaler Deception telemetry findingsThreatLabz observed malicious POST requests targeting the PHP2Shell exploitation path across multiple tools and stages of the attack chain. Every observed request is a multipart/form-data POST targeting PHP endpoints, specifically /, /index.php, /api/endpoint.php, and /app/upload.php.Exploitation payloads observed1. ShellFlow PHP2Shell named exploit toolThe most forensically significant artifact is the presence of a multipart boundary string that explicitly names the exploitation tool. This indicator should not be considered durable, as an adversary can trivially replace the known strings with something less obvious. At this time, the ShellFlow tool uses a known boundary value, so it is a useful indicator for detecting the unmodified tool. The exploit tool request is shown below. POST / HTTP/1.1 Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----shellflow-php2shell ------shellflow-php2shell Content-Disposition: form-data; name="PHPSESSID" sf618_ec172709c8b74601 ------shellflow-php2shell Content-Disposition: form-data; name="PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS" shellflow_poc ------shellflow-php2shell Content-Disposition: form-data; name="f"; filename="poc.bin" Content-Type: application/octet-stream AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA[...15485 bytes total...]The multipart boundary shellflow-php2shell identifies the attacking tool by name. The poc.bin file body contains more than 15k bytes of data along with a repeated AAAA... characters, a characteristic heap spray pattern used for memory layout control in the CVE-2026-109618 OOM corruption path.Notable characteristics:The boundary string shellflow-php2shell directly identifies the ShellFlow PHP2Shell attacking tool, which is publicly linked to CVE-2026-109618 scanning activity.The session ID sf618_ec172709c8b74601 contains sf618, possibly reflecting a developer’s shorthand reference to ShellFlow + CVE-2026-109618.The application/octet-stream upload with a repeating AAAAA... buffer is consistent with a heap spray technique used to influence the memory layout when the OOM condition is triggered.2. Active system() command execution payloadThese requests represent the strongest indication of automated exploitation attempts. The filename= field contains a fully formed PHP webshell instruction designed to be written into the PHP session file through the session.upload_progress handler and later executed, as shown in the example below.The filename= value [?php system('echo 'exploited digga' > pwned.txt');echo 'RCE';?] instructs the PHP runtime to:Execute the OS command echo 'exploited digga' > pwned.txt, writing a proof-of-compromise marker to disk.Echo the string RCE in the HTTP response body, providing an indication of successful code execution to the attacker. The RCE string may still be returned even if the preceding echo redirection fails.This payload pattern was observed in two separate requests with identical content, consistent with automated retry behavior commonly seen in exploit frameworks.3. The filename x|O:8:"stdClass":0:{} uses the PHP default session serialization format, where the | character separates a variable name from its serialized value.POST /app/upload.php HTTP/1.1 Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=--NeoMM2026 --NeoMM2026 Content-Disposition: form-data; name="PHPSESSID" neosc4n00000000000000002 --NeoMM2026 Content-Disposition: form-data; name="PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS" neo_obj_inject --NeoMM2026 Content-Disposition: form-data; name="f"; filename="x|O:8:\"stdClass\":0:{}" Content-Type: text/plain Z --NeoMM2026--Overall attack tool fingerprinting summaryThreatLabz identified multiple distinct attacker toolsets through analysis of numerous requests in our telemetry, as summarized in the table below:Tool / FrameworkIdentifying MarkersShellFlow PHP2ShellBoundary shellflow-php2shell; session ID prefix sf618; poc.bin heap sprayActive RCE OperatorBoundary --VERIFY; system() payload in filename=; pwned.txt writeNuclei CVE TemplatesBoundary prefix ------Nuclei; echo-test random token in filenameNeo ScannerBoundary --NeoMM2026b / --NeoMM2026; targets /api/endpoint.php, /app/upload.phpTable 1: Attacker tools and identifying markers observed in PHP2Shell exploitation activity. Affected VersionsAll PHP versions from 5.4 onward are vulnerable. Only currently supported branches received patches, but package maintainers may also backport the security patches to previous versions. Carefully review the instructions and release notes from the maintainers of your PHP installations to determine what version and release includes the necessary patch.PHP BranchVulnerable VersionsPatch AvailablePHP 8.58.5.0 – 8.5.11Yes (8.5.12)PHP 8.48.4.0 – 8.4.26Yes (8.4.27)PHP 8.38.3.0 – 8.3.35Yes (8.3.36)PHP 8.28.2.0 – 8.2.34Yes (8.2.35)PHP 8.1All versions (EOL)No (EOL — upgrade required)PHP 8.0All versions (EOL)No (EOL — upgrade required)PHP 7.xAll versions (EOL)No (EOL — upgrade required)PHP 5.4+All versions (EOL)No (EOL — upgrade required)Table 2: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 Affected PHP Versions and Patch Availability How It WorksBoth vulnerabilities are use-after-free memory safety flaws in PHP's core request-handling engine. All PHP installations serving web requests may be affected regardless of security controls. The vulnerabilities can allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on affected servers or read sensitive process memory; that memory may contain passwords, authentication tokens, API keys and certificates belonging to other requests or the server itself.CVE-2026-109618: OOM Corruption / Uninitialized Memory UseCVSS v4.0: 9.2 - CriticalRoot Cause: PHP uses longjmp() to abort a request when it hits its configured memory limit. When a web application receives form input, PHP records new entries in its internal POST data structure before finishing their initialization. If an out-of-memory (OOM) error fires while internal request data is only partially initialized, longjmp() bypasses normal control flow, leaving memory in an inconsistent/uninitialized state. During request cleanup, PHP misinterprets this invalid data as valid and follows an attacker-controlled code pointer, yielding control of execution.Exploit Vector: An attacker can intentionally trigger specific OOM conditions (e.g., via large memory allocations, deeply recursive calls, or maliciously crafted request payloads) to corrupt state and achieve unauthenticated RCE.Impact: Unauthenticated Remote Code ExecutionCVE-2026-109619: Use-After-Free / Stale Memory AccessCVSS v4.0: 9.2 - CriticalRoot Cause: When PHP encounters a fatal error and calls zend_bailout() (via longjmp()), request-owned internal state can survive in global memory after its backing allocation has been freed. PHP workers process multiple requests in sequence, and certain internal pointers persist between requests. If a request crashes or exhausts memory at the right moment, those pointers are left pointing to already-recycled memory. A subsequent request processed by the same worker may access this stale memory before re-initialization occurs.Exploit Vector: This vulnerability is chainable with CVE-2026-109618. The partial initialization in CVE-2026-109618 allows an attacker to shape the freed memory contents and gain control of the instruction pointer, potentially enabling RCE. Chaining these two CVEs requires no authentication and no user interaction.Impact: Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution and memory/credential disclosure ConclusionPHP2Shell represents a significant security issue because of the severity of the vulnerabilities and PHP’s broad deployment. The combination of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 could provide an unauthenticated path to RCE and potentially broader server compromise without user interaction.Organizations are strongly urged to treat this as an emergency patching event. Systems running EOL PHP branches must be migrated without delay. Full Text:
On Tuesday, October 20, threat actors gained advance visibility into two critical PHP vulnerabilities after details leaked ahead of the planned disclosure, accelerating the race between defenders and attackers. The flaws are tracked as Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) identifiers CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Together they’re known as PHP2Shell. Both carry a 9.2 rating on the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) version 4.0 scale. For both vulnerabilities, Arctic Wolf’s Aurora® Agentic SOC helps organizations rapidly identify affected assets, correlate exploitation signals across the environment, and accelerate investigation and response before attackers can establish persistence.

An unauthenticated attacker can use either flaw to run code on a vulnerable server. On Wednesday, October 21, the PHP project released patched versions. PHP2Shell shows how AI is changing the threat landscape. Attackers can now find and weaponize old flaws in widely used technology faster than ever before. Arctic Wolf recommends treating every PHP installation that serves web requests as at-risk presently. Internet-facing Linux web servers without endpoint monitoring carry the highest risk of quiet compromise.

Patching remains the recommended remediation. Security teams should assess exposure immediately, identify likely attack paths, and segment critical systems to limit an attacker’s ability to move through the environment. If attackers exploit PHP2Shell, Aurora Agentic SOC is designed to detect the activity that follows, including webshell deployment, unauthorized command execution, persistence attempts, and lateral movement, enabling rapid investigation and response before attacks can escalate.

Overview and Impact

All PHP installations that serve web requests are at risk. That includes PHP-FPM (FastCGI Process Manager), Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. PHP rates the risk highest for mod_php. In PHP’s demonstrated exploit, an unauthenticated request triggers the attack before any application code runs.

PHP runs WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, and control panels like cPanel and Plesk. Many vendor applications bundle PHP without saying so, which makes the affected assets hard to find. Bundled standalone binaries such as php.exe and php-cgi.exe on Windows are easy to miss.

Understanding the Root Cause

CVE-2026-109618 is an out-of-memory handling flaw. PHP can stop while internal request data is only partly set up. Request cleanup may then treat that invalid data as valid.

CVE-2026-109619 is a stale state flaw. Request-owned internal state can survive after its memory is freed. A later request on the same worker may use that stale state before normal setup resets it. The PHP session upload progress feature is one confirmed path to this flaw, and it’s enabled by default.

Guidance for Arctic Wolf Customers

Inventory every system that runs PHP. Include package-based installs, containers, appliances, and hosting panels. Include vendor software that bundles PHP. Include continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) images.

Identify the PHP branch and package source on each system.

Update to the patched version or confirm your vendor has backported both fixes. Patch internet-facing systems first.

Restart every affected service. That covers PHP-FPM, Apache, NGINX upstream pools, application workers, and containers.

Rebuild container images from patched upstream bases. Patching only the running containers leaves the image exposed.

Move end-of-life PHP to a supported branch.

Record the patched version, vendor advisory, restart time, and validation evidence for each host or image. If a workload can’t be patched right away, document compensating controls and an approved exception with an expiry date.

Use stopgaps to reduce exposure while you patch

Configuration changes such as memory_limit or session.upload_progress.enabled are not remediation. PHP states that only an update is a complete solution. The required fix is a patched PHP runtime or a vendor package that explicitly backports both fixes.

If you can’t update right away, PHP lists measures that reduce exposure to specific attack paths. These measures do not make an installation safe.

For CVE-2026-109618

Set memory_limit=-1 in a way applications can’t override, such as php_admin_value in the FPM pool or Apache configuration.

Set a low post_max_size. PHP suggests 8M for applications without uploads and 32M for those with uploads. Keep upload_max_filesize below it.

Enforce request size, field count, and header limits at the web server or proxy.

Fix attacker-reachable fatal errors and execution timeouts.

How Arctic Wolf Labs turns telemetry into outcomes

Arctic Wolf Labs is our threat intelligence and research team. Global SOC telemetry visibility drives a shared defense, while active network monitoring gives Labs an early warning system across our global customer base. Using telemetry from across the Arctic Wolf customer community, researchers identify spikes in scanning activity, analyze exploitation attempts, and uncover attacker payloads associated with PHP2Shell. We use those findings to develop and fine-tune detections to respond to malicious activity faster. This means customers gain coverage against PHP2Shell activity they may have not observed yet in their unique environment.

Labs researchers also replicate attacker techniques against PHP2Shell vulnerabilities in controlled environments. Arctic Wolf Labs leverages resulting artifacts from these simulations, as well as observed exploit techniques, attacker tradecraft, and emerging indicators of attack/compromise (IOA/IOC), to develop new detections, threat hunt queries, and inform customer remediation guidance

As threat behavior evolves, we continuously apply the latest intelligence across customer environments. Arctic Wolf Labs’ initial investigation has identified numerous scanning efforts as well as malicious exploitation attempts, including passing wget requests to retrieve both ELF and Golang binaries associated with commodity malware.

How the Aurora Superintelligence Platform keeps customers protected

The Aurora Superintelligence Platform helps organizations reduce PHP2Shell risk before and after exploitation. Aurora Vulnerability Management identifies and prioritizes affected assets using live exploit activity and threat intelligence, helping security teams focus remediation efforts where risk is highest.

The Aurora Agentic SOC monitors the behaviors attackers rely on after exploitation, including webshell deployment, suspicious processes spawned by PHP or web servers, malicious command execution, persistence activity, and lateral movement.

Together, these capabilities help organizations quickly identify exposed systems, prioritize remediation, detect malicious activity, investigate potential compromise, and contain threats while vulnerable systems are being patched. As the threat evolves, Arctic Wolf continuously incorporates new intelligence across the platform to strengthen proactive cyber risk remediation and detection and response capabilities for all customers.

Title: Keep Calm, and Patch PHP2Shell
Context: With a widely available patch for supported versions and the lifeline thrown for some legacy code, threat actors will weaponize these exploits against unpatched and end of life...
Full Text:
Keep Calm and Patch PHP2Shell

October 21, 2026

Justin Timothy

With contributions by the GuidePoint Security GRIT team

BLOG

10 min.

How to Respond to CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619

*Note: This is an actively developing situation and the information from this blog is accurate as of writing. Please refer to PHP’s official guidance for any newly released information and additional patching and mitigation recommendations.

The newly released ‘PHP2Shell’ vulnerabilities have become a hot topic hitting the desks, feeds and wires of every cybersecurity professional around the world. Starting October 20th, leaked details, disputed PoCs, conflicting exploitation reports and a patch that was scheduled but not yet released started circulating among security professionals online.

TL;DR – LPHP2Shell is a critical, highly exploitable set of two vulnerabilities that could potentially affect a massive percentage of internet facing websites. The patch is available and the time to patch is now.

CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, collectively nicknamed “PHP2Shell”, are critical severity vulnerabilities that require immediate attention.

Patches are available for supported versions of PHP. PHP supplied Linux distributions and LTS vendors the patches in advance. Experts recommend isolating or decommissioning systems running versions older than 7.4.

It’s important to patch internet-facing systems first, rebuild containers that contain PHP, restart all affected systems after patching and conduct retrospective threat hunts to ensure no threat actors slipped through before the patches were applied.

The instinct during these types of high-impact vulnerability disclosures is to either panic or wait for certainty. Panic can lead to uncoordinated patching and inconsistent workarounds. Waiting means the exploit code is circulating before you hit your change window.

It wasn’t until PHP released their official post announcing the two CVEs and the mitigation options that the world was able to definitively understand the impact and start implementing patch management strategies.

This is why a balanced approach works best: act on what’s confirmed, prepare for what’s coming and make deliberate decisions about the tradeoffs you’re accepting.

What We Know About PHP2Shell

All PHP installations serving web requests, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed are affected by these vulnerabilities. PHP considers the risk highest for mod_php, where the demonstrated exploit achieves unauthenticated remote code execution before application code runs. Both CVEs have been rated CVSS 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS v4.0 by PHP.

CVE-2026-109618: RCE via OOM Corruption

PHP handles out-of-memory (OOM) conditions, unwinding straight out of the current execution context and aborting the request. In certain early-request contexts, request-scoped memory is reachable before it has been fully initialized.

If any allocation fails in that window, the non-local exit skips the initialization and PHP’s error path does not account for the half-built state. The request shutdown routine then reads or branches on that memory. The failing allocation does not need to be related to the corrupted memory, so the trigger is generic: any OOM during the window is enough.

Several OOM-induction strategies trigger it consistently, which makes exploitation reliable and leads to Remote Code Execution (RCE).

CVE-2026-109619: RCE Via Stale Global State

PHP workers are long-lived and reused across requests and they keep some global state (error, session, object and extension data) that points to memory belonging to a single request. That state should be cleared before the request’s memory is freed. A fatal error can stop an operation before it cleans up.

Examples include running out of memory, hitting the execution time limit or a failed compile. A later warning during shutdown can also refill error state that was already cleared. The request’s memory is then freed while the worker still points to it, which is a use-after-free. When the same worker handles its next request, early steps that run before normal setup (input, configuration, session and error handling) can read, free or act on that stale pointer.

With a carefully crafted memory layout, an attacker can turn this into RCE, meaning they run their own code on the server. Exploitation takes two separate HTTP requests handled by the same worker: the first leaves stale state behind and the second uses it.

PHP2Shell encompasses two critical-severity vulnerabilities in one of the most widely deployed server-side runtimes on the internet. A patch has now been made available and we encourage all organizations to patch where possible.

Why PHP2Shell Deserves Your Attention

Not every vulnerability warrants immediate attention; however, this one does. The characteristics, including the potential impact and the exploitability demand quick action.

The parsing layer is the attack surface: Initial reporting indicates that the PHP2Shell vulnerability triggers during multipart/form-data parsing, before your application code executes. CMS maintenance modes, security plugins, authentication layers… none of it matters once it’s under attack. The request body gets parsed by PHP itself and that’s where the flaw lives.

The affected footprint is potentially enormous: PHP powers a significant portion of global websites with their server-side language. It’s embedded in WordPress, cPanel, WHM, Laravel-based internal tools, hosting panels, appliances and countless containerized microservices. Many organizations running PHP don’t think of themselves as PHP shops.

End-of-life PHP versions won’t get a fix: PHP 8.1 and earlier are considered end-of-life by the vendor. Any system running a legacy PHP version will not receive an official patch. If the claims about the vulnerability affecting versions as far back as PHP 5, many systems may face the need for rapid upgrade or decommissioning to ensure security.

The exploit interest is high and the details are public: The advisories are linked, the root causes are documented and the confirmed attack paths are described. The window between “patch available” and “weaponized exploit code circulating” is narrowing. We know from experience that threat actors weaponize large scale, public exploits within 24-48 hours of their disclosure.

How to Patch PHP2Shell

PHP has released the following versions that have addressed the vulnerabilities: PHP 8.5.12, PHP 8.4.27, PHP 8.3.36 and PHP 8.2.35.

Source downloads are available on php.net. Linux distributions and LTS vendors received the patches in advance, so check your vendor for updated packages.

Patching alone does not fully mitigate the possibility of exploitation. Keep in mind exploitability and follow this recommended execution sequence to reduce the highest risks first:

Patch internet-facing systems first: With systems that face the internet, the attack surface is remote and unauthenticated. Internet-facing PHP hosts are the front line. Secure them before all others to close the widest gap.

Confirm the fix through package changelogs, not version strings: Distributions frequently backport security fixes without changing the upstream version number. A system reporting PHP 8.4.26 might already contain the fix if the distribution backported it. Check the package changelog or the distribution’s security advisory for confirmation.

Restart everything: Patching the binary on disk doesn’t protect running processes. Restart PHP-FPM, Apache modules and every long-running PHP process. This includes queue workers, schedulers and daemons. Without a restart, these processes continue running the old, vulnerable binary.

Rebuild and redeploy container images: If PHP runs in containers, updating the host package isn’t enough. Rebuild images with the patched PHP version and redeploy. Every running container based on the old image remains vulnerable.

Watch your distribution’s timeline: Not every package repository will have the fix today. The volunteer-run Remi repository (widely used on RHEL-based servers) will not publish updates on October 21st. PHP’s advisory urges Remi users to switch to distribution packages or build from source so the fix can be applied immediately.

What to Do If You Can't Patch PHP2Shell Immediately

PHP’s guidance is clear: the only complete solution is an update.

PHP has published specific interim measures that reduce exposure to confirmed attack paths. These mitigations are not equivalent to patching. They mitigate the risk of exploitation, but they do not eliminate it completely.

The multi-part rejection workaround remains valid as an additional layer for both CVEs. Rejecting requests whose Content-Type contains multipart/form-data at the web server, before they reach PHP, is still a strong stopgap. Cover all HTTP methods, not just POST (PHP 8.4+ parses multipart bodies on other methods) and apply it to every virtual host and default server that passes requests to PHP. This breaks file uploads until removed.

For CVE-2026-109618 (OOM corruption):

Set memory_limit=-1, preferably in a way applications can’t override (e.g., php_admin_value in the FPM pool or Apache configuration). Verify that no pool, directory or application setting puts a finite limit back. This removes the controllable PHP memory limit failure, but an underlying allocation failure can still reach the vulnerable path.

Set a low post_max_size. For applications that don’t require file uploads, post_max_size = 8M. If file uploads are necessary, post_max_size = 32M. Keep upload_max_filesize below post_max_size. Enforce limits at the web server or proxy level for decoded request size, input field count, multipart part count, header count and nesting depth, including for requests without a usable Content-Length.

Use a container or cgroup limit as an availability boundary, preferably with a policy that kills only the affected worker. Do not substitute RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA, as these can cause vulnerable allocation failure.

For CVE-2026-109619 (stale global state):

Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and restart every worker. Use php.ini, an FPM pool or server configuration that applies before request parsing. Do not rely on ini_set() or FPM .user.ini. The setting needs to take effect before the parser runs.

On PHP 8.5, set fatal_error_backtraces=0 and restart every worker. This blocks the confirmed fatal backtrace path only.

Remove invalid or deprecated settings applied per request that emit diagnostics before initialization. Hiding diagnostics with error_reporting, display_errors or @ does not help.

The Systems That Won't Get an Official Fix (But Might Get Help)

PHP 8.1 and earlier are end-of-life, so normally, those versions would not receive updates. Notably, PHP published minimal source-backports for PHP 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1 to help organizations building from source or without access to an LTS vendor. This is not a full-support commitment. However, it is a valuable lifeline for teams that can compile from source and need to close the gap.

For systems that can’t be patched or compiled from backports (and especially for anything older than 7.4) the guidance from multiple regulatory boards and industry experts stands: isolate internet-facing PHP systems from public networks or take them offline entirely. That’s a hard conversation for teams running legacy applications on unsupported PHP versions and it’s a conversation that needs to happen today.

With a widely available patch for supported versions and the lifeline thrown for some legacy code, threat actors will weaponize these exploits against unpatched and end of life systems.

After Patching: Hunt Backwards

Patching closes the door, which reduces your risk going forward. However, it doesn’t guarantee that a threat actor wasn’t able to slip through the cracks while you were busy patching. A retrospective threat hunt based on these behavior signals can help you eliminate the possibility of infiltration:

PHP worker child processes spawning shells or download utilities (PHP-FPM, Apache or other PHP workers)

Unexplained worker crashes or segmentation faults in PHP-FPM and web server logs (plausible side effects of memory-corruption exploitation attempts)

Unusual multipart/form-data requests from October 20th, 15:00 UTC onward, particularly to endpoints that don’t accept uploads

New or modified files in web roots, upload directories, plugin directories and mu-plugins

Changes to .user.ini files or the auto_prepend_file setting

Persistence indicators: new cron entries, systemd units, Supervisor entries, SSH authorized_keys additions, newly created application admin accounts or unexpected outbound connections from PHP service accounts

A clean result doesn’t rule out compromise, but it does indicate that the available behavioral indicators didn’t fire. That’s a meaningful data point. That said: preserve your logs. Web server and PHP logs from October 20th, 15:00 UTC onward are your forensic baseline. Log rotation, redeployment and container rebuilds can destroy the evidence needed for a compromise assessment. Back them up before patching changes anything.

Stay Tuned for Updates

GuidePoint Security’s GRIT team is actively tracking PHP2Shell and its impact. We will provide updated advisories, emerging exploit techniques and confirmed indicators of compromise as they become available. If PHP workers are spawning shells, unexpected files appear in web roots or you discover persistence mechanisms on a PHP host, the GuidePoint Security Incident Response team is ready to help.

FAQs

What is PHP2Shell?

PHP2Shell is the collective name for two critical PHP vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) disclosed on October 20, 2026. Both are rated CVSS 9.2 (Critical) and can allow unauthenticated remote code execution on PHP web servers. CVE-2026-109618 exploits out-of-memory corruption during request processing and CVE-2026-109619 exploits stale global state that persists across requests within the same PHP worker process.

What PHP versions are affected by PHP2Shell?

All PHP installations serving web requests are affected, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. PHP considers mod_php the highest-risk configuration. Patched versions are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. PHP 8.1 and earlier are end-of-life and will not receive official patches, though PHP published minimal source-backports for PHP 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1. Unconfirmed reports indicate the vulnerabilities may affect versions as far back as PHP 5.

How do I patch PHP2Shell?

Update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35. Source downloads are available on php.net and Linux distributions and LTS vendors received patches in advance. After updating, restart PHP-FPM, Apache modules and all long-running PHP processes such as queue workers and schedulers; these continue running the old binary until restarted. Container images must be rebuilt and redeployed with the patched PHP version. Confirm the fix through package changelogs or vendor advisories rather than version strings, since distributions often backport fixes without changing the upstream version number.

What should I do if I can't patch PHP2Shell immediately?

PHP’s official position is that only a full update is a complete solution. Interim measures that reduce exposure include: rejecting requests whose Content-Type contains multipart/form-data at the web server before they reach PHP (covering all HTTP methods, not just POST); setting memory_limit=-1 to remove the controllable OOM trigger for CVE-2026-109618; and setting session.upload_progress.enabled=0 for CVE-2026-109619. For systems running PHP 8.1 or earlier that cannot be patched or compiled from PHP’s source-backports, the recommended action is isolation from public networks or taking them offline.

How do I detect PHP2Shell exploitation on my servers?

As of October 21, 2026, no vendor-published indicators of compromise exist yet, so detection relies on behavioral hunting. Look for PHP worker processes spawning shells or download utilities, unexplained worker crashes or segmentation faults in PHP-FPM and web server logs, unusual multipart/form-data requests (especially to endpoints that don’t accept uploads) from October 20, 2026 onward, new or modified files in web roots and upload directories, changes to .user.ini files or auto_prepend_file settings and new persistence indicators such as cron entries, SSH authorized_keys additions or unexpected outbound connections. Preserve web server and PHP logs from October 20 onward before patching or redeploying.

How does Aquasec protect PHP workloads?

Aquasec enforces security policies inside running workloads, allowing security teams to restrict supported unauthorized actions without depending exclusively on vulnerability specific signatures.

Four runtime control areas are particularly relevant to PHP workloads.

Restrict unauthorized process execution. Runtime policies can restrict PHP workloads from launching unnecessary shells and download utilities such as `sh`, `bash`, `curl` and `wget`. This can interrupt certain attempts to execute additional commands or retrieve malicious payloads.

Prevent unauthorized executable changes. Aquasec Drift Prevention can block execution of executable files that were not present in the original container image. This helps restrict newly introduced malicious binaries, although it does not independently prevent a PHP script from running through the existing interpreter.

Restrict unauthorized network activity. Appropriate runtime network controls can restrict unnecessary outbound connections and help limit certain reverse shell activities or communication with attacker controlled infrastructure.

Protect application files. File integrity monitoring can detect unauthorized modifications to sensitive application directories. File modification restrictions can prevent changes when properly configured, including changes to PHP web roots where malicious scripts might be introduced.

The effectiveness of these controls depends on workload coverage, policy configuration and the attack technique. In enforcement mode, validated policies can block supported unauthorized actions. They should not be represented as complete protection against either PHP2Shell vulnerability, particularly the reported memory disclosure path.

Title: Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today
Context: Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server
Full Text:
Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.

Image: Shutterstock.com, Sashkin.

The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.

Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.

OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”

Censys, a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.

Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].

“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”

The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.

The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.

“A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”

The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. Executive Summary

“Can you find about like what scam or thing they done in past like spoofing calls or somthing [sic],” the threat actor typed. The conversation was with one of several AI assistants that the actor was using to get advice on planning and executing a variety of cybercrime activities.

Our visibility into this specific actor's operational environment gives us unique insights into exactly how threat actors are building, testing and executing agentic attacks across multiple campaign types.

Unit 42’s investigation into the actor’s operational environment and activities makes two things clear:

The attacker used basic tooling and relied on AI-generated scripts and reconnaissance reports, suggesting they didn’t have the skills these activities would have required before the advent of readily available AI tools.

Despite some apparent bumbling, the actor had an impact, attacking a number of targets in India, including universities. The actor recovered thousands of records revealing personal information and mapped multiple organizations’ attack surfaces.

The attacker’s conversations with jailbroken AI tools included getting step by step advice on how to set up a fraudulent Voice over IP (VoIP) operation. One assistant “helpfully” generated a document including a “NEXT EXPLOIT OPPORTUNITIES” section, outlining planned followup attacks.

Unit 42 identified and investigated this threat actor's operational environment. There, we determined that they had weaponized an AI assistant across several types of cybercrime, including:

Credential theft and data exfiltration

VoIP telecommunications fraud

Wi-Fi password cracking

Cryptocurrency reconnaissance

Command-and-control (C2) operations

An actor operating under the handle BUGSTER configured the Hermes Agent framework with DeepSeek V4 as its reasoning engine and Cursor integrated development environment (IDE) as a secondary tool, both with safety controls disabled. The actor ran an AI-generated brute-force campaign against an Indian university’s website. Notably, the Wi-Fi cracking capability requires close physical proximity to the target, indicating the actor had local access to the targeted locations.

Multiple, unrelated actors are independently adopting the same Hermes + DeepSeek combination. This suggests we may be witnessing an increasingly prevalent toolchain of choice for cybercriminals adopting AI-enabled capabilities. We assess a key driver is low safety friction at low cost: DeepSeek models are inexpensive and easy to access, and readily jailbroken with a simple system-prompt override.

Title: PHP2Shell: AI uncovers critical RCE vulnerabilities affecting 70% of the Internet
Context: Core PHP engine flaws enable remote code execution and Heartbleed-style memory disclosure across the web.
Full Text:
Executive Summary

Wiz Research uncovered multiple critical vulnerabilities in core PHP, a popular general-purpose scripting language that powers 70% of all websites in the world. Successful exploitation could allow attackers to take control of affected servers, steal sensitive data, and deface the websites running on them.

PHP is a backbone of the web: it’s the programming language powering WordPress, Joomla, Drupal, Wikipedia’s MediaWiki, and many others.

These vulnerabilities include memory disclosure and unauthenticated remote code execution in PHP itself, independent of the application running on top of it, putting every affected website in immediate risk.

Every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities, going back to version 5.4. Attackers can exploit them remotely, in some cases fairly easily. Immediate patching is strongly advised.

On October 21, 2026, PHP released the patch fixing multiple memory-safety vulnerabilities in the core engine.

These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history. The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.

Overview

In this post, we explain how frontier AI helped us find and fix vulnerabilities that had remained hidden in the PHP codebase for more than a decade. The issues described below all stem from key architecture decisions, some made over a decade ago, and were grouped under two CVEs, with severity reaching CVSS 9.2. The work grew into a cross-industry effort to protect customers, find variants, deploy detections and mitigations, and verify a patch in time for coordinated disclosure.

Nearly every PHP version is affected by at least one of these issues, including releases dating back to PHP 5.4. The vulnerabilities can allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on affected servers or read sensitive process memory. That memory may contain passwords, authentication tokens, API keys and certificates belonging to other requests or the server itself.

PHP is the programming language behind much of the web, powering WordPress, Drupal and MediaWiki, the software that runs Wikipedia. A flaw in its core engine can affect websites across this ecosystem, even when their own application code is secure.

Some vulnerabilities become turning points because they challenge fundamental assumptions about security. In 2014, Heartbleed exposed the fragility of shared infrastructure securing the internet. In 2021, Log4Shell revealed how deeply embedded software dependencies could create widespread exposure that organizations struggled to identify. We believe PHP2Shell could mark a similar turning point for the AI era, illustrating how AI can change the practical exploitability of longstanding vulnerabilities. Building the exploit required chaining multiple flaws and adapting to each target’s memory layout through repeated testing and debugging. Frontier models were critical to making this process practical, enabling us to develop and adapt working exploits across multiple applications in hours. As the time and expertise required for this work decrease, complexity may no longer provide a meaningful barrier, changing how we define what is vulnerable in practice.

Wiz Research would like to thank the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI for their work on discovery, coordination and patch verification. OpenAI and Calif also published blogs containing details on the vulnerability – its history, technical details, and insight into the disclosure process. PHP posted as well.

We’d also like to express our sincere gratitude towards Automattic, Akamai, AWS, Cloudflare, Fastly, Google, Imperva, Microsoft, Vercel, and many others, for helping prepare guidance and out-of-the-box mitigations for customers who cannot apply the patch immediately.

The Vulnerabilities

All of the disclosed vulnerabilities are memory-safety issues that stem from bugs in how PHP handles fatal errors while processing requests, particularly out-of-memory errors. These bugs can leave a corrupted internal PHP state behind after a request ends unexpectedly. A later request or worker can reuse that stale state, leading to memory disclosure or corruption.

Below you can find a table that demonstrates what type of impact was demonstrated by each of the bugs we reported to PHP. The applications listed below are targets we chose for the RCE demonstrations. They are representative targets - exploitation does not require one of these CMSs, as the vulnerable code is in PHP itself.

While this blog covers only four instances of exploitable bugs (grouped under two CVEs) that follow this problematic pattern, there are other tracked, and likely untracked, variants of this issue in the PHP codebase. These variants have different requirements for exploitation and can lead to different types of impact. In any case, the patch provided by the PHP team fixes the issue at its core and eliminates all variants in the patched release.

Impact

We combined these vulnerabilities into a single exploit script, php2shell, and demonstrated that it could execute code remotely without authentication on deployments of WordPress (wordpress:latest), Drupal (drupal:latest), and Joomla (joomla:latest), using their latest container images at the time of testing.

These platforms illustrate the impact, but the vulnerabilities are in PHP itself. Exploitation does not depend on a flaw in the application’s code: even a simple “Hello World” application running on an affected PHP version can be vulnerable.

Separately, we demonstrated that attackers could read sensitive data from the PHP process’s memory, including passwords, tokens, and API keys, without needing to achieve remote code execution.

The AI inflection point

The vulnerable code had been present for more than a decade. Turning these flaws into working exploits required chaining multiple bugs and accounting for how PHP allocates and reuses memory across requests. Memory bugs are notoriously complex; differences in PHP versions, configurations and application behavior can break assumptions the exploit depends on. An attack that works against one deployment may need substantial adjustments to work against another, each requiring further analysis, testing and debugging. Pre-AI, this manual work would be difficult to implement and even harder to scale.

With AI this is no longer a barrier. LLMs can help adapt an exploit to different PHP versions, configurations and memory layouts. With testing and debugging tools, models can analyze failures and iterate on adjustments, reducing the specialist effort required for each target. This significantly lowers the barrier to scaling attacks across different deployments.

This changes the economics of both discovery and exploitation. As AI reduces the effort needed to develop and adapt complex exploits, vulnerabilities that once seemed impractical to exploit become viable targets.

We used Wiz Atlas, Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol throughout this research. Notably, Gemini 4 Argon made an invaluable contribution to finding the vulnerability, exploit development, attack detection, and validation of the patch.

Using Gemini 4 Argon, the team at Wiz has shown why frontier AI is a game-changer for cyber defense. For over a decade, these critical vulnerabilities remained unaddressed because vulnerability discovery and exploitation were incredibly complex. We're pleased to see Gemini 4 Argon help defenders bridge that gap, finding vulnerabilities and helping patch them.

Raluca Ada Popa, Head of Gemini Security, Google DeepMind

Industry-level collaborations

Prior to public disclosure, Wiz Research worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI on discovery, coordination and patch verification. We also partnered with Google Cloud, Cloudflare, AWS, Microsoft, Automattic, Fastly, Akamai, Imperva, Vercel and many others to prepare customer guidance, detections and out-of-the-box mitigations for organizations that cannot update immediately.

A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application. PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.

Technical deep dive

Bug: Upload-progress unserializer use-after-free

PHP's Session module can decode session data during upload-progress handling in the same pre-initialization window. The decoder stores request-owned bookkeeping in BG(unserialize). A fatal allocation failure can interrupt this path, destroy the request heap and leave the unserializer's global state published.

On a later request handled by the same worker, PHP can consume attacker-reclaimed memory as live unserializer bookkeeping. The stale state becomes a powerful memory-corruption primitive. We combined it with the memory disclosure to remove address uncertainty and achieved unauthenticated remote code execution on WordPress, Drupal and Joomla.

The WordPress, Drupal and Joomla chains are representative demonstrations. The underlying primitives exist at the PHP engine level and can affect any PHP application running on a vulnerable version.

These issues execute below the application layer, so application logs may contain little context. Until systems are patched, defenders should pay particular attention to unusual multipart requests followed by memory-limit errors or repeated HTTP 500 responses, unexpectedly large or malformed PHPSESSID response cookies, and unexplained PHP worker churn. These signals can guide an investigation. Applying the PHP security update remains the only complete remediation.

Bug: Remote process-memory disclosure

PHP parses RFC1867 multipart requests during request startup, before normal module initialization has completed. Session upload-progress handling can initialize Session state at this early stage and publish a session ID in PS(id). An out-of-memory error can abort the request before cleanup completes. PHP then destroys the request heap and may leave PS(id) pointing to the freed allocation.

A later multipart request handled by the same worker can reach the upload-progress cleanup path before normal Session initialization resets that pointer. PHP trusts the stale pointer and length as a live zend_string and URL-encodes the reclaimed heap contents into a PHPSESSID response cookie. The attack works even when the application never calls session_start(), making the issue application-agnostic. We demonstrated unauthenticated disclosure of an attacker-sized region of live worker memory containing data from outside the attacker's request.

Bug: Fatal-error backtrace use-after-free

In affected versions, PHP retains the backtrace of the most recent fatal error in EG(last_fatal_error_backtrace). A fatal out-of-memory error can destroy the request heap without undefining that executor-global value. The worker survives with a global that still points to memory from the previous request.

If the same worker emits a diagnostic early in the next request, it can access the pointer before the executor reinitializes that state. PHP then destroys or updates the dangling backtrace and follows attacker-reclaimed memory. The resulting cross-request use-after-free can be developed into controlled memory corruption. We demonstrated unauthenticated remote code execution against Drupal using this primitive.

Bug: OPcache type confusion

OPcache persists compiled PHP structures in shared memory and assigns indices into per-worker runtime-pointer maps. Workers coordinate those indices through a shared frontier. During zend_accel_script_persist(), PHP advances the process-local CG(map_ptr_last) frontier. It publishes the corresponding shared frontier only after persistence completes. An allocation failure between those two events leaves the process-local advance in place and partially persisted objects referring to slots that the shared state still considers available.

When another worker later reuses one of those slots for a different runtime object, stale shared metadata resolves to a pointer of the wrong type. The mismatch creates a cross-worker type confusion and corrupts shared OPcache state. We used this primitive to build an unauthenticated RCE chain against WordPress.

There are other variants outside of these four bugs. While we initially reported these four to PHP, through this research we realized the vulnerability is deeply rooted in the PHP codebase and will require a comprehensive fix. Other variants should also fold under the same two CVEs.

How Can Wiz Help?

Wiz customers should refer to the Wiz Threat Intel Center advisory for PHP2Shell, which includes built-in coverage for agentless and runtime vulnerability detection, exploitation detection via Wiz Defend and Sensor, and automatic response policies, alongside remediation and threat hunting guidance.

Sensor customers using the newest version (1.0.12768) can also enable a built-in response policy to automatically terminate processes exhibiting behaviors typical of PHP2Shell exploitation:

Conclusion

With 70% of the Internet affected, the impact of PHP2Shell cannot be overstated. It marks an AI inflection point. The vulnerable code had been there for more than a decade – what AI changed was the ability to understand the weaknesses and turn them into a working exploit. With frontier AI models and the right tools, a single researcher completed in a week what previously would have taken a world-class team months of work.

This changes the economics of both discovery and exploitation. Vulnerabilities that once seemed impractical to exploit become viable targets. These same capabilities also give defenders a chance to uncover and fix flaws that have survived years of scrutiny.

Wiz used Wiz Atlas, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol throughout this research, with Argon making a particularly significant contribution to finding and helping to remediate the vulnerability.

The opportunity is to make this work routine: systematically finding flaws in existing software and catching new ones before they reach production. Our coordinated efforts with PHP, OpenAI and Calif advance that goal, applying AI to strengthen the software foundations we all share.

Title: Cloudflare deploys protections against php2shell vulnerability
Context: The php2shell protections are the first managed detections we have released using this capability
Full Text:
Update - On October 23, the PHP project published an informational advisory for a related vulnerability, CVE-2026-115560, in PHP's session upload progress feature. It affects fully patched PHP releases, including 8.5.12, and will be fixed in PHP's next regular release.

All Cloudflare WAF customers are protected against known exploit attempts if their site uses PHP's default upload progress field name. Customers who have changed session.upload_progress.name are not covered by the WAF rule.

The existing rules "PHP Remote Code Execution Attack (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) #6" protects against this vulnerability.

More information to follow.

October 21, Calif.io, Wiz, OpenAI and Quarkslab disclosed two vulnerabilities in PHP, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and known as php2shell. The vulnerabilities affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later and they may allow an attacker to cause denial of service, remote code execution, and data exposure when an application processes specially crafted HTTP traffic.

Cloudflare has been part of a coordinated effort to deploy mitigations to protect the Internet, working with PHP foundation, OpenAI and Wiz among others. Cloudflare has developed and deployed web application firewall (WAF) protections since early October 2026, which were deployed about 9 hours ahead of public disclosure. Starting on October 21 3:02 am UTC, Cloudflare customers using our free or paid WAF were protected by default against php2shell.

Cloudflare successfully deployed multiple mitigations for all its customers while the vulnerability was leaked before the official release date and we observed attack traffic targeting our customers. We observed how attackers were mutating the attack payload to try to bypass our protections by tracking the volume of matches and cross-referencing with the rule logic.

Protecting against php2shell required more than standard request-based rules. Request data alone does not always provide enough evidence to distinguish an exploit from legitimate traffic. The origin’s response adds context, helping identify whether an exploit succeeded while reducing the risk of false positives.

To deliver this protection, we developed full transaction detection, a new Cloudflare WAF capability that combines signals from the request and response within the same HTTP transaction. Response rules can then block a matching origin response before it reaches the requester. The php2shell protections are the first managed detections we have released using this capability.

Customers should patch their PHP repos even with WAF protections providing an additional layer of defense-in-depth mitigation. Our security analysts continue monitoring attack activity and update the rules when and if new techniques and variations emerge in the hours and days ahead. You can track new rules in the changelog.

The protections are available and deployed automatically on all plans with WAF deployed, including Free users.

What we know about the vulnerabilities

PHP is used by almost 70% of websites. The php2shell vulnerabilities affect the PHP runtime itself and can allow attackers to execute malicious code on vulnerable servers, expose customer data, or disrupt services. Because PHP underpins widely used platforms such as WordPress and Magento, these flaws could potentially affect a large number of applications across the Internet.

The two vulnerabilities involve how PHP handles memory when something goes wrong while processing a HTTP request. Normally, PHP allocates memory to store the data it needs to process a request, then releases it when that work finishes. If processing stops unexpectedly, for example because it runs out of memory, PHP fails to clean up the memory safely. These vulnerabilities arise when PHP handles an error and then tries to use data that was not fully set up or memory that has already been released.

An attacker can send specially crafted HTTP requests to trigger these conditions. Large requests are one way to put memory under pressure, but the problem goes beyond consuming server resources. By manipulating the data PHP encounters in this invalid memory, an attacker may be able to crash a PHP process, expose sensitive information, or execute code provided by the attacker.

The two vulnerabilities differ in when the unsafe memory access happens:

Vulnerability

What goes wrong

CVE-2026-109618

PHP runs out of memory and interrupts its work before some internal data has been properly initialized. During cleanup of that request, PHP may use this unfinished data as though it were valid.

CVE-2026-109619

A fatal error interrupts a request, leaving PHP holding references to memory that is released when the request ends. When the same PHP process handles a later request, it may follow those outdated references and access memory that is no longer valid and expose sensitive data.

These flaws are in the PHP runtime, so updating website code or a plugin(s) alone does not fix these vulnerabilities. Administrators need to update the PHP software running their applications. If a hosting provider manages PHP, ask the provider to apply the security update.

Administrators can follow the PHP advisory for affected versions and remediation instructions. Keep Cloudflare WAF protections enabled while patching. Restricting unnecessary uploads and limiting upload sizes can also reduce exposure, but these measures do not replace the PHP fix.

For Free customers, new rules have been released under the Cloudflare Managed Free Ruleset (Ruleset ID 77454fe2d30c4220b5701f6fdfb893ba). Free customers don’t have to take any actions to enable the protection. To override the ruleset behavior, you can refer to our documentation.
